q: A law is silent on when it takes effect. Under Article 2 of the Civil Code, as amended by Executive Order No. 200, when does it take effect?
choices: Immediately upon approval by the President
Fifteen days after the completion of its publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation
Fifteen days after its approval by the President
hints: Approval alone is never enough; something must happen first.
Count fifteen days from the completion of publication.
why: Under Art. 2, as amended by EO 200, a law takes effect after fifteen days following the completion of its publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation, unless it provides otherwise.
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2, as amended by EO 200, Sec. 1

q: Congress passed a law providing that it "shall take effect immediately upon approval." The President approved it on 2 March. It was published in a newspaper of general circulation only on 20 March. On 10 March, Ramon was charged with violating it. Ramon argues that the law was not yet in force on 10 March. Is Ramon correct? Explain.

alac.answer: Yes, Ramon is correct. The law was not yet in force on 10 March.
alac.basis: Under Article 2 of the Civil Code, as amended by Executive Order No. 200, laws take effect after fifteen days following the completion of their publication in the Official Gazette or in a newspaper of general circulation, unless it is otherwise provided. In Tañada v. Tuvera, G.R. No. L-63915, December 29, 1986, the Supreme Court held that the clause "unless it is otherwise provided" refers only to the fifteen-day period, not to the requirement of publication. Publication is indispensable; a law may take effect immediately after publication, but never without it.
alac.application: Here, the law said it would take effect immediately upon approval. This could shorten the fifteen-day period, but it could not do away with publication. The law was published only on 20 March, so on 10 March it had not been published and was not yet effective.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ramon cannot be held liable for an act done on 10 March under a law that took effect only upon its publication on 20 March.

keyPoints: Publication is indispensable (Tañada v. Tuvera)
"Unless otherwise provided" refers to the 15-day period only
Law effective only upon publication on 20 March
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2, as amended by EO 200; Tañada v. Tuvera, G.R. No. L-63915, December 29, 1986

q: Complete Article 3 of the Civil Code: "Ignorance of the law excuses ______ from compliance therewith."
hints: The rule has no exceptions based on who the person is.
Two words: the opposite of "everyone".
why: Art. 3: ignorance of the law excuses no one from compliance with it.

q: Rosa, who did not finish elementary school, failed to file her claim within the period fixed by law because she did not know that the law set a deadline. She asks the court to excuse the delay because she is unschooled and could not have known the law. Should the court grant her plea? Would your answer be different if Rosa, in good faith, had possessed land on the basis of a mistaken reading of a doubtful and difficult question of law?

alac.answer: No, the court should not excuse the delay. But a mistake on a doubtful or difficult question of law may support good faith in possession.
alac.basis: Article 3 of the Civil Code provides that ignorance of the law excuses no one from compliance therewith. The rule applies to everyone, whatever his education. However, Article 526 of the Civil Code provides that mistake upon a doubtful or difficult question of law may be the basis of good faith.
alac.application: Here, Rosa's lack of schooling does not excuse her from complying with the period fixed by law, because everyone is presumed to know the law. In the second situation, if her possession rested on an honest mistake about a doubtful or difficult question of law, the law itself allows that mistake to be the basis of her good faith as a possessor.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Rosa's late claim is not excused, but her possession based on an honest mistake on a doubtful or difficult question of law may be treated as possession in good faith.

keyPoints: Ignorance of the law excuses no one (Art. 3)
Education does not matter
Exception: mistake on a doubtful or difficult question of law may be the basis of good faith (Art. 526)

q: Laws as a rule have no retroactive effect (Art. 4, Civil Code). Which of the following is a recognized exception that may be applied to pending cases?
choices: A law that impairs vested rights
A penal law that is unfavorable to the accused
A law that is silent and creates new obligations
hints: No one has a vested right in a rule of procedure.
Penal laws may apply retroactively only when they favor the accused.
why: Art. 4 makes laws prospective unless the contrary is provided. Procedural and remedial laws are a recognized exception because there is no vested right in rules of procedure; penal laws apply retroactively only if favorable to the accused.

q: On 1 June 2026 a new law required that every lease of a house be notarized to be valid. The law said nothing about leases already signed. Lito leased his house to Mina on 1 January 2026 in a private, un-notarized contract. In July 2026, Lito claims the lease is void under the new law and asks Mina to leave. Is Lito correct?

alac.answer: No, Lito is not correct. The lease remains valid.
alac.basis: Article 4 of the Civil Code provides that laws shall have no retroactive effect, unless the contrary is provided. The validity of a contract is governed by the law in force when it was entered into.
alac.application: Here, the new law took effect on 1 June 2026 and does not say that it applies to leases already signed. The lease between Lito and Mina was perfected on 1 January 2026, before the new law, when no notarization was required. Applying the new law to it would give the law a retroactive effect that the law itself does not provide.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the lease is valid and Lito cannot eject Mina on the ground that the lease was not notarized.

keyPoints: Laws are prospective unless the contrary is provided (Art. 4)
Validity is judged by the law at the time of the contract
The new law is silent on retroactivity

q: Under Article 5 of the Civil Code, acts executed against the provisions of mandatory or prohibitory laws are:
choices: Void, except when the law itself authorizes their validity
hints: It is the most serious kind of defect.
The only exception is when the law itself says the act is valid.
why: Art. 5: acts against mandatory or prohibitory laws are void, except when the law itself authorizes their validity.

q: In 2020, Ana sold her residential lot in Quezon City to Mr. Chen, a Chinese citizen who has lived in the Philippines for 30 years. Is the sale valid?

alac.answer: No, the sale is void.
alac.basis: Article XII, Section 7 of the 1987 Constitution provides that, save in cases of hereditary succession, no private lands shall be transferred or conveyed except to individuals, corporations, or associations qualified to acquire or hold lands of the public domain. Article 5 of the Civil Code provides that acts executed against the provisions of mandatory or prohibitory laws shall be void, except when the law itself authorizes their validity.
alac.application: Here, Mr. Chen is a foreigner and is not qualified to acquire or hold lands of the public domain. His long residence does not change his citizenship. The sale is not a case of hereditary succession. The sale therefore violates a prohibitory provision of the Constitution, and no law authorizes its validity.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale of the lot to Mr. Chen is void.

keyPoints: Constitutional ban on transfer of private land to aliens (Art. XII, Sec. 7)
Only exception: hereditary succession
Act against a prohibitory law is void (Art. 5)
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Sec. 7; Civil Code, Art. 5

q: Which of the following may validly be waived under the Civil Code?
choices: The right to prescribe in the future
Prescription already obtained, by a person with capacity to alienate property
A right whose waiver would prejudice a third person with a right recognized by law
hints: Art. 6 forbids waivers contrary to law or prejudicial to third persons.
Art. 1112 treats prescription already obtained differently from prescription in the future.
why: Rights may be waived unless the waiver is contrary to law or prejudicial to third persons (Art. 6). Art. 1112 allows a person with capacity to alienate to renounce prescription already obtained, but not the right to prescribe in the future; contracts on future inheritance are not allowed (Art. 1347).

q: While their father Pedro was still alive, Jose signed a notarized document waiving his future share in Pedro's estate in favor of his sister Maria, in exchange for P500,000. When Pedro died, Jose claimed his share as an heir. Maria invoked the waiver. Is the waiver valid?

alac.answer: No, the waiver is void, and Jose may claim his share in Pedro's estate.
alac.basis: Article 6 of the Civil Code provides that rights may be waived, unless the waiver is contrary to law, public order, public policy, morals, or good customs, or prejudicial to a third person with a right recognized by law. Article 1347 provides that no contract may be entered into upon future inheritance except in cases expressly authorized by law.
alac.application: Here, Jose waived his share while Pedro was still alive. At that time, the inheritance was a mere future inheritance, and no law expressly authorizes such a waiver. The waiver, made for a price, is a contract upon future inheritance and is contrary to law.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the waiver produces no effect, and Jose may claim his share as Pedro's heir.

keyPoints: Waiver contrary to law is void (Art. 6)
No contract upon future inheritance (Art. 1347)
Inheritance was still future when the waiver was signed

q: Under Article 7 of the Civil Code, laws are repealed only by:
choices: Custom or practice to the contrary
hints: Non-observance does not repeal a law.
Only a law can undo a law.
why: Art. 7: laws are repealed only by subsequent ones; disuse, custom or contrary practice does not excuse their violation.

q: Carlo's written loan from Bank X fell due in 2010. In 2015, a law suspended all collection suits against small farmers, including Carlo. Relying on that law, Bank X did not sue. In 2021, the Supreme Court declared the law unconstitutional. Bank X sued Carlo in 2022. Carlo argues that the action has prescribed, counting ten years from 2010, because an unconstitutional law is void and has no effect. Decide.

alac.answer: The action has not prescribed.
alac.basis: Article 1144 of the Civil Code requires an action upon a written contract to be brought within ten years from the time the right of action accrues. Article 7 provides that when the courts declare a law to be inconsistent with the Constitution, the former shall be void. Under the operative fact doctrine, however, the actual existence of a statute before it is declared unconstitutional is an operative fact whose consequences cannot justly be ignored (Serrano de Agbayani v. Philippine National Bank, G.R. No. L-23127, April 29, 1971).
alac.application: Here, the bank's right of action accrued in 2010. From 2015 to 2021, the bank could not sue because the law suspended collection suits, and it relied on that law in good faith. Under the operative fact doctrine, that period is not counted. Excluding the six years of suspension, only about six years ran before the suit in 2022, less than ten years.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Bank X's action was filed on time and has not prescribed.

keyPoints: Ten years for a written contract (Art. 1144)
Unconstitutional law is void (Art. 7)
Operative fact doctrine: period of suspension excluded (Serrano de Agbayani v. PNB)
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 7 and 1144; Serrano de Agbayani v. Philippine National Bank, G.R. No. L-23127, April 29, 1971

q: Under Article 8 of the Civil Code, judicial decisions applying or interpreting the laws or the Constitution:
choices: Are laws passed by the courts
Form part of the legal system of the Philippines
Bind only the parties to the case
May be disregarded by lower courts
hints: Courts do not legislate, but their rulings still matter beyond the case.
Read the last words of Art. 8.
why: Art. 8: judicial decisions applying or interpreting the laws or the Constitution form part of the legal system of the Philippines.

q: In 2019, relying on a Supreme Court doctrine that holders of a certain government permit could lawfully carry firearms, Dante carried a firearm with that permit. In 2022, the Supreme Court abandoned that doctrine and held that the permit gives no such authority. Dante is now prosecuted for illegal possession of a firearm for his act in 2019. Should he be convicted?

alac.answer: No, Dante should be acquitted.
alac.basis: Article 8 of the Civil Code provides that judicial decisions applying or interpreting the laws or the Constitution shall form a part of the legal system of the Philippines. Article 4 provides that laws shall have no retroactive effect, unless the contrary is provided. In People v. Jabinal, G.R. No. L-30061, February 27, 1974, the Supreme Court held that when a doctrine is overruled, the new doctrine should be applied prospectively and should not prejudice those who relied on the old doctrine.
alac.application: Here, in 2019 the prevailing doctrine of the Supreme Court formed part of the law and allowed holders of the permit to carry firearms. Dante acted in good faith under that doctrine. The 2022 ruling that abandoned it may be applied only to acts done after it, not to Dante's act in 2019.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Dante cannot be convicted for carrying the firearm in 2019.

keyPoints: Judicial decisions form part of the legal system (Art. 8)
New doctrine applies prospectively (People v. Jabinal)
Good-faith reliance on the old doctrine
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 4 and 8; People v. Jabinal, G.R. No. L-30061, February 27, 1974

q: Under Section 31, Book I of the Administrative Code of 1987, a "year" is understood to be:
hints: The Administrative Code counts in months, not days.
The Supreme Court held this rule prevails over Art. 13 of the Civil Code.
why: EO 292, Book I, Sec. 31: a year is twelve calendar months. In CIR v. Primetown Property Group, Inc., G.R. No. 162155, August 28, 2007, the Court held that this provision governs over Art. 13 of the Civil Code (365 days).
cite: EO 292 (Administrative Code of 1987), Book I, Sec. 31; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Primetown Property Group, Inc., G.R. No. 162155, August 28, 2007

q: A law gave Liza two years from 15 April 2022 to file a claim. She filed it on 15 April 2024. The agency rejected it as late, reasoning that two years of 365 days each, or 730 days, ended on 14 April 2024 because 2024 is a leap year. Was the claim filed on time?

alac.answer: Yes, the claim was filed on time.
alac.basis: Section 31, Book I of the Administrative Code of 1987 provides that a "year" shall be understood to be twelve calendar months. In Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Primetown Property Group, Inc., G.R. No. 162155, August 28, 2007, the Supreme Court held that this provision, being the later law, governs over Article 13 of the Civil Code, which counted a year as 365 days. Article 13 also provides that in computing a period, the first day shall be excluded, and the last day included.
alac.application: Here, two years means twenty-four calendar months, regardless of the number of days in a leap year. Excluding the first day, 15 April 2022, the period ended on 15 April 2024, which is included. Liza filed on that last day.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Liza's claim was filed within the two-year period.

keyPoints: A year is twelve calendar months (EO 292, Book I, Sec. 31)
EO 292 prevails over Art. 13's 365-day rule (CIR v. Primetown)
First day excluded, last day included
cite: EO 292, Book I, Sec. 31; Civil Code, Art. 13; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Primetown Property Group, Inc., G.R. No. 162155, August 28, 2007

q: Under Article 14 of the Civil Code, penal laws and those of public security and safety are obligatory upon:
choices: All who live or sojourn in Philippine territory, subject to the principles of public international law and treaty stipulations
hints: The rule follows territory, not citizenship.
There are exceptions under international law and treaties.
why: Art. 14: penal laws and laws of public security and safety bind all who live or sojourn in the Philippines, subject to public international law and treaty stipulations.

q: John, an American tourist on a one-week visit to Manila, was caught stealing a phone. He argues that Philippine penal laws apply only to Filipinos and residents. On the same day, the accredited ambassador of a foreign state was involved in a fistfight. Can both be prosecuted in Philippine courts?

alac.answer: John can be prosecuted, but the ambassador, as a rule, cannot.
alac.basis: Article 14 of the Civil Code provides that penal laws and those of public security and safety shall be obligatory upon all who live or sojourn in the Philippine territory, subject to the principles of public international law and to treaty stipulations.
alac.application: Here, John sojourns in the Philippines as a tourist, so Philippine penal laws bind him even if he is neither a citizen nor a resident. The ambassador, on the other hand, enjoys diplomatic immunity from criminal jurisdiction under the principles of public international law, which Article 14 expressly respects.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, John may be prosecuted for theft, while the ambassador is immune from prosecution unless his state waives the immunity.

keyPoints: Penal laws bind all who live or sojourn in the Philippines (Art. 14)
Citizenship and residence do not matter
Exception: public international law, e.g. diplomatic immunity

q: Under Article 37 of the Civil Code, juridical capacity is:
choices: The power to do acts with legal effect, which may be lost
The fitness to be the subject of legal relations, inherent in every natural person and lost only through death
Acquired only upon reaching the age of majority
hints: Juridical capacity is passive; capacity to act is active.
Only one event ends juridical capacity.
why: Art. 37: juridical capacity is the fitness to be the subject of legal relations; it is inherent in every natural person and lost only through death. Capacity to act is the power to do acts with legal effect, which is acquired and may be lost.

q: Andres and his only son Benjo died in the same plane crash. There is no evidence of who died first. Benjo's wife, Celia, claims that Benjo inherited from Andres a moment before he died, so that she now receives part of Andres's estate through Benjo. Andres's brother objects. Is Celia's claim correct?

alac.answer: No, Celia's claim is not correct.
alac.basis: Article 43 of the Civil Code provides that if there is a doubt, as between two or more persons who are called to succeed each other, as to which of them died first, whoever alleges the death of one prior to the other shall prove the same; in the absence of proof, it is presumed that they died at the same time and there shall be no transmission of rights from one to the other.
alac.application: Here, Andres and Benjo were called to succeed each other as father and son, and there is no evidence of who died first. Celia, who alleges that Andres died first, has no proof of it. They are therefore presumed to have died at the same time, and no rights passed from Andres to Benjo.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Celia cannot receive any part of Andres's estate through Benjo.

keyPoints: Persons called to succeed each other (Art. 43)
Burden of proof on whoever alleges prior death
Presumed simultaneous death; no transmission of rights

q: Under Article 44 of the Civil Code, the State and its political subdivisions, such as provinces and municipalities, are:
choices: Juridical persons only when sued abroad
hints: Art. 44 lists three kinds of juridical persons.
The State is first on the list.
why: Art. 44(1) lists the State and its political subdivisions as juridical persons; Art. 45 says they are governed by the laws creating or recognizing them.

q: The Municipality of San Isidro, through its mayor duly authorized by the Sangguniang Bayan, bought a lot for a public market and later sued the seller in the municipality's own name for failure to deliver. The seller moved to dismiss, arguing that a municipality is not a person and cannot own property or sue. Rule on the motion.

alac.answer: The motion should be denied.
alac.basis: Article 44 of the Civil Code provides that the State and its political subdivisions are juridical persons. Article 45 provides that they are governed by the laws creating or recognizing them. Section 22 of the Local Government Code (RA 7160) provides that every local government unit, as a corporation, shall have the power, among others, to sue and be sued, to acquire and convey real or personal property, and to enter into contracts.
alac.application: Here, the Municipality of San Isidro is a political subdivision and therefore a juridical person. The Local Government Code, the law that governs it, expressly gives it the power to acquire property, to enter into contracts, and to sue in its corporate name.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the municipality validly bought the lot and may sue the seller in its own name; the motion to dismiss should be denied.

keyPoints: Political subdivisions are juridical persons (Art. 44(1))
Governed by the laws creating them (Art. 45)
LGC Sec. 22: sue and be sued, acquire property, contract
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 44 and 45; Local Government Code (RA 7160), Sec. 22

q: Under Section 18 of the Revised Corporation Code, a private corporation commences its corporate existence and juridical personality from:
choices: The date the incorporators sign the articles of incorporation
The date the SEC issues the certificate of incorporation under its official seal
The date of its first board meeting
The date it opens a bank account
hints: Juridical personality is granted by the State, not by the incorporators.
Look for the act of the Securities and Exchange Commission.
why: RA 11232, Sec. 18: a private corporation commences its corporate existence and juridical personality from the date the SEC issues the certificate of incorporation under its official seal.

q: Five friends signed articles of incorporation for "Bright Bakes, Inc." and filed them with the SEC on 1 March. On 10 March, before the SEC issued any certificate, they signed a supply contract in the name of "Bright Bakes, Inc." The SEC issued the certificate of incorporation on 30 March. Was Bright Bakes, Inc. a juridical person when the contract was signed on 10 March?

alac.answer: No, Bright Bakes, Inc. was not yet a juridical person on 10 March.
alac.basis: Section 2 of the Revised Corporation Code defines a corporation as an artificial being created by operation of law. Article 44(3) of the Civil Code recognizes as juridical persons corporations for private interest to which the law grants a juridical personality. Section 18 of the Revised Corporation Code provides that a private corporation commences its corporate existence and juridical personality from the date the Commission issues the certificate of incorporation under its official seal.
alac.application: Here, the SEC issued the certificate of incorporation only on 30 March. Signing and filing the articles on 1 March did not create the corporation. On 10 March, when the supply contract was signed, the law had not yet granted Bright Bakes, Inc. a juridical personality.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Bright Bakes, Inc. was not a juridical person on 10 March; its corporate existence began only on 30 March.

keyPoints: A corporation is created by operation of law (RCC Sec. 2)
Juridical personality granted by law (Civil Code Art. 44(3))
Existence begins on issuance of the SEC certificate (RCC Sec. 18)
cite: Revised Corporation Code (RA 11232), Secs. 2 and 18; Civil Code, Art. 44(3)

q: Under Article 16 of the Philippine Cooperative Code of 2008 (RA 9520), a cooperative acquires juridical personality from:
choices: The date of its first general assembly
The date the members pay their share capital
The date the Cooperative Development Authority issues a certificate of registration under its official seal
The date it starts doing business
hints: Like a corporation, a cooperative needs a government certificate.
The agency is the Cooperative Development Authority.
why: RA 9520, Art. 16: a cooperative acquires juridical personality from the date the Authority (CDA) issues a certificate of registration under its official seal.

q: Twenty residents formed the "Kapitbahayan Savings Cooperative" and adopted bylaws, but they never registered it with the Cooperative Development Authority. The cooperative later sued a member in its own name to collect a loan. The member moved to dismiss on the ground that the cooperative has no juridical personality. Rule on the motion.

alac.answer: The motion should be granted.
alac.basis: Article 3 of the Philippine Cooperative Code of 2008 defines a cooperative as an autonomous and duly registered association of persons. Article 16 provides that a cooperative acquires juridical personality from the date the Authority issues a certificate of registration under its official seal. Under Rule 3, Section 1 of the Rules of Court, only natural or juridical persons, or entities authorized by law, may be parties in a civil action.
alac.application: Here, the Kapitbahayan Savings Cooperative was never registered with the Cooperative Development Authority. It therefore never acquired juridical personality, and no law authorizes an unregistered cooperative to sue in its own name.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the cooperative cannot sue in its own name, and the motion to dismiss should be granted; the members who made the loan may sue in their own names instead.

keyPoints: A cooperative must be duly registered (RA 9520, Art. 3)
Juridical personality from the CDA certificate of registration (Art. 16)
Only natural or juridical persons may be parties (Rule 3, Sec. 1)
cite: Philippine Cooperative Code of 2008 (RA 9520), Arts. 3 and 16; Rules of Court, Rule 3, Sec. 1

q: Under Article 38 of the Civil Code, minority, insanity or imbecility, the state of being a deaf-mute, prodigality and civil interdiction are:
choices: Mere restrictions on capacity to act, which do not exempt the person from certain obligations
Grounds that make all acts of the person void
Circumstances that apply only to juridical persons
hints: Juridical capacity is lost only through death.
The person may still be bound, e.g. by obligations arising from his acts or from property relations.
why: Art. 38: these are mere restrictions on capacity to act and do not exempt the person from certain obligations, such as those arising from his acts or from property relations.

q: Years before, Fely had been discharged from government service after being diagnosed with schizophrenia. Later, she donated a lot to her sister. After Fely's death, her other relatives sued to annul the donation, arguing that her past diagnosis shows she lacked capacity. No evidence was presented about her mental condition on the day of the donation. Should the donation be annulled?

alac.answer: No, the donation should not be annulled.
alac.basis: Article 37 of the Civil Code provides that capacity to act, which is the power to do acts with legal effect, is acquired and may be lost. The law presumes that a person of age has capacity to act, and whoever alleges incapacity must prove it as of the time of the act. In Catalan v. Basa, G.R. No. 159567, July 31, 2007, the Supreme Court held that a prior diagnosis of a mental illness does not by itself prove that the donor lacked capacity when the donation was made.
alac.application: Here, the relatives rely only on Fely's diagnosis years before. They presented no evidence that she was incapacitated on the day she made the donation. The presumption that she had capacity to act was not overcome.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the donation is valid and should not be annulled.

keyPoints: Capacity to act is presumed
Burden of proof on the one alleging incapacity, as of the time of the act
A past diagnosis alone is not enough (Catalan v. Basa)
cite: Civil Code, Art. 37; Catalan v. Basa, G.R. No. 159567, July 31, 2007

q: Under Article 234 of the Family Code, as amended by RA 6809, majority commences at the age of:
hints: RA 6809 lowered the age of majority.
It is the same age at which one may vote.
why: Art. 234, as amended by RA 6809: emancipation takes place by the attainment of majority, which commences at eighteen, unless otherwise provided.
cite: Family Code, Art. 234, as amended by RA 6809

q: Carla, 19 and single, sold the car she inherited from her grandmother without asking her parents. A month later, she married her boyfriend, also 19, before a judge, without the consent of her parents. Is the sale valid? What is the status of the marriage?

alac.answer: The sale is valid. The marriage is valid but voidable.
alac.basis: Article 234 of the Family Code, as amended by RA 6809, provides that majority commences at the age of eighteen years. Article 236, as amended, provides that the emancipated child is qualified and responsible for all acts of civil life, save the exceptions established by law, and that contracting marriage shall require parental consent until the age of twenty-one. Article 45(1) of the Family Code provides that a marriage may be annulled if the party was eighteen years of age or over but below twenty-one and the marriage was solemnized without the consent of the parents.
alac.application: Here, Carla is 19, so she is emancipated and may sell her own car without her parents' consent. However, she is below 21 and married without parental consent. That marriage is valid until annulled, but it may be annulled under Article 45(1), unless after reaching 21 she freely cohabits with her husband.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale of the car is valid, while the marriage is voidable and may be annulled for lack of parental consent.

keyPoints: Majority at 18 (Art. 234, as amended by RA 6809)
Emancipated: qualified for all acts of civil life (Art. 236)
Marriage between 18 and 21 without parental consent is voidable (Art. 45(1))
cite: Family Code, Arts. 234 and 236, as amended by RA 6809; Art. 45(1)

q: Under RA 11596 (Prohibition of Child Marriage Law), a marriage in which one party is 17 years old is:
choices: Valid if celebrated under customary rites
hints: RA 11596 defines a child as anyone under eighteen.
Parental consent and custom do not cure it.
why: RA 11596, Sec. 6: child marriage is void ab initio. Sec. 3(b) covers marriages solemnized in civil or church proceedings or in any traditional, cultural or customary manner.

q: In 2024, Rico, 25, and Lani, 16, were married in a traditional ceremony officiated by a community elder, with the consent and active arrangement of Lani's parents. What is the status of the marriage, and who may be held criminally liable under RA 11596?

alac.answer: The marriage is void ab initio. Lani's parents, the officiating elder and Rico may be held criminally liable.
alac.basis: Under Section 3(b) of RA 11596, child marriage refers to any marriage where one or both parties are children, solemnized in civil or church proceedings, or in any recognized traditional, cultural or customary manner; a child is any person under eighteen. Section 6 provides that child marriage is void ab initio. Section 4 punishes (a) any person who causes, fixes, facilitates, or arranges a child marriage, with a higher penalty and perpetual loss of parental authority if the offender is a parent; (b) any person who performs or officiates a child marriage; and (c) an adult partner who cohabits with a child outside wedlock. Section 5 declares these public crimes.
alac.application: Here, Lani was 16, a child under the law, so the marriage is a child marriage even though it was traditional and her parents consented. Lani's parents arranged it, the elder officiated it, and Rico, an adult, lives with a child in a union that is void and therefore outside a valid marriage. Since these are public crimes, any concerned person may initiate the case.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the marriage is void ab initio; Lani's parents may be liable for facilitating it and lose parental authority, the elder for officiating it, and Rico as an adult cohabiting with a child.

keyPoints: Child = under 18; includes traditional or customary marriages (Sec. 3)
Child marriage is void ab initio (Sec. 6)
Facilitation, solemnization and adult cohabitation punished (Sec. 4); public crimes (Sec. 5)

q: Under Article 1 of the Family Code, the nature, consequences and incidents of marriage are:
choices: Freely agreed upon by the spouses
Governed by law and not subject to stipulation, except that marriage settlements may fix the property relations
Governed by the religion of the spouses
hints: Marriage is a special contract, unlike ordinary contracts.
The spouses may agree only on one thing: their property relations.
why: Art. 1: marriage is an inviolable social institution whose nature, consequences and incidents are governed by law and not subject to stipulation, except that marriage settlements may fix the property relations.
cite: Family Code, Art. 1; 1987 Constitution, Art. XV, Sec. 2

q: Before their wedding, Leo and Mia signed a notarized agreement stating that (a) their marriage would automatically end after ten years unless renewed in writing, and (b) they would have complete separation of property. Are these stipulations valid?

alac.answer: Stipulation (a) is void, but stipulation (b) is valid.
alac.basis: Article XV, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution provides that marriage, as an inviolable social institution, is the foundation of the family and shall be protected by the State. Article 1 of the Family Code defines marriage as a special contract of permanent union, whose nature, consequences, and incidents are governed by law and not subject to stipulation, except that marriage settlements may fix the property relations during the marriage within the limits provided by the Code.
alac.application: Here, stipulation (a) tries to make the marriage temporary and to end it by the spouses' own agreement. This goes against the permanent nature of marriage, which the law alone governs. Stipulation (b), on the other hand, only fixes their property relations, which the law allows the future spouses to agree upon in a marriage settlement executed before the wedding.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the ten-year term is void and the marriage continues, while the agreement on complete separation of property is valid.

keyPoints: Marriage is a permanent union (Art. 1)
Nature and incidents of marriage are not subject to stipulation
Only property relations may be fixed in marriage settlements
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XV, Sec. 2; Family Code, Art. 1

q: Which of the following is an ESSENTIAL (not formal) requisite of marriage under the Family Code?
choices: Consent freely given in the presence of the solemnizing officer
A marriage ceremony with at least two witnesses
hints: Art. 2 lists the essential requisites; Art. 3 lists the formal ones.
Essential requisites concern the parties themselves.
why: Art. 2: the essential requisites are legal capacity of the parties, who must be a male and a female, and consent freely given in the presence of the solemnizing officer. The other choices are formal requisites under Art. 3.

q: Ana lives in Pasig and Ben lives in Taguig. They obtained their marriage license from the Local Civil Registrar of Makati, where neither of them resides, and were married by a judge in Makati with two witnesses. A year later, Ana sought a declaration that the marriage is void because the license was issued in the wrong place. Will her petition prosper?

alac.answer: No, the petition will not prosper. The marriage is valid.
alac.basis: Article 3 of the Family Code lists the formal requisites of marriage, including a valid marriage license. Article 9 provides that a marriage license shall be issued by the local civil registrar of the city or municipality where either contracting party habitually resides. Under Article 4, only the absence of an essential or formal requisite makes a marriage void; an irregularity in the formal requisites does not affect the validity of the marriage, but the party or parties responsible for the irregularity are civilly, criminally and administratively liable.
alac.application: Here, Ana and Ben had a marriage license, so the formal requisite was not absent. Its issuance by the civil registrar of Makati, where neither of them resides, violates Article 9, but this is only an irregularity in the formal requisite. All the other requisites were present.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the marriage is valid, although the persons responsible for the irregular issuance of the license may be held liable.

keyPoints: A license was issued, so the requisite was not absent
Wrong place of issuance (Art. 9) is a mere irregularity
Irregularity does not affect validity; responsible persons liable (Art. 4)

q: Under Article 73 of the Family Code, may a spouse practice a legitimate profession without the consent of the other spouse?
choices: No, the consent of the other spouse is always required
Yes, and the other spouse may object only on valid, serious, and moral grounds
No, unless the court first authorizes it
hints: The Family Code treats both spouses equally.
The other spouse may object, but only on limited grounds.
why: Art. 73: either spouse may exercise any legitimate profession, occupation, business or activity without the consent of the other, who may object only on valid, serious, and moral grounds.

q: Ramon accepted a five-year job in Dubai and demanded that his wife Tess resign from her teaching job in Cebu and move with him. Tess refused because their two children are in school in Cebu and she wants to keep her job. Ramon asked the court to order Tess to live with him in Dubai. How should the court rule?

alac.answer: The court may exempt Tess from living with Ramon in Dubai and may decide the family domicile.
alac.basis: Article 68 of the Family Code obliges the husband and wife to live together. Article 69 provides that the husband and wife shall fix the family domicile, and in case of disagreement, the court shall decide. The court may exempt one spouse from living with the other if the latter should live abroad or there are other valid and compelling reasons for the exemption, but not if the exemption is not compatible with the solidarity of the family. Article 73 allows either spouse to exercise a legitimate profession without the consent of the other.
alac.application: Here, the spouses disagree on the domicile, so the court decides. Ramon will live abroad, which is a ground for exempting Tess from living with him. The children's schooling in Cebu and Tess's right to keep her profession are valid reasons, and keeping the children's home in Cebu is compatible with the solidarity of the family.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court may decline to order Tess to move to Dubai and may exempt her from living with Ramon abroad.

keyPoints: Duty to live together (Art. 68)
Court decides the domicile and may exempt a spouse if the other lives abroad (Art. 69)
Right to exercise a profession (Art. 73); solidarity of the family

q: Under the first paragraph of Article 26 of the Family Code, a marriage solemnized abroad and valid where celebrated is:
choices: Valid in the Philippines, except those prohibited under certain articles such as marriages where a party is below 18 and bigamous marriages
Valid only if registered with the Philippine embassy
Valid only if both parties are foreigners
hints: The rule follows the law of the place of celebration (lex loci celebrationis).
There are exceptions for marriages that offend strong Philippine policy.
why: Art. 26, par. 1: marriages valid where celebrated are valid here, except those prohibited under Arts. 35(1), (4), (5) and (6), 36, 37 and 38.

q: Jun and Lea, both Filipino citizens aged 17, travelled to a country whose law allows persons aged 16 to marry with parental consent. With their parents' consent, they were married there in full compliance with that country's law. Is their marriage valid in the Philippines?

alac.answer: No, the marriage is void in the Philippines.
alac.basis: Under Article 26 of the Family Code, all marriages solemnized outside the Philippines in accordance with the laws in force in the country where they were solemnized, and valid there as such, shall also be valid in this country, except those prohibited under Articles 35(1), (4), (5) and (6), 36, 37 and 38. Article 35(1) declares void those marriages contracted by any party below eighteen years of age even with the consent of parents or guardians.
alac.application: Here, the marriage was valid under the law of the country where it was celebrated. However, both Jun and Lea were below eighteen. Their marriage falls under the exception in Article 26 for marriages prohibited by Article 35(1), and the consent of their parents does not cure the defect.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the marriage of Jun and Lea is void in the Philippines.

keyPoints: Lex loci celebrationis: valid abroad, valid here (Art. 26)
Exception: Art. 35(1), party below 18
Parental consent does not cure it

q: Under the second paragraph of Article 26 of the Family Code, a Filipino spouse may remarry under Philippine law when:
choices: Any divorce is obtained anywhere by either Filipino spouse of a marriage between two Filipinos
A marriage between a Filipino and a foreigner was validly celebrated and a divorce is validly obtained abroad capacitating the foreign spouse to remarry
The spouses have lived apart for five years
The foreign spouse dies abroad without leaving a will
hints: The rule applies to mixed marriages.
The divorce must capacitate the foreign spouse to remarry.
why: Art. 26, par. 2: when a marriage between a Filipino and a foreigner is validly celebrated and a divorce is validly obtained abroad capacitating the alien spouse to remarry, the Filipino spouse also has capacity to remarry.
cite: Family Code, Art. 26, par. 2 (as amended by EO 227)

q: Marites, a Filipina, married Kenji, a Japanese citizen, in Manila. Later, Marites herself filed for divorce in Japan, and the Japanese court granted it. Back in the Philippines, Marites wants to remarry. Kenji has already remarried in Japan. Can Marites remarry, and what must she do first?

alac.answer: Yes, Marites may remarry, after the Japanese divorce decree is recognized by a Philippine court.
alac.basis: The second paragraph of Article 26 of the Family Code provides that where a marriage between a Filipino citizen and a foreigner is validly celebrated and a divorce is thereafter validly obtained abroad by the alien spouse capacitating him or her to remarry, the Filipino spouse shall have capacity to remarry under Philippine law. In Republic v. Manalo, G.R. No. 221029, April 24, 2018, the Supreme Court held that the provision applies even if it was the Filipino spouse who initiated the foreign divorce proceeding. A foreign divorce decree and the foreign law allowing it must be proved, and the decree judicially recognized in the Philippines, before it takes effect here.
alac.application: Here, the marriage was a mixed marriage validly celebrated in Manila, and a valid divorce was obtained in Japan, which allowed Kenji to remarry. Under Manalo, it does not matter that Marites, the Filipino spouse, filed the divorce. She must first file a petition in a Philippine court for recognition of the Japanese divorce decree, proving the decree and the Japanese law on divorce.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, once the Japanese divorce is judicially recognized in the Philippines, Marites has capacity to remarry.

keyPoints: Mixed marriage validly celebrated; valid foreign divorce (Art. 26, par. 2)
Applies even if the Filipino spouse initiated the divorce (Republic v. Manalo)
Judicial recognition of the foreign decree and proof of foreign law needed
cite: Family Code, Art. 26, par. 2; Republic v. Manalo, G.R. No. 221029, April 24, 2018

q: Under Article 46 of the Family Code, which of the following does NOT constitute fraud that is a ground for annulment of marriage?
choices: Concealment by the wife that she was pregnant by another man at the time of the marriage
Concealment of a sexually transmissible disease existing at the time of the marriage
Misrepresentation by a spouse about his wealth and family background
Non-disclosure of a previous conviction by final judgment of a crime involving moral turpitude
hints: Art. 46 gives a closed list.
The last paragraph of Art. 46 excludes misrepresentation as to character, health, rank, fortune or chastity.
why: Art. 46 lists the only kinds of fraud that allow annulment; misrepresentation as to character, health, rank, fortune or chastity is not one of them.

q: Two years after his wedding, Edgar discovered that at the time of the marriage his wife Rina had been pregnant by another man and had hidden it from him. Upon learning this, Edgar moved out at once. Three years after the discovery, he filed a petition to annul the marriage. Will the petition prosper?

alac.answer: Yes, the petition will prosper.
alac.basis: Article 45(3) of the Family Code provides that a marriage may be annulled if the consent of either party was obtained by fraud, unless the party, with full knowledge of the facts constituting the fraud, freely cohabited with the other as husband and wife. Article 46(2) provides that concealment by the wife of the fact that at the time of the marriage she was pregnant by a man other than her husband constitutes such fraud. Article 47(3) provides that the action must be filed by the injured party within five years after the discovery of the fraud.
alac.application: Here, Rina concealed that she was pregnant by another man when they married, which is fraud under Article 46(2). Edgar did not ratify the marriage, because he moved out as soon as he learned the truth. He filed the petition three years after discovering the fraud, within the five-year period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the marriage is voidable, and Edgar's petition for annulment will prosper.

keyPoints: Fraud as ground for annulment (Art. 45(3))
Concealment of pregnancy by another man is fraud (Art. 46(2))
Filed within five years from discovery; no free cohabitation after discovery (Art. 47(3))

q: Under Article 63 of the Family Code, what is the effect of a decree of legal separation on the marriage bond?
choices: The marriage is dissolved and both may remarry
The spouses may live separately, but the marriage bonds are not severed
Only the innocent spouse may remarry
hints: Legal separation is not divorce.
Neither spouse may remarry.
why: Art. 63(1): the spouses are entitled to live separately, but the marriage bonds are not severed.

q: In 2023, Lorna discovered that her husband Victor was having an affair. She filed a petition for legal separation in 2024 on the ground of sexual infidelity. At the trial, Victor proved that Lorna herself had been having an affair since 2022. Should the court grant the petition?

alac.answer: No, the petition should be denied.
alac.basis: Article 55(8) of the Family Code makes sexual infidelity a ground for legal separation. However, Article 56(4) provides that the petition for legal separation shall be denied where both parties have given ground for legal separation. Article 57 requires the action to be filed within five years from the time of the occurrence of the cause.
alac.application: Here, Lorna filed on time, within five years from Victor's infidelity, and his infidelity is a ground for legal separation. But Victor proved that Lorna had also committed sexual infidelity. Both spouses therefore gave ground for legal separation, a situation known as recrimination or mutual guilt.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should deny Lorna's petition under Article 56(4).

keyPoints: Sexual infidelity is a ground (Art. 55(8))
Petition denied where both parties gave ground (Art. 56(4))
Filed within five years (Art. 57)

q: Under Article 77 of the Family Code, a marriage settlement must be:
choices: Oral or written, executed any time during the marriage
In writing, signed by the parties and executed before the celebration of the marriage
Approved by the court before the wedding
Executed within one year after the wedding
hints: Timing is essential.
It must also be in writing and signed.
why: Art. 77: marriage settlements and their modifications must be in writing, signed by the parties and executed before the celebration of the marriage; they bind third persons only if registered.

q: Paolo and Grace were married on 1 June 2025. On 2 June 2025, they signed a notarized "prenuptial agreement" adopting complete separation of property. In 2026, Paolo claimed that a lot Grace bought with her salary in 2025 is hers alone under their agreement. What property regime governs their marriage?

alac.answer: The absolute community of property governs, and the lot forms part of the community.
alac.basis: Article 77 of the Family Code requires that marriage settlements be in writing, signed by the parties and executed before the celebration of the marriage. Article 75 provides that in the absence of a marriage settlement, or when the regime agreed upon is void, the system of absolute community of property shall govern. Article 91 provides that the community property consists of all the property owned by the spouses at the time of the celebration of the marriage or acquired thereafter, unless otherwise provided.
alac.application: Here, the agreement was signed on 2 June 2025, a day after the wedding. It is not a valid marriage settlement because it was not executed before the celebration of the marriage, and the spouses could not change their property regime during the marriage by mere agreement. With no valid marriage settlement, the absolute community of property governs. The lot was bought by Grace during the marriage with her salary.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the lot belongs to the absolute community, not to Grace alone.

keyPoints: Settlement must be executed before the wedding (Art. 77)
No valid settlement: absolute community (Art. 75)
Property acquired during the marriage is community property (Art. 91)

q: Future spouses agree in their marriage settlement on complete separation of property. Under Article 84 of the Family Code, how much of their present property may they donate to each other in the marriage settlement?
hints: The limit applies when they choose a regime other than absolute community.
Any excess is void.
why: Art. 84: if the future spouses agree on a regime other than absolute community, they cannot donate to each other in their marriage settlements more than one-fifth of their present property; the excess is void.

q: A month before the planned wedding of Dan and Ivy, Dan's father Tomas donated a house and lot to Ivy, in a public instrument accepted by her, "in consideration of her coming marriage to my son Dan." The wedding was called off and never took place. May Tomas revoke the donation?

alac.answer: Yes, Tomas may revoke the donation.
alac.basis: Article 82 of the Family Code defines donations by reason of marriage as those made before its celebration, in consideration of the same, and in favor of one or both of the future spouses. Article 86(1) provides that a donation by reason of marriage may be revoked by the donor if the marriage is not celebrated.
alac.application: Here, the donation was made before the wedding, in consideration of the marriage, and in favor of Ivy, a future spouse. It is therefore a donation by reason of marriage. Since the wedding was called off and never celebrated, the ground for revocation under Article 86(1) exists.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Tomas may revoke the donation of the house and lot to Ivy.

keyPoints: Donation propter nuptias: before the wedding, in consideration of it, to a future spouse (Art. 82)
Revocable if the marriage is not celebrated (Art. 86(1))
Donation was made by a third person, not in a marriage settlement

q: Spouses married in 2020 without a marriage settlement. During the marriage, the wife inherited a parcel of land from her mother. Under Article 92 of the Family Code, the land is:
choices: Part of the absolute community because it was acquired during the marriage
Excluded from the community, being acquired by gratuitous title, unless the decedent provided otherwise
Owned in common by the wife and her siblings forever
Part of the conjugal partnership of gains
hints: With no settlement, the regime is absolute community (Art. 75).
Art. 92 excludes property acquired by gratuitous title.
why: Art. 92(1): property acquired during the marriage by gratuitous title (such as inheritance), and its fruits and income, are excluded from the community, unless the donor, testator or grantor expressly provides otherwise.

q: Spouses Rey and Joy, married in 2015 without a marriage settlement, bought a lot during their marriage. In 2025, Rey sold the lot to Nilo without Joy's knowledge or written consent and without court authority. Joy learned of the sale and refused to agree to it. Is the sale valid?

alac.answer: No, the sale is void.
alac.basis: Under Article 75 of the Family Code, absent a marriage settlement, the absolute community of property governs, and Article 91 includes in the community all property acquired during the marriage. Article 96 provides that the administration and enjoyment of the community property belong to both spouses jointly, and that a disposition or encumbrance without the authority of the court or the written consent of the other spouse is void. However, the transaction is construed as a continuing offer on the part of the consenting spouse and the third person, which may be perfected as a binding contract upon the acceptance by the other spouse or authorization by the court before the offer is withdrawn.
alac.application: Here, the lot was acquired during the marriage and is community property. Rey sold it without Joy's written consent and without court authority. Joy did not accept the continuing offer; she refused to agree to the sale.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale to Nilo is void, and Joy may recover the lot for the community.

keyPoints: Absolute community governs absent a settlement (Arts. 75, 91)
Disposition without written consent or court authority is void (Art. 96)
Continuing offer, perfected only if the other spouse accepts before withdrawal

q: Under Article 150 of the Family Code, which of the following is NOT a "family relation"?
choices: Among brothers and sisters of the half blood
hints: Art. 150 has a short, closed list of three.
Cousins are relatives, but not "family relations" under Art. 150.
why: Art. 150: family relations include those between husband and wife, between parents and children, and among brothers and sisters, whether of the full or half blood. Cousins are not included.

q: Pedro sued his brother Juan to recover a parcel of land. The complaint did not allege that any earnest effort toward a compromise had been made. Juan moved to dismiss the complaint. Rule on the motion.

alac.answer: The motion should be granted.
alac.basis: Article 151 of the Family Code provides that no suit between members of the same family shall prosper unless it should appear from the verified complaint or petition that earnest efforts toward a compromise have been made, but that the same have failed. Under Article 150, family relations include those among brothers and sisters.
alac.application: Here, Pedro and Juan are brothers, so they are members of the same family. Pedro's complaint does not show that earnest efforts toward a compromise were made and failed. This is a condition that must be complied with before a suit between family members may prosper.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the complaint should be dismissed for failure to comply with the condition required by Article 151.

keyPoints: Brothers are members of the same family (Art. 150)
Complaint must show earnest efforts at compromise (Art. 151)
Non-compliance: suit will not prosper

q: Under Article 163 of the Family Code, filiation of children may be:
choices: By nature or by adoption; natural filiation may be legitimate or illegitimate
hints: There are two sources of filiation.
Natural filiation is further divided into two.
why: Art. 163: filiation may be by nature or by adoption; natural filiation may be legitimate or illegitimate.

q: Spouses Ken and Lyn could not have children. Before their child was born, they signed and recorded a written instrument authorizing the artificial insemination of Lyn with the sperm of an anonymous donor. Lyn gave birth to Mia. Later, Ken's brother claimed that Mia is not Ken's legitimate child because Ken is not her biological father. Is the brother correct?

alac.answer: No, the brother is not correct. Mia is the legitimate child of Ken and Lyn.
alac.basis: Article 164 of the Family Code provides that children conceived or born during the marriage of the parents are legitimate. Children conceived as a result of artificial insemination of the wife with the sperm of the husband or that of a donor or both are likewise legitimate children of the husband and his wife, provided that both of them authorized or ratified such insemination in a written instrument executed and signed by them before the birth of the child.
alac.application: Here, Mia was conceived during the marriage through artificial insemination with a donor's sperm. Both Ken and Lyn signed a written authorization before her birth. The law itself makes such a child the legitimate child of the husband and wife, even if the husband is not the biological father.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Mia is the legitimate child of Ken and Lyn.

keyPoints: Conceived or born during the marriage: legitimate (Art. 164)
Artificial insemination with donor sperm: legitimate
Condition: written authorization or ratification signed by both before birth

q: Under Article 172 of the Family Code, which of the following is PRIMARY evidence of filiation?
choices: Open and continuous possession of the status of a child
The record of birth appearing in the civil register, or a final judgment
Photographs of the child with the parent
hints: Art. 172 has a first paragraph and a second paragraph.
The second paragraph applies only in the absence of the first.
why: Art. 172, par. 1: filiation is established by the record of birth in the civil register or a final judgment, or by an admission in a public document or a signed private handwritten instrument. Open and continuous possession of status is secondary evidence (par. 2).

q: Toni claims to be the illegitimate son of the late Mr. Cruz. Mr. Cruz never signed Toni's birth certificate or any written admission. One year after Mr. Cruz died, Toni sued his estate to establish his filiation, relying only on proof that Mr. Cruz openly treated him as his son for years. Will the action prosper?

alac.answer: No, the action will not prosper.
alac.basis: Under Article 175 of the Family Code, illegitimate children may establish their filiation in the same way and on the same evidence as legitimate children, but when the action is based on the second paragraph of Article 172, the action may be brought only during the lifetime of the alleged parent. The second paragraph of Article 172 covers the open and continuous possession of the status of a child and any other means allowed by the Rules of Court and special laws.
alac.application: Here, Toni has no record of birth signed by Mr. Cruz and no written admission by him. He relies only on open and continuous possession of the status of a child, which falls under the second paragraph of Article 172. He filed the action after Mr. Cruz had already died.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Toni's action is barred because it was not brought during the lifetime of the alleged father.

keyPoints: Primary vs secondary evidence of filiation (Art. 172)
Action based on secondary evidence must be filed during the alleged parent's lifetime (Art. 175)
Filed after death: barred

q: Under Article 176 of the Family Code, as amended by RA 9255, the legitime of each illegitimate child is:
choices: Equal to that of a legitimate child
One-half of the legitime of a legitimate child
One-third of the legitime of a legitimate child
Nothing, unless given in a will
hints: Illegitimate children are compulsory heirs, but receive less.
The fraction is the simplest one.
why: Art. 176: the legitime of each illegitimate child consists of one-half of the legitime of a legitimate child.
cite: Family Code, Art. 176, as amended by RA 9255

q: Andy acknowledged his illegitimate son Paolo in Paolo's record of birth. Paolo uses the surname of his mother, Joan, and lives with her. Andy sued to have Paolo's surname changed to his own and to obtain parental authority and custody, arguing that since he recognized Paolo, the child must carry his name. Decide.

alac.answer: Andy's suit should be dismissed. Joan keeps parental authority, and Paolo cannot be compelled to use Andy's surname.
alac.basis: Article 176 of the Family Code, as amended by RA 9255, provides that illegitimate children shall use the surname and shall be under the parental authority of their mother, but may use the surname of their father if their filiation has been expressly recognized by the father. In Grande v. Antonio, G.R. No. 206248, February 18, 2014, the Supreme Court held that the word "may" is permissive: the father cannot compel the use of his surname, and parental authority over an illegitimate child belongs to the mother.
alac.application: Here, Paolo is illegitimate. Although Andy recognized him in the record of birth, the law only gives Paolo the option to use Andy's surname; it does not give Andy the right to impose it. Parental authority belongs to Joan, the mother, with whom Paolo lives.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Andy cannot compel the change of Paolo's surname, and parental authority and custody remain with Joan.

keyPoints: Illegitimate child: mother's surname and parental authority (Art. 176)
Use of father's surname is optional when recognized (RA 9255)
Father cannot compel it (Grande v. Antonio)
cite: Family Code, Art. 176, as amended by RA 9255; Grande v. Antonio, G.R. No. 206248, February 18, 2014

q: Under Article 170 of the Family Code, if the husband lives in the city where the child's birth took place, the action to impugn the child's legitimacy must be filed within:
choices: One year from knowledge of the birth or its recording
hints: The period depends on where the husband lives.
Living in the same place gives the shortest period.
why: Art. 170: one year if the husband resides where the birth took place or was recorded; two years if elsewhere in the Philippines; three years if abroad.

q: Raul worked continuously in Saudi Arabia for two years and never came home. During that time his wife Bea, who stayed in Manila, gave birth to a child. Raul, still residing in Saudi Arabia, learned of the birth and filed an action to impugn the child's legitimacy two and a half years after learning of it. Was the action filed on time, and does he have a ground?

alac.answer: Yes, the action was filed on time, and Raul has a ground to impugn the child's legitimacy.
alac.basis: Article 166(1)(b) of the Family Code allows legitimacy to be impugned if it was physically impossible for the husband to have sexual intercourse with his wife within the first 120 days of the 300 days which immediately preceded the birth because the husband and wife were living separately in such a way that sexual intercourse was not possible. Article 170 requires the action to be brought within one year if the husband resides where the birth took place, two years if he resides elsewhere in the Philippines, and three years if he resides abroad, counted from knowledge of the birth or its recording.
alac.application: Here, Raul was in Saudi Arabia the whole time and never came home, so intercourse with Bea during the period of conception was physically impossible. Raul resides abroad, so he had three years from knowledge of the birth. He filed after two and a half years.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Raul's action was filed within the three-year period and is based on a valid ground under Article 166(1)(b).

keyPoints: Ground: physical impossibility of intercourse in the first 120 of 300 days (Art. 166(1)(b))
Three-year period when the husband resides abroad (Art. 170)
Counted from knowledge of the birth

q: Under Article 180 of the Family Code, the effects of legitimation retroact to:
choices: The date of the parents' marriage
The time of the child's birth
The date of registration of the legitimation
The time of the child's conception
hints: Legitimated children are treated as if they had always been legitimate.
Think of the earliest date the child had civil personality.
why: Art. 180: the effects of legitimation retroact to the time of the child's birth; Art. 179: legitimated children enjoy the same rights as legitimate children.

q: Jay and Kim were both 17 and single when their son Leo was conceived and born. When they turned 20, they validly married each other. Is Leo legitimated, and what are his rights?

alac.answer: Yes, Leo is legitimated and has the same rights as a legitimate child from his birth.
alac.basis: Article 177 of the Family Code, as amended by RA 9858, provides that children conceived and born outside of wedlock of parents who, at the time of conception, were not disqualified by any impediment to marry each other, or were so disqualified only because either or both of them were below eighteen years of age, may be legitimated. Article 178 provides that legitimation takes place by a subsequent valid marriage between the parents. Article 179 grants legitimated children the same rights as legitimate children, and Article 180 makes the effects retroact to the time of the child's birth.
alac.application: Here, Jay and Kim were disqualified from marrying when Leo was conceived only because both were below eighteen. Under RA 9858, this no longer prevents legitimation. They later validly married each other.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Leo was legitimated by his parents' subsequent valid marriage and enjoys all the rights of a legitimate child from the time of his birth.

keyPoints: Age below 18 no longer bars legitimation (Art. 177, as amended by RA 9858)
Legitimation by subsequent valid marriage (Art. 178)
Same rights as legitimate children, retroactive to birth (Arts. 179-180)
cite: Family Code, Arts. 177 (as amended by RA 9858), 178, 179 and 180

q: Under Article 182 of the Family Code, who may impugn a legitimation, and within what period?
choices: Only those prejudiced in their rights, within five years from the time their cause of action accrues
Only the child, within one year from majority
Only the Solicitor General, within ten years
hints: Only those who are hurt by it may question it.
The period is the same as for many family actions: five years.
why: Art. 182: legitimation may be impugned only by those who are prejudiced in their rights, within five years from the time their cause of action accrues.

q: When Nina was conceived, her father Oscar was still married to his first wife, Pia. After Pia died, Oscar married Nina's mother, and Nina was recorded as legitimated. When Oscar died, his legitimate children by Pia questioned Nina's legitimation. Will their challenge prosper?

alac.answer: Yes, the challenge will prosper if filed on time. Nina was not legitimated.
alac.basis: Article 177 of the Family Code, as amended by RA 9858, allows the legitimation only of children whose parents, at the time of conception, were not disqualified by any impediment to marry each other, other than being below eighteen years of age. Article 182 provides that legitimation may be impugned only by those who are prejudiced in their rights, within five years from the time their cause of action accrues.
alac.application: Here, when Nina was conceived, Oscar was still married to Pia. That existing marriage was an impediment to his marrying Nina's mother, so Nina could not be legitimated by their later marriage. Oscar's legitimate children are prejudiced in their rights because Nina's claimed legitimate status would increase her share in Oscar's estate. Their cause of action accrued upon Oscar's death, and they may impugn the legitimation within five years from then.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Nina remains an illegitimate child, and the challenge of Oscar's legitimate children will prosper if filed within five years from their cause of action.

keyPoints: Only children of parents with no impediment at conception may be legitimated (Art. 177)
A subsisting prior marriage is an impediment
Impugned by those prejudiced, within five years (Art. 182)
cite: Family Code, Arts. 177 (as amended by RA 9858) and 182

q: Under RA 11642, a Filipino citizen who wishes to adopt must, among other qualifications, be at least:
choices: 18 years old and 10 years older than the adoptee
21 years old and 15 years older than the adoptee
25 years old and 16 years older than the adoptee, unless waived in the cases allowed by law
30 years old and 20 years older than the adoptee
hints: RA 11642 sets a minimum age of a quarter-century.
The age gap may be waived for a biological parent or the spouse of the adoptee's parent.
why: RA 11642, Sec. 21(a): at least 25 years old and at least 16 years older than the adoptee; the age gap may be waived if the adopter is the biological parent of the adoptee or the spouse of the adoptee's parent.

q: Mark, a 40-year-old Filipino, is married to Rose. He wants to adopt his 8-year-old nephew, whose parents abandoned him. Rose does not want to join the adoption. May Mark adopt the child alone?

alac.answer: No, Mark may not adopt alone. Spouses must adopt jointly.
alac.basis: Section 21 of RA 11642 provides that spouses shall jointly adopt, except: (a) if one spouse seeks to adopt the legitimate child of the other; (b) if one spouse seeks to adopt his or her own illegitimate child, provided the other spouse has signified consent; or (c) if the spouses are legally separated from each other.
alac.application: Here, Mark is married to Rose and wants to adopt his nephew. The nephew is not Rose's legitimate child, not Mark's own illegitimate child, and the spouses are not legally separated. None of the exceptions applies.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Mark cannot adopt his nephew alone; the adoption must be joint with Rose.

keyPoints: General rule: spouses jointly adopt (RA 11642, Sec. 21)
Three exceptions: legitimate child of spouse; own illegitimate child with consent; legal separation
Adopting a nephew is not an exception

q: Under RA 11642, may a Filipino of legal age be adopted?
choices: No, only minors may be adopted
Yes, if before the adoption the person has been consistently considered and treated by the adopters as their own child for at least three years
Yes, but only by a foreigner
Yes, if the person consents, without any other condition
hints: Adult adoption is allowed, with one condition.
The condition concerns how long the adopters treated the person as their own.
why: RA 11642, Sec. 22(d): a Filipino of legal age may be adopted if, prior to the adoption, the person has been consistently considered and treated by the adopters as their own child for at least three years.

q: Ben, married to Carol, has a 6-year-old illegitimate daughter, Dina, with another woman. Ben wants to adopt Dina to improve her status. Carol agrees in writing but does not want to adopt Dina herself. May Dina be adopted by Ben alone, and what will her status be?

alac.answer: Yes, Ben alone may adopt Dina, and she will be considered his legitimate child.
alac.basis: Section 22(c) of RA 11642 provides that an illegitimate child may be adopted by a qualified adopter to improve the child's status of legitimacy. Section 21 requires spouses to adopt jointly, except, among others, if one spouse seeks to adopt his own illegitimate child, provided the other spouse has signified consent. Section 41 provides that the adoptee shall be considered the legitimate child of the adopter for all intents and purposes.
alac.application: Here, Dina is Ben's illegitimate child, and the purpose of the adoption is to improve her status. Although Ben is married, the joint-adoption rule does not apply because he is adopting his own illegitimate child and Carol has consented in writing.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ben may adopt Dina alone, and upon adoption she becomes his legitimate child for all intents and purposes.

keyPoints: Illegitimate child may be adopted to improve status (Sec. 22(c))
Exception to joint adoption: own illegitimate child, with spouse's consent (Sec. 21)
Adoptee is a legitimate child of the adopter (Sec. 41)

q: Under RA 11642, where is a petition for domestic administrative adoption filed?
choices: The Regional Trial Court (Family Court) where the child resides
The Regional Alternative Child Care Office (RACCO) of the city or municipality where the prospective adoptive parents reside
hints: RA 11642 made domestic adoption administrative, not judicial.
The office is a regional office of the National Authority for Child Care.
why: RA 11642, Sec. 31: the petition is filed with the RACCO of the city or municipality where the prospective adoptive parents reside; the NACC decides it without adversarial proceedings (Sec. 32).

q: Spouses Rico and Liz filed a petition to adopt Jomar, their 12-year-old foster child. Jomar gave his written consent. The spouses' own legitimate son, Carlo, who is 11, refused to sign a written consent. Can the adoption be granted without Carlo's written consent?

alac.answer: No, the adoption cannot be granted without Carlo's written consent.
alac.basis: Section 23 of RA 11642 requires, after proper counseling, the written consent of the adoptee if ten years of age or over, and of the legitimate and adopted children, ten years of age or over, of the adopters, among others. Children under ten are only counseled and consulted.
alac.application: Here, Jomar is 12 and has given his written consent. But Carlo, the adopters' legitimate son, is 11, which is ten years of age or over, so his written consent is required. Carlo refused to give it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, without Carlo's written consent, the adoption cannot be granted.

keyPoints: Written consent of an adoptee 10 or over (Sec. 23(a))
Written consent of the adopters' legitimate children 10 or over (Sec. 23(c))
Under 10: counseled and consulted only

q: Under Section 41 of RA 11642, the legitimate filiation created between the adopter and the adoptee extends to:
choices: The adopter's parents, legitimate siblings, and legitimate descendants
hints: This is one of the major changes of RA 11642.
The adoptee becomes part of the adopter's wider family.
why: RA 11642, Sec. 41: the adoptee is the legitimate child of the adopter, and the legitimate filiation extends to the adopter's parents, legitimate siblings, and legitimate descendants.

q: Five years after an Order of Adoption made Spouses Lim the parents of Ella, Ella's biological mother, now financially stable, asked for Ella's return and the restoration of her parental authority. Will her request prosper?

alac.answer: No, the biological mother's request will not prosper.
alac.basis: Section 42 of RA 11642 provides that upon the issuance of the Order of Adoption, the adoptive parents shall have full parental authority over the child, and, except where the biological parent is the spouse of the adopter, all legal ties between the biological parents and the adoptee shall be severed and vested on the adopters. Section 41 makes the adoptee the legitimate child of the adopter for all intents and purposes.
alac.application: Here, the Order of Adoption has been issued. Ella's biological mother is not the spouse of either adopter. All legal ties between her and Ella were severed, and full parental authority is now with Spouses Lim. Her improved finances do not revive those ties.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the biological mother cannot recover Ella or regain parental authority over her.

keyPoints: Adoptive parents have full parental authority (Sec. 42)
Legal ties with biological parents severed, unless the biological parent is the adopter's spouse
Adoptee is a legitimate child of the adopters (Sec. 41)

q: Under RA 11642, who may petition for the rescission of an administrative adoption?
choices: The adoptee (with the assistance of the social welfare office if a minor, or through a guardian if incapacitated)
hints: Adoption is for the best interest of the child.
The adopter has another remedy: disinheritance.
why: RA 11642, Sec. 47: the adoption may be rescinded only upon the petition of the adoptee; the adopter cannot rescind it but may disinherit the adoptee for causes under Art. 919 of the Civil Code.

q: Tess adopted Rob when he was a child. Now 22, Rob physically assaulted Tess during an argument over money. Tess wants to rescind the adoption. What is her remedy?

alac.answer: Tess cannot rescind the adoption, but she may disinherit Rob.
alac.basis: Section 47 of RA 11642 provides that the adoption may be rescinded only upon the petition of the adoptee, on grounds committed by the adopter, and that the adoption, being in the best interest of the child, shall not be subject to rescission by the adopter. However, the adopter may disinherit the adoptee for causes provided in Article 919 of the Civil Code.
alac.application: Here, Tess is the adopter, so the law does not allow her to rescind the adoption, whatever Rob did. Her remedy is to disinherit Rob in a will, if his act falls under the causes in Article 919 of the Civil Code, such as maltreatment of the testator by word or deed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Tess's remedy is disinheritance under Article 919, not rescission of the adoption.

keyPoints: Only the adoptee may seek rescission (Sec. 47)
Adopter cannot rescind
Adopter may disinherit under Civil Code Art. 919

q: Under RA 8043, intercountry adoption of a Filipino child is allowed:
choices: Only as a last resort, after all possibilities of adoption in the Philippines have been exhausted and it is in the child's best interest
Only if the child's parents are foreigners
hints: The law prefers placing the child in the Philippines.
Look at the title of Section 7.
why: RA 8043, Sec. 7: intercountry adoption is a last resort; all possibilities of adoption in the Philippines must first be exhausted, and it must be in the best interest of the child.

q: John and Mary, American citizens aged 26 and 30, live in the United States. They wish to adopt a 2-year-old Filipino orphan through intercountry adoption. Are they qualified as to age, and what must first be shown before the child is placed with them?

alac.answer: John is not qualified as to age, and intercountry adoption requires that domestic adoption options be exhausted first.
