alac.basis: Section 9 of RA 8043 allows an alien or a Filipino citizen permanently residing abroad to apply for intercountry adoption if he or she is at least twenty-seven years of age and at least sixteen years older than the child at the time of application, unless the adopter is the parent by nature of the child or the spouse of such parent. Section 7 makes intercountry adoption a last resort: all possibilities of adoption in the Philippines must first be exhausted, and it must be in the best interest of the child. Under RA 11642, these functions are now exercised by the National Authority for Child Care.
alac.application: Here, John is only 26, below the minimum age of 27; Mary, at 30, meets the age requirement and is more than sixteen years older than the child. Since spouses adopt jointly, John's lack of age qualification is a problem for the joint application. In any case, before the child may be placed abroad, it must be shown that no suitable adoption in the Philippines is possible and that intercountry adoption serves the child's best interest.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, John does not yet meet the minimum age, and the child may be placed with the couple only as a last resort after domestic adoption options are exhausted.

keyPoints: Minimum age 27 and 16 years older than the child (RA 8043, Sec. 9)
Intercountry adoption is a last resort (Sec. 7)
Functions now with the NACC under RA 11642
cite: RA 8043, Secs. 7 and 9, as amended by RA 11642

q: Under RA 11767, a foundling found in the Philippines is:
choices: Presumed a natural-born Filipino citizen, regardless of the status or circumstances of birth
A Filipino only if adopted by Filipinos
hints: RA 11767 settled the issue raised in a famous election case.
The presumption is of the highest class of citizenship.
why: RA 11767, Sec. 5: a foundling found in the Philippines is presumed a natural-born Filipino citizen regardless of the status or circumstances of birth.

q: Grace was found as a newborn in a church in Iloilo and was raised by the couple who found her; they had registered her birth as if she were their own child. Now 40, she runs for a post that requires natural-born citizenship. An opponent argues that she is not natural-born because her parents are unknown and her birth certificate was simulated. Decide.

alac.answer: Grace is a natural-born Filipino citizen.
alac.basis: Section 5 of RA 11767 provides that a foundling found in the Philippines is presumed a natural-born Filipino citizen regardless of the status or circumstances of birth. The presumption may not be impugned in any proceeding unless substantial proof of foreign parentage is shown, and the natural-born status of a foundling is not affected by the fact that the birth certificate was simulated. This is consistent with Poe-Llamanzares v. Commission on Elections, G.R. No. 221697, March 8, 2016.
alac.application: Here, Grace was found in the Philippines as a newborn, so she is presumed natural-born. Her opponent shows only that her parents are unknown and that her birth record was simulated; he offers no substantial proof of foreign parentage. The simulated birth certificate does not affect her status.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the presumption stands, and Grace is a natural-born Filipino citizen qualified as to citizenship.

keyPoints: Foundling presumed natural-born (RA 11767, Sec. 5)
Rebuttable only by substantial proof of foreign parentage
Simulated birth certificate does not affect status
cite: RA 11767, Sec. 5; Poe-Llamanzares v. Commission on Elections, G.R. No. 221697, March 8, 2016

q: Under RA 11767, which documents are required before a foundling may be registered with the local civil registrar?
choices: The affidavit of the finder; a certification of the barangay captain or police on the circumstances of discovery; and a report of the NACC
hints: There are three documents.
One comes from the finder, one from the barangay or police, one from the NACC.
why: RA 11767, Sec. 10: the affidavit of the finder, a certification of the barangay captain or police authority, and the report of the NACC.

q: Lorna found a newborn baby in a box near her house. The next day she went to the local civil registrar, presented only her own affidavit, and asked that the baby be registered with a certificate of live birth. Should the registrar register the baby on that basis?

alac.answer: No, the registrar should not register the baby on Lorna's affidavit alone.
alac.basis: Section 10 of RA 11767 requires the following before a foundling may be registered: (a) the affidavit of the finder; (b) a certification of the barangay captain or police authority on the circumstances surrounding the discovery; and (c) a report of the NACC attesting that the birth and parentage of the foundling are unknown despite a diligent search. The NACC fills out and submits the application for registration to the local civil registrar.
alac.application: Here, Lorna presented only her affidavit as finder. There is no barangay or police certification and no NACC report showing a diligent search for the baby's parents. The application should also be prepared and submitted by the NACC.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the registrar should not yet register the baby; the other two documents must first be obtained through the barangay or police and the NACC.

keyPoints: Three required documents (RA 11767, Sec. 10)
NACC report after diligent search
NACC submits the application for registration

q: Under RA 11767, when may a foundling be declared legally available for adoption?
choices: When the biological parents cannot be identified and located
Only after the foundling turns seven
Never; foundlings may only be placed in foster care
hints: A search for the parents comes first.
Adoption follows if the search fails.
why: RA 11767, Sec. 6: if the biological parents cannot be identified and located, the foundling shall be declared legally available for adoption, considering the best interest of the child.

q: Spouses Dizon found an abandoned baby boy and want to adopt him. They ask what steps must be taken before they can file a petition for adoption. Advise them.

alac.answer: The child must first be declared legally available for adoption after a failed search for his parents; then the spouses may adopt under RA 11642.
alac.basis: Section 6 of RA 11767 provides that if the biological parents of a foundling cannot be identified and located, the foundling shall be declared legally available for adoption, taking into consideration the best interest of the child. Under RA 11642, a child who has been issued a Certification Declaring a Child Legally Available for Adoption (CDCLAA) may be adopted (Section 22(a)), and the petition for administrative adoption is filed with the RACCO where the prospective adoptive parents reside (Section 31).
alac.application: Here, the baby is a foundling. The authorities must first conduct a diligent search for his parents. If the parents cannot be identified and located, the child will be declared legally available for adoption through a CDCLAA. Only then may Spouses Dizon, if qualified, go through matching, supervised trial custody and the administrative adoption process with the RACCO.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the spouses must wait for the search and the CDCLAA before filing their petition for administrative adoption under RA 11642.

keyPoints: Search for the biological parents first
Declaration of availability for adoption (RA 11767, Sec. 6; CDCLAA)
Then administrative adoption under RA 11642 (Secs. 22(a), 31)

q: Under RA 11767, the biological parents of a foundling who wish to recover legal custody and restore parental authority should petition:
choices: The National Authority for Child Care (NACC)
hints: The same agency handles alternative child care and adoption.
It replaced the Inter-Country Adoption Board.
why: RA 11767, Sec. 12: the biological parents or legal guardian may petition the NACC; the best interest of the child is the paramount consideration.

q: Jenny abandoned her newborn daughter at a hospital. Three years later, after the child had been legally adopted by another couple, Jenny petitioned the NACC to recover custody and restore her parental authority. Will her petition prosper?

alac.answer: No, Jenny's petition will not prosper.
alac.basis: Section 12 of RA 11767 allows the biological parents of a foundling to petition the NACC to recover legal custody and restore parental authority, with the best interest of the child as the paramount consideration. However, if the child is already adopted, all legal ties between the biological parents and the child are severed and vested on the adopters.
alac.application: Here, the child had already been legally adopted when Jenny filed her petition. Her legal ties with the child were therefore severed and vested in the adoptive parents.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Jenny can no longer recover custody or parental authority over the child.

keyPoints: Biological parents may petition the NACC (RA 11767, Sec. 12)
Best interest of the child is paramount
If already adopted, legal ties are severed

q: Under the safe haven provision of RA 11767, a parent who relinquishes an infant to a licensed child-caring agency, a church, or a DOH-accredited health facility is exempt from criminal liability if the infant is:
hints: The rule protects newborns.
The limit is about one month.
why: RA 11767, Sec. 13: a parent who relinquishes an infant thirty days old and younger to the listed persons or entities is exempt from criminal liability.

q: Maria left her 20-day-old baby inside a parish church during a regular Sunday Mass, where the parish staff took the child in. Her neighbor Liza left her 2-month-old baby at a roadside waiting shed. Both are charged with abandonment of a minor. Are they exempt from criminal liability under RA 11767?

alac.answer: Maria is exempt from criminal liability, but Liza is not.
alac.basis: Section 13 of RA 11767 provides that, notwithstanding Articles 276 and 277 of the Revised Penal Code and RA 7610, any parent who relinquishes an infant thirty days old and younger to a licensed child-caring or child-placing agency, a church (a place devoted to religious worship held with regularity), a DOH-accredited health facility, a local social welfare office, or a DSWD- or LGU-managed residential care facility shall be exempt from criminal liability.
alac.application: Here, Maria's baby was only 20 days old, and she left the baby in a parish church where worship is regularly held, which is a safe haven under the law. Liza's baby was two months old, beyond the thirty-day limit, and a roadside waiting shed is not one of the places listed in the law.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Maria is exempt from criminal liability under the safe haven provision, while Liza may be held liable.

keyPoints: Infant thirty days old and younger (RA 11767, Sec. 13)
Relinquished to a listed safe haven, e.g. a church with regular worship
Older infant or unlisted place: no exemption

q: Under Article 194 of the Family Code, does support include education beyond the age of majority?
choices: Yes, education includes schooling or training for a profession, trade or vocation, even beyond the age of majority
Only if the parents agree in writing
hints: Support is "in keeping with the financial capacity of the family."
Read the second sentence of Art. 194.
why: Art. 194: support includes education, which covers schooling or training for some profession, trade or vocation, even beyond the age of majority.

q: Lea's son Jun was born in 2020. His father, Ariel, never gave support. Lea first sent Ariel a written demand for support in January 2024, and sued him in 2025. She asks for support starting from Jun's birth in 2020. From when may support be awarded?

alac.answer: Support may be awarded only from January 2024, the date of the first written demand.
alac.basis: Article 203 of the Family Code provides that the obligation to give support shall be demandable from the time the person who has a right to receive the same needs it for maintenance, but it shall not be paid except from the date of judicial or extrajudicial demand. Article 201 provides that the amount of support shall be in proportion to the resources or means of the giver and to the necessities of the recipient.
alac.application: Here, Jun needed support from his birth in 2020, but no demand was made until Lea's written demand in January 2024, which is an extrajudicial demand. Support in arrears before that date cannot be recovered.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ariel may be ordered to pay support from January 2024, in an amount proportionate to his means and Jun's needs.

keyPoints: Support is demandable when needed but payable only from judicial or extrajudicial demand (Art. 203)
A written demand letter is an extrajudicial demand
Amount in proportion to means and needs (Art. 201)

q: Under Article 153 of the Family Code, when is a family home deemed constituted?
choices: Upon registration with the Registry of Deeds
From the time the house and lot are occupied as a family residence
hints: Under the Family Code, no judicial or extrajudicial constitution is needed.
Actual occupancy is the key.
why: Art. 153: the family home is deemed constituted from the time it is occupied as a family residence.

q: In 2018, Rudy borrowed P1 million from Sam without any security. In 2020, Rudy and his family began living in a house and lot he owned. In 2025, Sam won a collection case and sought to levy on the house. Rudy claims it is exempt as a family home. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, Rudy is not correct. The house may be levied upon.
alac.basis: Article 153 of the Family Code provides that the family home is deemed constituted from the time it is occupied as a family residence, and from then it is exempt from execution, forced sale or attachment, except as provided by law. Article 155(2) provides that the family home is not exempt from execution for debts incurred prior to the constitution of the family home.
alac.application: Here, the house became a family home only in 2020, when Rudy's family began living there. Rudy's debt to Sam was incurred in 2018, before the family home was constituted. The debt therefore falls under the exception in Article 155(2).
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the family home is not exempt, and Sam may levy on it to satisfy the judgment.

keyPoints: Family home constituted upon occupancy (Art. 153)
Exempt from execution, with exceptions (Art. 155)
Debt incurred before constitution: not exempt (Art. 155(2))

q: Under Article 213 of the Family Code, when parents separate, a child under seven years of age:
choices: Shall not be separated from the mother unless the court finds compelling reasons to order otherwise
Chooses which parent to live with
hints: This is called the tender-age presumption.
The child's own choice matters only when over seven.
why: Art. 213: no child under seven years of age shall be separated from the mother unless the court finds compelling reasons to order otherwise.

q: Spouses Dan and Faye separated in fact. Their 5-year-old daughter stayed with Dan, who has a higher income. Faye, a fit and loving mother with a steady but modest job, petitioned for custody. Dan argues that he can give the child a better life. Who should be given custody?

alac.answer: Faye should be given custody of the child.
alac.basis: Article 213 of the Family Code provides that in case of separation of the parents, parental authority shall be exercised by the parent designated by the court, taking into account all relevant considerations. However, no child under seven years of age shall be separated from the mother unless the court finds compelling reasons to order otherwise.
alac.application: Here, the child is five years old, so the tender-age presumption in favor of the mother applies. Faye is fit and loving, and no compelling reason, such as neglect, abandonment or unfitness, was shown. Dan's higher income alone is not a compelling reason to separate the child from her mother.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, custody should be awarded to Faye.

keyPoints: Court designates the parent upon separation (Art. 213)
Child under seven not separated from the mother absent compelling reasons
Higher income of the father is not a compelling reason

q: Under Article 408 of the Civil Code, which of the following is NOT among the matters entered in the civil register?
choices: Judgments declaring marriages void from the beginning
hints: The civil register records civil status (Art. 407).
Property transactions go to a different registry.
why: Arts. 407-408: acts, events and judicial decrees concerning civil status are recorded in the civil register, e.g., births, marriages, deaths, legal separations, annulments, judgments of nullity, legitimations, adoptions, naturalization, changes of name. Sales of land are recorded in the Registry of Deeds.

q: Arman obtained a final judgment declaring his first marriage void. Without recording the judgment in the civil registry, and without the partition of the properties and delivery of the children's presumptive legitimes being recorded, he married Bianca. What is the status of his marriage to Bianca?

alac.answer: Arman's marriage to Bianca is void.
alac.basis: Article 408 of the Civil Code requires judgments declaring marriages void from the beginning to be entered in the civil register. Article 52 of the Family Code provides that the judgment of annulment or of absolute nullity, the partition and distribution of the properties of the spouses, and the delivery of the children's presumptive legitimes shall be recorded in the appropriate civil registry and registries of property. Article 53 provides that either former spouse may marry again only after compliance with Article 52; otherwise, the subsequent marriage shall be null and void.
alac.application: Here, Arman had a final judgment of nullity, but neither the judgment nor the partition and delivery of presumptive legitimes was recorded as required. He remarried before complying with Article 52.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Arman's subsequent marriage to Bianca is null and void under Article 53.

keyPoints: Judgments of nullity are entered in the civil register (Civil Code Art. 408)
Recording of judgment, partition and presumptive legitimes (Family Code Art. 52)
Remarriage without compliance is void (Art. 53)
cite: Civil Code, Art. 408; Family Code, Arts. 52 and 53

q: Under RA 11222, persons who simulated a child's birth before the law took effect are exempt from criminal, civil and administrative liability if, among others:
choices: The simulation was made for the best interest of the child, the child has been consistently treated as their own, and they file a petition for adoption with rectification within ten years from the law's effectivity
The biological mother agrees in writing
hints: The law is an amnesty with conditions.
There is a deadline counted from the law's effectivity.
why: RA 11222, Sec. 4: no liability if the simulation was for the best interest of the child, the child was consistently treated as their own, and a petition for adoption with rectification is filed within ten years from effectivity.

q: In 2010, Spouses Reyes found a baby girl at their doorstep and registered her birth as if she were their own child. They raised her as their daughter. In 2025, wanting to set things right, they ask whether they can still regularize her status without being prosecuted. Advise them.

alac.answer: Yes, they may avail of RA 11222 by filing a petition for adoption with rectification of the simulated birth record within ten years from the law's effectivity.
alac.basis: Section 4 of RA 11222 exempts from criminal, civil or administrative liability persons who simulated the birth of a child before the law took effect, provided the simulation was for the best interest of the child, the child has been consistently treated as their own, and they file a petition for adoption with an application for rectification of the simulated birth record within ten years from the effectivity of the Act. Section 5 allows administrative adoption and rectification, provided the child has been living with them for at least three years before the effectivity of the Act and a certification declaring the child legally available for adoption (CDCLAA) is issued.
alac.application: Here, the spouses simulated the birth in 2010, before RA 11222 took effect in 2019. They did it to care for an abandoned baby, which is in her best interest, and they have consistently treated her as their daughter. She has lived with them since 2010, more than three years before the law took effect. Filing in 2025 is still within ten years from the law's effectivity.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, once a CDCLAA is issued for the child, the spouses may file a petition for adoption with rectification of the simulated birth record and will be exempt from liability.

keyPoints: Simulation before effectivity, for the child's best interest (RA 11222, Sec. 4)
Child consistently treated as own; living with them 3 years before effectivity; CDCLAA (Sec. 5)
Petition within ten years from effectivity

q: Under RA 9048, as amended by RA 10172, which of the following may be corrected by the city or municipal civil registrar without a court order?
choices: A change of the person's nationality
A change of the person's legitimacy status
A clerical error in the day and month of birth that is patently clear
A change of the person's age by several years
hints: Only harmless, obvious clerical errors may be corrected administratively.
No correction may change nationality, age, or status.
why: RA 9048, as amended by RA 10172: clerical or typographical errors, change of first name or nickname, and the day and month of birth or sex where the error is patently clear may be corrected administratively; no correction may involve a change of nationality, age, or status.
cite: RA 9048, Secs. 1 and 2(3), as amended by RA 10172

q: After their father died, the legitimate children of Mr. Ruiz filed a Rule 108 petition to correct the birth record of their half-brother Paco, to delete Mr. Ruiz as his father and to have Paco declared illegitimate, claiming that Mr. Ruiz's marriage to Paco's mother was void. Will the petition prosper?

alac.answer: No, the petition will not prosper.
alac.basis: Article 412 of the Civil Code provides that no entry in a civil register shall be changed or corrected without a judicial order. A petition under Rule 108 of the Rules of Court is not the proper remedy to attack legitimacy, filiation or the validity of a marriage. In Braza v. City Civil Registrar of Himamaylan City, G.R. No. 181174, December 4, 2009, the Supreme Court held that the validity of a marriage and the legitimacy and filiation of a child cannot be collaterally attacked in a petition for correction of entries; they must be raised in a direct action.
alac.application: Here, the petition asks the court, through a correction of entries, to change Paco's filiation and status and to rule, in effect, that his parents' marriage was void. These are matters of personal status that may not be attacked collaterally in a Rule 108 proceeding. They must be raised in a direct action, such as an action to impugn filiation or a petition concerning the validity of the marriage, filed by the proper party.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the Rule 108 petition should be dismissed.

keyPoints: No change of civil register entries without a judicial order (Art. 412)
Status, legitimacy and validity of marriage cannot be collaterally attacked in Rule 108 (Braza v. City Civil Registrar)
Must be raised in a direct action
cite: Civil Code, Art. 412; Rules of Court, Rule 108; Braza v. City Civil Registrar of Himamaylan City, G.R. No. 181174, December 4, 2009

q: Under Article 1156 of the Civil Code, an obligation is:
choices: A moral duty to help others
A juridical necessity to give, to do or not to do
A duty imposed only by contract
hints: The key word is "juridical": the law can enforce it.
There are three kinds of prestation.
why: Art. 1156: an obligation is a juridical necessity to give, to do or not to do. Its elements are an active subject (creditor), a passive subject (debtor), the prestation (object), and the juridical tie (vinculum juris).

q: Dina promised her best friend Joy that she would attend Joy's birthday dinner. Dina did not come, and Joy, embarrassed before her guests, sued Dina for breach of obligation. Will the suit prosper?

alac.answer: No, the suit will not prosper.
alac.basis: Article 1156 of the Civil Code defines an obligation as a juridical necessity to give, to do or not to do. An obligation requires a juridical tie (vinculum juris) that the law recognizes and enforces, arising from one of the sources listed in Article 1157: law, contracts, quasi-contracts, acts or omissions punished by law, and quasi-delicts.
alac.application: Here, Dina's promise to attend a birthday dinner is a purely social undertaking. The friends did not intend to create a legal tie, and no law, contract, quasi-contract, crime or quasi-delict makes attendance at a party a juridical necessity. Without a juridical tie, there is no enforceable obligation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Joy has no cause of action against Dina for not attending the dinner.

keyPoints: Obligation = juridical necessity (Art. 1156)
Juridical tie must come from a source in Art. 1157
A purely social promise creates no obligation

q: Which of the following is NOT a source of obligations under Article 1157 of the Civil Code?
choices: Acts or omissions punished by law
hints: Art. 1157 lists five sources.
Morality alone does not create a civil obligation.
why: Art. 1157: obligations arise from law, contracts, quasi-contracts, acts or omissions punished by law, and quasi-delicts. Purely moral duties are not listed.

q: Identify the source of each obligation: (a) Ramon's duty to support his minor son; (b) Liza's duty to pay rent under a lease of an apartment; (c) the duty of a store to return P5,000 that a customer paid twice by mistake; (d) a driver's duty to pay for injuries he negligently caused to a pedestrian, where no criminal case is filed.

alac.answer: (a) Law; (b) contract; (c) quasi-contract; (d) quasi-delict.
alac.basis: Article 1157 of the Civil Code provides that obligations arise from law, contracts, quasi-contracts, acts or omissions punished by law, and quasi-delicts.
alac.application: Here, (a) the duty to support a minor child is imposed by the Family Code, so it arises from law. (b) Rent is due because Liza agreed to it in the lease, so it arises from contract. (c) The store received something not due to it through mistake, so its duty to return the money arises from the quasi-contract of solutio indebiti. (d) The driver caused damage by negligence, with no pre-existing contract and no criminal case, so his liability arises from quasi-delict.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sources are, in order: law, contract, quasi-contract, and quasi-delict.

keyPoints: Five sources (Art. 1157)
Support: law; lease: contract
Payment by mistake: quasi-contract; negligence without contract: quasi-delict

q: In a reciprocal obligation where one party fails to comply, Article 1191 of the Civil Code allows the injured party to:
choices: Choose between fulfillment and rescission, with damages in either case
Take the law into his own hands
hints: The power to rescind is implied in reciprocal obligations.
Damages may be claimed whichever remedy is chosen.
why: Art. 1191: the injured party may choose between fulfillment and rescission of the obligation, with the payment of damages in either case; he may still seek rescission if fulfillment becomes impossible.

q: Bea ordered a wedding gown from a designer, to be delivered on 9 May because her wedding was on 10 May. The designer delivered it only on 12 May. Bea had to rent another gown at a high price. The designer argues that he was not in delay because Bea never made a demand. Is the designer liable?

alac.answer: Yes, the designer is liable for damages.
alac.basis: Article 1169 of the Civil Code provides that those obliged to deliver or to do something incur in delay from the time the obligee judicially or extrajudicially demands fulfillment. However, demand is not necessary when from the nature and circumstances of the obligation it appears that the designation of the time when the thing is to be delivered was a controlling motive for the establishment of the contract. Article 1170 makes those who are guilty of delay liable for damages.
alac.application: Here, the gown was ordered for a wedding on 10 May, and delivery by 9 May was the very reason for the contract. Time was a controlling motive, so no demand was needed for the designer to be in delay. He delivered only on 12 May, causing Bea to spend for another gown.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the designer was in delay without need of demand and is liable to Bea for damages.

keyPoints: Delay generally requires demand (Art. 1169)
Exception: time is a controlling motive of the contract
Liability for damages for delay (Art. 1170)

q: Under Article 1174 of the Civil Code, a debtor IS liable for a fortuitous event when:
choices: The law expressly so provides, the parties so stipulate, or the nature of the obligation requires the assumption of risk
hints: The general rule is no liability for fortuitous events.
Art. 1174 lists three exceptions.
why: Art. 1174: no one is responsible for fortuitous events, except when expressly specified by law, declared by stipulation, or when the nature of the obligation requires the assumption of risk.

q: Nico sold his specific car to Ana, to be delivered on 1 August. On 2 August, Ana sent Nico a written demand to deliver. Nico did not deliver. On 20 August, a typhoon flooded Nico's garage and destroyed the car. Nico claims the obligation was extinguished by a fortuitous event. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, Nico is not correct. He remains liable.
alac.basis: Article 1262 of the Civil Code provides that an obligation to deliver a determinate thing is extinguished if the thing is lost without the fault of the debtor and before he has incurred in delay. Article 1165 provides that if the obligor delays, he shall be responsible for any fortuitous event until he has effected the delivery. Under Article 1169, the debtor incurs in delay from the time of judicial or extrajudicial demand.
alac.application: Here, Nico was obliged to deliver a specific car. Ana made a written demand on 2 August, so Nico was in delay from then. The typhoon destroyed the car on 20 August, while he was already in delay. A debtor in delay answers even for fortuitous events.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the obligation was not extinguished, and Nico is liable to Ana for damages.

keyPoints: Loss of a determinate thing extinguishes the obligation only if before delay (Art. 1262)
Debtor in delay is liable even for fortuitous events (Art. 1165)
Delay began upon written demand (Art. 1169)

q: Under Article 1179 of the Civil Code, an obligation whose performance does not depend on a future or uncertain event, or on a past event unknown to the parties, is:
hints: This is the definition of a pure obligation.
There is no condition and no period.
why: Art. 1179: a pure obligation is demandable at once; so is an obligation with a resolutory condition, without prejudice to the effects of the happening of the event.

q: Rey signed a promissory note: "I promise to pay Ben P50,000, payable on demand." One week later, Ben demanded payment. Rey refused, saying that no due date had been fixed and that Ben must first ask the court to fix a period. Is Rey correct?

alac.answer: No, Rey is not correct. The obligation is pure and demandable at once.
alac.basis: Article 1179 of the Civil Code provides that every obligation whose performance does not depend upon a future or uncertain event, or upon a past event unknown to the parties, is demandable at once. A court fixes a period under Article 1197 only when the obligation does not fix a period but one was intended, or when the period depends on the will of the debtor.
alac.application: Here, the note is payable on demand. Its performance does not depend on any future or uncertain event, and the parties did not intend any period; payment was to be made whenever Ben asked for it. There is nothing for the court to fix.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the obligation became demandable when Ben made his demand, and Rey must pay.

keyPoints: Pure obligation: no condition, no period (Art. 1179)
"Payable on demand" is demandable at once
Court fixes a period only in cases under Art. 1197

q: Under Article 1182 of the Civil Code, a conditional obligation is void when the fulfillment of the condition depends upon:
choices: The will of a third person
The sole will of the debtor
The sole will of the creditor
hints: A debtor who may decide whether to be bound is not really bound.
This is a purely potestative condition.
why: Art. 1182: when the fulfillment of the condition depends upon the sole will of the debtor, the conditional obligation is void; if it depends on chance or the will of a third person, it takes effect.

q: Uncle Fred wrote to his nephew Jon: (a) "I will give you P100,000 if you pass the 2026 Bar Examinations"; and (b) "I will also give you my old car if I feel like it." Jon passed the 2026 Bar. Fred refuses to give either. Can Jon demand the P100,000 and the car?

alac.answer: Jon can demand the P100,000, but not the car.
alac.basis: Article 1181 of the Civil Code provides that in conditional obligations, the acquisition of rights depends upon the happening of the event which constitutes the condition. Article 1182 provides that when the fulfillment of the condition depends upon the sole will of the debtor, the conditional obligation shall be void.
alac.application: Here, promise (a) depends on a future and uncertain event, Jon's passing the 2026 Bar. That event has happened, so Jon acquired the right to the P100,000. Promise (b) depends only on whether Fred "feels like it," which is the sole will of the debtor, so it is a purely potestative condition. (A promise to give for nothing in return must also comply with the forms of donation to be enforceable; that is a separate issue.)
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the obligation to give the P100,000 is valid and demandable, while the promise of the car is void.

keyPoints: Rights acquired upon happening of the suspensive condition (Art. 1181)
Condition depending on the debtor's sole will makes the obligation void (Art. 1182)
Passing the Bar is a valid casual or mixed condition

q: "I will pay you P10,000 on the day my father dies." Under Article 1193 of the Civil Code, this obligation is:
choices: Conditional, because the date is unknown
With a period, because the day must necessarily come although it is not known when
Void, for being contrary to morals
hints: Death is certain; only its date is uncertain.
A day certain is one that must necessarily come.
why: Art. 1193: a day certain is that which must necessarily come, although it may not be known when. Death is certain to come, so the obligation has a period.

q: Carlo borrowed P200,000 from Dan and signed a note: "I will pay when my means permit me to do so." Two years later, Dan sued to collect. Carlo argues that he cannot be compelled to pay because his means do not yet permit. What should the court do?

alac.answer: The court should fix the period within which Carlo must pay.
alac.basis: Article 1180 of the Civil Code provides that when the debtor binds himself to pay when his means permit him to do so, the obligation shall be deemed to be one with a period, subject to Article 1197. Article 1197 provides that the courts shall fix the duration of the period when it depends upon the will of the debtor.
alac.application: Here, Carlo promised to pay "when my means permit." The law treats this as an obligation with a period, not a condition that depends on Carlo's will. Since the period depends on Carlo's will, the court must fix it, considering what the parties probably contemplated.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should fix a period for payment; once it lapses, Carlo must pay Dan.

keyPoints: "When my means permit" is an obligation with a period (Art. 1180)
Court fixes the period when it depends on the debtor's will (Art. 1197)
Not a void potestative condition

q: In an alternative obligation, unless the right of choice has been expressly granted to the creditor, the choice belongs to:
choices: A third person chosen by lot
hints: Art. 1200 states the default rule.
The person who must perform usually chooses how.
why: Art. 1200: the right of choice belongs to the debtor, unless it has been expressly granted to the creditor; the choice takes effect only from the time it is communicated (Art. 1201).

q: Lito obliged himself to deliver to Mara either his pickup truck or P800,000, at his option. On the due date, Lito tendered P400,000 in cash plus a half share in the pickup truck. Mara refused. Was her refusal proper?

alac.answer: Yes, Mara's refusal was proper.
alac.basis: Article 1199 of the Civil Code provides that a person alternatively bound by different prestations shall completely perform one of them, and the creditor cannot be compelled to receive part of one and part of the other undertaking. Article 1200 gives the right of choice to the debtor unless expressly granted to the creditor.
alac.application: Here, Lito had the right to choose between delivering the truck and paying P800,000. But whichever he chose, he had to perform it completely. Offering half the money and a half share in the truck is part of one and part of the other prestation, which Mara cannot be compelled to accept.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Mara validly refused the tender; Lito must deliver the truck or pay the full P800,000.

keyPoints: Debtor must completely perform one prestation (Art. 1199)
Creditor cannot be compelled to accept part of each
Choice belongs to the debtor (Art. 1200)

q: Under Article 1207 of the Civil Code, when two or more debtors concur in one obligation, the obligation is solidary only when:
choices: There are more than two debtors
The obligation expressly so states, or the law or the nature of the obligation requires solidarity
hints: The presumption is that the obligation is joint.
Solidarity is not presumed.
why: Art. 1207: solidary liability exists only when the obligation expressly so states, or when the law or the nature of the obligation requires solidarity; otherwise the obligation is presumed joint (Art. 1208).

q: Ana, Ben and Cora signed a promissory note: "We promise to pay Dante P300,000 on 1 March 2026." The note says nothing more. When the debt fell due, Dante sued only Ana for the entire P300,000 because Ben and Cora had no money. How much can Dante collect from Ana?

alac.answer: Dante can collect only P100,000 from Ana.
alac.basis: Article 1207 of the Civil Code provides that the concurrence of two or more debtors in one obligation does not imply that each is bound to render entire compliance; there is solidary liability only when the obligation expressly so states, or when the law or the nature of the obligation requires solidarity. Article 1208 provides that, if the contrary does not appear, the debt shall be presumed to be divided into as many shares as there are debtors.
alac.application: Here, the note merely says "we promise to pay." It does not state that the debtors are bound solidarily (for example, "jointly and severally" or "individually and collectively"), and no law or the nature of the obligation requires solidarity. The obligation is therefore joint, and the P300,000 debt is divided equally among the three debtors.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Dante can collect from Ana only her share of P100,000; the insolvency of Ben and Cora does not increase her liability.

keyPoints: Solidarity is not presumed (Art. 1207)
Joint debt divided into equal shares (Art. 1208)
"We promise to pay" alone is joint

q: Under Article 1225 of the Civil Code, which obligation is DIVISIBLE?
choices: To build a house, where the parties intended a single complete work
To work for 30 days at a daily rate
hints: Obligations to give definite things are indivisible.
Work by days or metrical units is susceptible of partial performance.
why: Art. 1225: obligations to give definite things and those not susceptible of partial performance are indivisible; obligations for a number of days of work or work by metrical units are divisible, unless the law or the parties provide otherwise.

q: Three brothers, Al, Bo and Cy, jointly agreed to deliver their co-owned racehorse to Dino for P900,000. On the due date, Al and Bo were ready to deliver, but Cy refused. Dino could not get the horse and suffered P300,000 in damages. Who is liable for the damages, and how much?

alac.answer: Cy alone is liable for the damages; Al and Bo are not liable beyond their share in the price.
alac.basis: Article 1225 of the Civil Code provides that an obligation to give a definite thing is indivisible. Article 1224 provides that a joint indivisible obligation gives rise to indemnity for damages from the time anyone of the debtors does not comply with his undertaking, and that the debtors who may have been ready to fulfill their promises shall not contribute to the indemnity beyond the corresponding portion of the price of the thing.
alac.application: Here, the obligation to deliver a specific racehorse is indivisible, and the three brothers are bound jointly. Because Cy refused, the obligation could not be fulfilled, and damages arose from his non-compliance. Al and Bo were ready to deliver, so they cannot be made to contribute to the indemnity beyond their respective portions of the price.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Cy must answer for the P300,000 in damages, while Al and Bo are not liable for damages beyond their portion of the price.

keyPoints: Obligation to give a definite thing is indivisible (Art. 1225)
Joint indivisible obligation: damages from non-compliance of anyone (Art. 1224)
Debtors ready to comply do not contribute beyond their portion of the price

q: Under Article 1226 of the Civil Code, in obligations with a penal clause, the penalty generally:
choices: Is added to damages and interest
Substitutes the indemnity for damages and the payment of interest, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary
hints: The penalty is meant to fix damages in advance.
Damages may still be paid in certain cases, such as fraud.
why: Art. 1226: the penalty substitutes the indemnity for damages and the payment of interest in case of noncompliance, unless otherwise stipulated; damages are still paid if the obligor refuses to pay the penalty or is guilty of fraud.

q: A builder contracted to finish a house for P5 million by 30 June, with a penalty equal to the full contract price if he failed. He completed 95% of the work by 30 June and the rest two weeks later. The owner demands the full P5 million penalty. Should the court award it?

alac.answer: No, the court should equitably reduce the penalty.
alac.basis: Article 1226 of the Civil Code allows the parties to stipulate a penalty that substitutes the indemnity for damages. However, Article 1229 provides that the judge shall equitably reduce the penalty when the principal obligation has been partly or irregularly complied with by the debtor, and that even without performance, the penalty may be reduced if it is iniquitous or unconscionable.
alac.application: Here, the builder had completed 95% of the work on the due date and finished the rest only two weeks late. The obligation was partly complied with. A penalty equal to the entire contract price for a short delay on the last 5% is also iniquitous and unconscionable.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should reduce the penalty to an amount that is fair in relation to the delay and the damage actually suffered by the owner.

keyPoints: Penalty substitutes damages (Art. 1226)
Mandatory reduction for partial or irregular compliance (Art. 1229)
Reduction also when iniquitous or unconscionable

q: Under Article 1423 of the Civil Code, natural obligations:
choices: Give a right of action to compel performance
Do not give a right of action, but after voluntary fulfillment, authorize the retention of what was delivered
Are enforceable only by the State
hints: They rest on equity and natural law, not positive law.
What matters is what happens after voluntary payment.
why: Art. 1423: natural obligations do not grant a right of action, but after voluntary fulfillment by the obligor, they authorize the retention of what has been delivered or rendered.

q: Joel owed Kris P80,000 under a written contract that fell due in 2010. Kris never sued. In 2024, Joel, knowing that the debt had prescribed, voluntarily paid Kris the P80,000. Later, Joel's lawyer told him he did not have to pay, so Joel sued to recover the money. Will the suit prosper?

alac.answer: No, the suit will not prosper.
alac.basis: Article 1423 of the Civil Code provides that natural obligations do not grant a right of action to enforce their performance, but after voluntary fulfillment by the obligor, they authorize the retention of what has been delivered. Article 1424 provides that when a right to sue upon a civil obligation has lapsed by extinctive prescription, the obligor who voluntarily performs the contract cannot recover what he has delivered.
alac.application: Here, Kris's action to collect prescribed ten years after 2010, so Joel's debt became a natural obligation. Joel then paid voluntarily, knowing that the debt had prescribed. Kris may therefore keep what she received.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Joel cannot recover the P80,000 he voluntarily paid.

keyPoints: Natural obligations: no action, but retention after voluntary payment (Art. 1423)
Prescribed debt paid voluntarily cannot be recovered (Art. 1424)
Payment was voluntary

q: Under Article 1236 of the Civil Code, is a creditor bound to accept payment from a third person who has no interest in the fulfillment of the obligation?
choices: No, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary
Yes, if the payment is in cash
No, never, even with a stipulation
hints: The rule protects the creditor's choice of who pays.
A stipulation may change the rule.
why: Art. 1236: the creditor is not bound to accept payment by a third person who has no interest in the fulfillment of the obligation, unless otherwise stipulated.

q: A supplier was obliged to deliver 100 sacks of rice to Rosa's store. He delivered only 95 sacks. Rosa counted them, knew there were only 95, accepted them without any protest or objection, and paid in full. A month later, she sued the supplier for the 5 missing sacks. Will she succeed?

alac.answer: No, Rosa will not succeed.
alac.basis: Article 1233 of the Civil Code provides that a debt is not understood to have been paid unless the thing or service has been completely delivered or rendered. However, Article 1235 provides that when the obligee accepts the performance, knowing its incompleteness or irregularity, and without expressing any protest or objection, the obligation is deemed fully complied with.
alac.application: Here, the supplier's delivery of 95 sacks was incomplete. But Rosa knew it was incomplete, accepted it, and made no protest or objection. Her acceptance under these circumstances is treated by law as full compliance.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the obligation is deemed fully complied with, and Rosa cannot demand the 5 missing sacks.

keyPoints: Payment requires complete delivery (Art. 1233)
Acceptance with knowledge of incompleteness and without protest (Art. 1235)
Obligation deemed fully complied with

q: Under Article 1263 of the Civil Code, in an obligation to deliver a generic thing (e.g., 50 sacks of rice of a certain kind), the loss of the debtor's rice by fire:
choices: Does not extinguish the obligation, because the genus never perishes
Converts it into a natural obligation
hints: Generic things can be replaced by others of the same kind.
Latin maxim: genus nunquam perit.
why: Art. 1263: in an obligation to deliver a generic thing, the loss or destruction of anything of the same kind does not extinguish the obligation.

q: Ely sold his specific horse, "Kidlat," to Fe, with delivery due on 15 May. On 10 May, Kidlat was killed by lightning while grazing in Ely's properly fenced pasture. Fe demands that Ely deliver another horse of the same breed or pay damages. Must Ely comply?

alac.answer: No, Ely need not comply. His obligation was extinguished.
alac.basis: Article 1262 of the Civil Code provides that an obligation which consists in the delivery of a determinate thing shall be extinguished if it should be lost or destroyed without the fault of the debtor, and before he has incurred in delay. Article 1174 provides that, as a rule, no person is responsible for events which could not be foreseen or which, though foreseen, were inevitable.
alac.application: Here, the obligation was to deliver a specific horse, Kidlat, a determinate thing. It was killed by lightning, a fortuitous event, without any fault of Ely, whose pasture was properly fenced. The loss happened on 10 May, before the due date, so Ely was not in delay. No law or stipulation made him liable for fortuitous events.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ely's obligation was extinguished, and he need not deliver another horse or pay damages.

keyPoints: Loss of a determinate thing without fault and before delay extinguishes the obligation (Art. 1262)
Lightning is a fortuitous event (Art. 1174)
A specific horse cannot be replaced by another

q: Under Article 1270 of the Civil Code, condonation or remission of a debt:
choices: Is onerous and needs no acceptance
Is essentially gratuitous and requires the acceptance of the obligor
Is valid only if made in a will
hints: Condonation is like a donation of the credit.
The debtor must accept it.
why: Art. 1270: condonation is essentially gratuitous and requires acceptance by the obligor; it may be express or implied; express condonation must comply with the forms of donation.

q: Gina lent Hugo P60,000, evidenced by a private promissory note. Gina later voluntarily handed the original note to Hugo, saying nothing. A year later, she sued Hugo to collect. What is the effect of her having handed the note to Hugo?

alac.answer: The voluntary delivery of the note implies that Gina renounced her action against Hugo.
alac.basis: Article 1271 of the Civil Code provides that the delivery of a private document evidencing a credit, made voluntarily by the creditor to the debtor, implies the renunciation of the action which the former had against the latter. Article 1270 provides that condonation may be made expressly or impliedly.
alac.application: Here, the promissory note is a private document evidencing Gina's credit. Gina handed it to Hugo voluntarily. The law treats this act as an implied renunciation, or condonation, of her action to collect. Unless Gina proves that the delivery was not voluntary or not meant as a renunciation, the presumption stands.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Gina's suit should be dismissed because she impliedly condoned the debt.

keyPoints: Voluntary delivery of a private document of credit implies renunciation (Art. 1271)
Implied condonation (Art. 1270)
Applies to private, not public, documents

q: Under Article 1275 of the Civil Code, an obligation is extinguished by confusion or merger when:
choices: The characters of creditor and debtor are merged in the same person
The debtor transfers to another city
hints: No one can be his own creditor.
Think of a debtor who inherits the credit against himself.
why: Art. 1275: the obligation is extinguished from the time the characters of creditor and debtor are merged in the same person.

q: Ivan borrowed P500,000 from his father, with his uncle Jun as guarantor. The father died, and in the settlement of his estate, the credit against Ivan was adjudicated to Ivan himself. The father's estate later had no other claims. Is Ivan's debt extinguished, and is Jun still liable as guarantor?

alac.answer: Yes, the debt is extinguished by confusion, and Jun is released as guarantor.
alac.basis: Article 1275 of the Civil Code provides that the obligation is extinguished from the time the characters of creditor and debtor are merged in the same person. Article 1276 provides that merger which takes place in the person of the principal debtor or creditor benefits the guarantors.
alac.application: Here, upon the adjudication of the credit to Ivan, Ivan became both the creditor and the debtor of the same P500,000 obligation. The characters of creditor and debtor merged in him, so the obligation was extinguished. Because the merger took place in the person of the principal debtor, it benefits the guarantor, Jun.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ivan's debt is extinguished by confusion, and Jun's liability as guarantor is also extinguished.

keyPoints: Confusion extinguishes the obligation (Art. 1275)
Merger in the principal debtor benefits the guarantor (Art. 1276)
The guaranty is accessory to the principal obligation

q: Which of the following is NOT a requisite of legal compensation under Article 1279 of the Civil Code?
choices: Each party is bound principally and is at the same time a principal creditor of the other
Both debts are due, liquidated and demandable
Both debts arise from the same contract
Neither debt is subject to a retention or controversy commenced by third persons and communicated to the debtor
hints: Art. 1279 lists five requisites.
The debts may come from different sources.
why: Art. 1279 requires that both parties be principal debtors and creditors of each other, that both debts be of money (or the same kind of consumables), due, liquidated and demandable, and free from any third-party retention or controversy. They need not arise from the same contract.

q: Kara has a P500,000 savings deposit in Bank X. She also owes Bank X P300,000 on a loan that is already due. Without Kara's consent, Bank X debited P300,000 from her savings account to pay the loan. Kara complains that the bank had no right to do so. Is she correct?

alac.answer: No, Kara is not correct. Legal compensation took place.
alac.basis: Article 1980 of the Civil Code provides that savings deposits of money in banks are governed by the provisions concerning simple loan, so the bank is the debtor of the depositor. Article 1278 provides that compensation takes place when two persons, in their own right, are creditors and debtors of each other. Under Article 1290, when all the requisites of Article 1279 are present, compensation takes effect by operation of law and extinguishes both debts to the concurrent amount, even though the parties are not aware of it.
alac.application: Here, Bank X is Kara's debtor for her P500,000 deposit, and Kara is the bank's debtor for the P300,000 loan. Both are principal debtors and creditors of each other, both debts are in money, due, liquidated and demandable, and no third person has claimed either. All the requisites of Article 1279 are present.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, compensation took place by operation of law to the extent of P300,000, and the bank validly applied the deposit to the loan.

keyPoints: Bank deposits are simple loans; bank is the debtor (Art. 1980)
Requisites of legal compensation present (Art. 1279)
Takes effect by operation of law, even without consent (Art. 1290)

q: Under Article 1292 of the Civil Code, an obligation is extinguished by novation only when:
choices: The parties agree to a new due date
It is declared in unequivocal terms, or the old and new obligations are on every point incompatible
The creditor accepts a partial payment
The debtor signs a new receipt
hints: Novation is never presumed.
There are two ways: express or implied (total incompatibility).
why: Art. 1292: to extinguish an obligation by substituting another, it must be declared in unequivocal terms (express novation) or the old and new obligations must be incompatible on every point (implied novation).

q: Lara owed Mon P1 million, due on 1 January 2026, secured by a guaranty of Nestor. In December 2025, Lara and Mon agreed in writing to move the due date to 1 June 2026 and to lower the interest rate, without saying anything about extinguishing the old obligation. Lara contends that the original obligation was novated and extinguished. Is she correct?

alac.answer: No, Lara is not correct. There was no novation that extinguished the obligation.
alac.basis: Article 1291 of the Civil Code provides that obligations may be modified by changing their object or principal conditions. Article 1292 provides that an obligation is extinguished by another which substitutes it only if it is so declared in unequivocal terms, or if the old and the new obligations are on every point incompatible with each other.
alac.application: Here, the parties did not declare in unequivocal terms that the old obligation was extinguished. The changes, a later due date and a lower interest rate, are not incompatible on every point with the original obligation; Lara still owes the same P1 million to the same creditor. These are mere modifications of incidental terms.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the original obligation subsists, as modified, and was not extinguished by novation.

keyPoints: Novation must be express or by total incompatibility (Art. 1292)
Extension of time and change in interest are mere modifications (Art. 1291)
Same debtor, creditor and principal obligation

q: Under Article 1293 of the Civil Code, substitution of a new debtor in place of the original one (expromision) may be made:
choices: Without the consent of the creditor
Even without the knowledge or against the will of the original debtor, but not without the consent of the creditor
Only if the original debtor is insolvent
hints: The creditor must agree to a new debtor.
The original debtor need not even know.
why: Art. 1293: novation by substituting a new debtor may be made even without the knowledge or against the will of the original debtor, but not without the consent of the creditor.

q: Omar owed Pia P400,000. Omar proposed that Quin take his place as debtor, and Pia agreed, releasing Omar. At that time, Omar knew that Quin was already insolvent, but Pia did not. Quin never paid. Can Pia go after Omar?

alac.answer: Yes, Pia can go after Omar.
alac.basis: Delegacion is the substitution of a new debtor proposed by the original debtor and accepted by the creditor. Article 1295 of the Civil Code provides that the insolvency of the new debtor, who has been proposed by the original debtor and accepted by the creditor, shall not revive the action of the creditor against the original obligor, except when said insolvency was already existing and of public knowledge, or known to the debtor, when he delegated his debt. By contrast, under Article 1294, in expromision the new debtor's insolvency gives rise to no liability of the original debtor.
alac.application: Here, Omar himself proposed Quin, and Pia accepted, so this was delegacion. Quin was already insolvent when Omar delegated the debt, and Omar knew it. The exception in Article 1295 therefore applies.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Pia's action against Omar is revived, and she may collect from him.

keyPoints: Delegacion: new debtor proposed by the old debtor, accepted by the creditor
Insolvency of the new debtor revives the action if existing and known to the old debtor (Art. 1295)
Contrast: expromision (Art. 1294)

q: Under Article 1301 of the Civil Code, conventional subrogation of a third person requires the consent of:
choices: The original parties and the third person
hints: Conventional subrogation is by agreement.
Everyone involved must agree.
why: Art. 1301: conventional subrogation requires the consent of the original parties (creditor and debtor) and of the third person.

q: Rico borrowed P1 million from Bank Y, secured by a mortgage on his land and by the guaranty of his friend Sol. When Rico defaulted, Sol paid the bank in full, without Rico's knowledge. Can Sol foreclose the mortgage on Rico's land?

alac.answer: Yes, Sol may foreclose the mortgage.
alac.basis: Article 1302(3) of the Civil Code presumes legal subrogation when, even without the knowledge of the debtor, a person interested in the fulfillment of the obligation pays. Article 1303 provides that subrogation transfers to the person subrogated the credit with all the rights thereto appertaining, either against the debtor or against third persons, be they guarantors or possessors of mortgages.
alac.application: Here, Sol, as guarantor, is a person interested in the fulfillment of the obligation, because she is liable if Rico does not pay. She paid the bank even without Rico's knowledge. She is therefore legally subrogated to the bank's rights, including its rights under the mortgage.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Sol steps into the shoes of the bank and may foreclose the mortgage on Rico's land.

keyPoints: Legal subrogation when an interested person pays, even without the debtor's knowledge (Art. 1302(3))
A guarantor is an interested person
Subrogation carries all rights, including the mortgage (Art. 1303)

q: Under Article 1431 of the Civil Code, through estoppel, an admission or representation is:
choices: Rendered conclusive upon the person making it, and cannot be denied or disproved as against the person relying on it
Valid only if in a public document
hints: Estoppel protects the person who relied on the representation.
The one who made it cannot take it back against that person.
why: Art. 1431: through estoppel an admission or representation is conclusive upon the person making it and cannot be denied or disproved as against the person relying on it.

q: In 2023, Tomas sold and delivered a parcel of land to Ursula, claiming to be its owner, although it actually belonged to his father. In 2025, the father died and Tomas inherited the land. Tomas now claims the land as his own, arguing that the 2023 sale was void because he did not own the land then. Who owns the land?

alac.answer: Ursula owns the land.
alac.basis: Article 1434 of the Civil Code provides that when a person who is not the owner of a thing sells or alienates and delivers it, and later the seller or grantor acquires title thereto, such title passes by operation of law to the buyer or grantee. This is an application of estoppel under Article 1431, which makes a representation conclusive upon the person making it as against the person relying on it.
alac.application: Here, Tomas sold and delivered the land to Ursula in 2023, representing himself as owner, although he was not. In 2025, he acquired title by inheritance. By operation of law, that title passed to Ursula, and Tomas is estopped from denying the sale he made.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ursula owns the land, and Tomas cannot recover it.

keyPoints: Seller who later acquires title: title passes to the buyer by operation of law (Art. 1434)
Estoppel (Art. 1431)
Seller cannot deny his own representation

q: Under Article 1305 of the Civil Code, a contract is:
choices: A meeting of minds between two persons whereby one binds himself, with respect to the other, to give something or to render some service
Any written document signed by one person
hints: A contract needs at least two parties.
The core is the meeting of minds.
why: Art. 1305: a contract is a meeting of minds between two persons whereby one binds himself, with respect to the other, to give something or to render some service.

q: Ana offered in writing to sell her car to Ben for P500,000. Ben replied, "I accept, but at P450,000." Ana did not answer. A week later, Ben tendered P500,000, but Ana had already sold the car to Cora. Ben sued Ana for breach of contract. Will he win?

alac.answer: No, Ben will not win. No contract was perfected between him and Ana.
alac.basis: Article 1305 of the Civil Code defines a contract as a meeting of minds between two persons. Article 1319 provides that consent is manifested by the meeting of the offer and the acceptance upon the thing and the cause; the offer must be certain and the acceptance absolute, and a qualified acceptance constitutes a counter-offer.
alac.application: Here, Ben's reply changed the price from P500,000 to P450,000. It was not an absolute acceptance but a counter-offer, which rejected Ana's original offer. Ana never accepted the counter-offer. Ben's later tender of P500,000 could not revive an offer that no longer existed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, there was no meeting of minds and no contract, so Ana was free to sell the car to Cora.

keyPoints: Contract = meeting of minds (Art. 1305)
Acceptance must be absolute; a qualified acceptance is a counter-offer (Art. 1319)
Counter-offer was never accepted

q: Under Article 1306 of the Civil Code, contracting parties may establish any stipulations they deem convenient, provided they are NOT contrary to:
choices: Law, morals, good customs, public order, or public policy
The opinion of a notary public
hints: This is the principle of autonomy of contracts.
The limits are the same as for waivers (Art. 6).
why: Art. 1306: parties may establish stipulations, clauses, terms and conditions as they deem convenient, provided they are not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public order, or public policy.

q: A supply contract between Dela Corp. and Eco Inc. states: "Eco Inc. waives any action against Dela Corp. for any fraud Dela Corp. may commit in performing this contract." Later, Dela Corp. deliberately delivered fake goods. Can Eco Inc. sue despite the waiver?

alac.answer: Yes, Eco Inc. can sue. The waiver is void.
alac.basis: Article 1306 of the Civil Code allows the parties to establish stipulations they deem convenient, provided they are not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public order, or public policy. Article 1171 provides that responsibility arising from fraud is demandable in all obligations, and any waiver of an action for future fraud is void.
alac.application: Here, the stipulation waives in advance Eco Inc.'s action for fraud that Dela Corp. might commit in the future. Such a waiver is expressly declared void by law, so the autonomy of the parties does not protect it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the waiver has no effect, and Eco Inc. may hold Dela Corp. liable for its fraud.

keyPoints: Autonomy of contracts is limited by law, morals, etc. (Art. 1306)
Waiver of action for future fraud is void (Art. 1171)
Fraud liability demandable in all obligations

q: Under Article 1308 of the Civil Code, the validity or compliance of a contract:
choices: May be left to the will of the stronger party
Cannot be left to the will of one of the contracting parties
hints: This is the principle of mutuality.
A contract must bind both parties.
why: Art. 1308: the contract must bind both contracting parties; its validity or compliance cannot be left to the will of one of them.

q: A loan agreement between Fe and Lending Co. allows Lending Co. to increase the interest rate "at any time, at its sole discretion, without notice to or consent of the borrower." Lending Co. later raised the rate from 12% to 36% a year. Is Fe bound by the increase?

alac.answer: No, Fe is not bound by the unilateral increase.
alac.basis: Article 1308 of the Civil Code provides that the contract must bind both contracting parties, and its validity or compliance cannot be left to the will of one of them. Under this principle of mutuality, a stipulation allowing one party to change a principal term such as the interest rate at its sole will, without the other's consent, is void.
alac.application: Here, the clause allows Lending Co. to raise the interest at its sole discretion, without notice to or consent of Fe. The interest rate is a principal term of the loan. Leaving it to the will of the lender alone violates the mutuality of contracts.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the escalation clause and the increase to 36% are void, and Fe remains bound only to the originally agreed rate of 12%.

keyPoints: Mutuality of contracts (Art. 1308)
Interest rate cannot be changed at the sole will of one party
Unilateral increase without consent is void

q: Under Article 1311 of the Civil Code, contracts generally take effect only between:
choices: The parties, their assigns and heirs
The parties and all their relatives
The parties and the general public
hints: This is the principle of relativity.
Heirs are bound, but not beyond the value of what they received.
why: Art. 1311: contracts take effect only between the parties, their assigns and heirs, except when the rights and obligations are not transmissible; the heir is not liable beyond the value of the property received.

q: Gil sold his house to Hana. Their deed provides that Hana will pay P500,000 of the price directly to Ivy, Gil's sister, "as Gil's gift to her." Ivy wrote Hana accepting the benefit. Afterwards, Gil and Hana agreed to delete the clause. Can Ivy still demand the P500,000 from Hana?

alac.answer: Yes, Ivy can demand the P500,000.
alac.basis: Article 1311 of the Civil Code provides that contracts take effect only between the parties, their assigns and heirs. However, if a contract contains a stipulation in favor of a third person, he may demand its fulfillment provided he communicated his acceptance to the obligor before its revocation. The contracting parties must have clearly and deliberately conferred a favor upon the third person.
alac.application: Here, the deed clearly and deliberately conferred a benefit on Ivy, a third person. Ivy communicated her acceptance to Hana, the obligor, before Gil and Hana tried to revoke the clause. The later agreement to delete it came too late.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the stipulation pour autrui became binding, and Ivy may demand payment of the P500,000 from Hana.

keyPoints: Relativity of contracts (Art. 1311)
Exception: stipulation pour autrui
Acceptance communicated to the obligor before revocation

q: Under Article 1315 of the Civil Code, contracts are generally perfected:
hints: This is the principle of consensuality.
Real contracts are the exception.
why: Art. 1315: contracts are perfected by mere consent, and the parties are then bound to what was stipulated and to all consequences in keeping with good faith, usage and law.

q: Jake orally agreed to sell his motorcycle to Kim for P80,000. Kim paid P20,000 on the spot, and they agreed on delivery the next week. Jake later changed his mind, arguing that there was no written contract. Can Kim compel Jake to deliver?

alac.answer: Yes, Kim can compel Jake to deliver the motorcycle.
alac.basis: Article 1315 of the Civil Code provides that contracts are perfected by mere consent. Under Article 1403(2)(d), an agreement for the sale of goods at a price not less than five hundred pesos is unenforceable unless in writing, unless the buyer accepts and receives part of the goods or pays at the time some part of the purchase money.
alac.application: Here, Jake and Kim agreed on the motorcycle and its price, so the sale was perfected by their consent. Although it was not in writing, Kim paid P20,000 of the price at the time of the agreement. That partial payment takes the sale out of the Statute of Frauds.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale is perfected and enforceable, and Kim may compel Jake to deliver the motorcycle upon payment of the balance.

keyPoints: Perfection by mere consent (Art. 1315)
Statute of Frauds for sale of goods of P500 or more (Art. 1403(2)(d))
Partial payment takes it out of the Statute of Frauds

q: Under Article 1159 of the Civil Code, obligations arising from contracts:
choices: Have the force of law between the contracting parties and should be complied with in good faith
May be ignored if they become costly
hints: This is the principle of obligatory force (pacta sunt servanda).
Good faith is required in compliance.
why: Art. 1159: obligations arising from contracts have the force of law between the contracting parties and should be complied with in good faith.

q: Lina contracted to supply 1,000 sacks of rice to a school at a fixed price for one year. Midway, the price of rice rose by 10%, and she asked to be released from the contract, citing Article 1267 of the Civil Code. Should she be released?

alac.answer: No, Lina should not be released.
alac.basis: Article 1159 of the Civil Code provides that obligations arising from contracts have the force of law between the contracting parties and should be complied with in good faith. Article 1267 allows release only when the service has become so difficult as to be manifestly beyond the contemplation of the parties.
alac.application: Here, a 10% rise in the price of rice is an ordinary business risk that the parties could have anticipated when they fixed the price for a whole year. It makes Lina's performance more costly, but not so difficult as to be manifestly beyond what the parties contemplated.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Lina remains bound to supply the rice at the agreed price.

keyPoints: Contracts have the force of law (Art. 1159)
Release only if performance is manifestly beyond the parties' contemplation (Art. 1267)
Ordinary price increase is not enough

q: Under Article 1316 of the Civil Code, which of the following is a REAL contract, perfected only upon delivery of the object?
hints: Real contracts are the exception to consensuality.
Art. 1316 names deposit, pledge and commodatum.
why: Art. 1316: real contracts, such as deposit, pledge and commodatum, are not perfected until the delivery of the object of the obligation.

q: Mia promised in writing to lend her car to Nora, free of charge, for Nora's out-of-town wedding. Nora accepted. On the eve of the trip, Mia refused to hand over the car. Was a commodatum perfected? Does Nora have any remedy?

alac.answer: No commodatum was perfected, but Nora may enforce Mia's accepted promise to lend.
alac.basis: Article 1316 of the Civil Code provides that real contracts, such as commodatum, are not perfected until the delivery of the object. Article 1934 provides that an accepted promise to deliver something by way of commodatum or simple loan is binding upon the parties, but the commodatum or simple loan itself shall not be perfected until the delivery of the object of the contract.
alac.application: Here, the car was never delivered, so the commodatum itself was not perfected. However, Mia made a promise to lend, and Nora accepted it. That accepted promise is a consensual contract that binds Mia.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, while there is no commodatum yet, Nora may hold Mia liable for breach of her accepted promise to lend.

keyPoints: Commodatum is a real contract, perfected by delivery (Art. 1316)
An accepted promise to lend is binding (Art. 1934)
Remedy is on the promise, not on the commodatum

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the essential requisites of a contract under Article 1318 of the Civil Code?
choices: Object certain which is the subject matter of the contract
Cause of the obligation which is established
hints: There are three essential requisites.
Form is generally not essential.
why: Art. 1318: there is no contract unless consent, object certain, and cause concur. Notarization is not an essential requisite.

q: While Olga was abroad, her nephew forged her signature on a deed selling her land to Pete, who paid the nephew. Pete now claims ownership. Olga sues to recover the land. Who should win?

alac.answer: Olga should win. The forged deed produced no contract.
alac.basis: Article 1318 of the Civil Code provides that there is no contract unless consent of the contracting parties, object certain, and cause concur. A deed bearing a forged signature carries no consent of the supposed seller, so it is void and transfers no title.
alac.application: Here, Olga never consented to the sale; her signature was forged by her nephew. Without Olga's consent, the essential requisite of consent is absent, and no contract of sale came into existence between Olga and Pete. Pete could not acquire from the nephew rights that the nephew did not have.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the forged deed is void, and Olga may recover her land; Pete's remedy is against the nephew.

keyPoints: Consent is an essential requisite (Art. 1318)
A forged signature means no consent
Void deed transfers no title

q: Under Article 1356 of the Civil Code, as a rule, contracts are obligatory:
choices: Only if in a public document
In whatever form they may have been entered into, provided all the essential requisites for their validity are present
hints: Form is generally not required for validity.
Some contracts are exceptions where the law requires a form.
why: Art. 1356: contracts are obligatory in whatever form they were entered into, provided the essential requisites are present; when the law requires a form for validity or enforceability, that requirement is absolute.

q: Quino sold his lot to Rina in a private, un-notarized deed signed by both, and Rina paid in full. Rina asked Quino to sign a notarized deed so she could register the sale, but he refused, claiming the sale is void because it is not in a public document. Is he correct? What can Rina do?

alac.answer: No, Quino is not correct. The sale is valid, and Rina may compel him to execute a public document.
alac.basis: Article 1356 of the Civil Code provides that contracts are obligatory in whatever form they may have been entered into, provided all the essential requisites are present. Article 1358 requires acts and contracts transmitting real rights over immovable property to appear in a public document, but this requirement is for convenience and effectivity against third persons, not for validity. Article 1357 provides that the contracting parties may compel each other to observe that form once the contract has been perfected.
alac.application: Here, Quino and Rina agreed on the lot and its price, and Rina paid in full, so a valid sale was perfected and is in writing. The lack of a public document does not make it void. It only means that Rina cannot yet register it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale is valid, and Rina may file an action to compel Quino to execute a notarized deed of sale.

keyPoints: Contracts valid in whatever form if essentials present (Art. 1356)
Public document for real rights over immovables is for convenience (Art. 1358)
Parties may compel each other to observe the form (Art. 1357)

q: Under Article 1359 of the Civil Code, if mistake or fraud has PREVENTED a meeting of the minds, the proper remedy is:
hints: Reformation presupposes that there was a meeting of minds.
If there was no real agreement, the contract itself is defective.
why: Art. 1359: reformation is proper when there was a meeting of minds but the instrument does not express the true intention; if mistake, fraud, inequitable conduct or accident prevented a meeting of minds, the remedy is annulment.

q: Sara agreed to sell Lot 5 to Tony, and both inspected Lot 5. Through a typing error that neither noticed, the deed of sale described Lot 6, which Sara also owns. What is Tony's remedy?

alac.answer: Tony may ask for the reformation of the deed of sale.
alac.basis: Article 1359 of the Civil Code provides that when, there having been a meeting of the minds of the parties to a contract, their true intention is not expressed in the instrument by reason of mistake, fraud, inequitable conduct or accident, one of the parties may ask for the reformation of the instrument.
