Article 1361 provides that when a mutual mistake of the parties causes the failure of the instrument to disclose their real agreement, the instrument may be reformed.
alac.application: Here, Sara and Tony agreed on the sale of Lot 5, so there was a meeting of minds. Because of a mutual typing error, the deed described Lot 6 instead. The instrument fails to express their true agreement.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Tony's proper remedy is an action for reformation of the instrument so that the deed describes Lot 5.

keyPoints: Meeting of minds existed (Art. 1359)
Mutual mistake in the instrument (Art. 1361)
Remedy: reformation, not annulment

q: Under Article 1370 of the Civil Code, if the terms of a contract are clear and leave no doubt as to the intention of the parties:
choices: The literal meaning of its stipulations shall control
The interpretation favorable to the weaker party prevails
hints: Clear words need no interpretation.
If words contradict the evident intention, intention prevails.
why: Art. 1370: if the terms are clear, the literal meaning controls; if the words appear contrary to the parties' evident intention, the intention prevails.

q: An insurance company prepared a printed policy which Uma signed without any chance to negotiate. A clause excluded coverage for "water damage," without saying whether this included flood. Uma's house was flooded. The insurer denied the claim. How should the clause be interpreted?

alac.answer: The clause should be interpreted against the insurer and in favor of coverage.
alac.basis: Article 1377 of the Civil Code provides that the interpretation of obscure words or stipulations in a contract shall not favor the party who caused the obscurity. This applies with special force to contracts of adhesion, which are prepared by one party and merely signed by the other.
alac.application: Here, the insurer drafted the printed policy, and Uma could not negotiate its terms. The phrase "water damage" is obscure as to whether it includes flood. Since the insurer caused the obscurity, the doubt must be resolved against it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the exclusion should be read as not covering flood, and the insurer should pay Uma's claim, subject to the other terms of the policy.

keyPoints: Obscurity construed against the party who caused it (Art. 1377)
Contract of adhesion drafted by the insurer
Doubt resolved in favor of coverage

q: Under Article 1389 of the Civil Code, the action to claim rescission of a rescissible contract must be commenced within:
hints: It is the same period as for annulment of voidable contracts.
For wards and absentees, it is counted from the end of incapacity or when the domicile is known.
why: Art. 1389: the action to claim rescission must be commenced within four years.

q: Vic owed Wen P2 million. After Wen sued him, Vic sold his only property, a house worth P3 million, to his brother for P500,000. Vic has no other assets. Can Wen ask that the sale be rescinded?

alac.answer: Yes, Wen may ask that the sale be rescinded.
alac.basis: Article 1381(3) of the Civil Code makes rescissible contracts undertaken in fraud of creditors when the latter cannot in any other manner collect the claims due them. Article 1383 provides that the action for rescission is subsidiary and cannot be instituted except when the party suffering damage has no other legal means to obtain reparation. Article 1389 requires the action to be commenced within four years.
alac.application: Here, Vic sold his only property, for far less than its value, to his own brother after Wen had already sued him. These circumstances show that the sale was made in fraud of Wen. Vic has no other assets, so Wen has no other legal means to collect.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Wen may file an action within four years to rescind the sale, so that the house may answer for Vic's debt.

keyPoints: Contracts in fraud of creditors are rescissible (Art. 1381(3))
Rescission is subsidiary: no other means to collect (Art. 1383)
Four-year period (Art. 1389)

q: Under Article 1390 of the Civil Code, voidable contracts are:
choices: Binding unless annulled by a proper action in court, and susceptible of ratification
hints: Voidable contracts are valid until set aside.
They can be ratified.
why: Art. 1390: voidable contracts (incapacity of a party, or consent vitiated by mistake, violence, intimidation, undue influence or fraud) are binding unless annulled by a proper court action and are susceptible of ratification.

q: In 2020, Xia bought a used car from Yul, who assured her it had never been in a flood. Xia would not have bought it otherwise. In 2024, a mechanic discovered that the car had been submerged in a flood. Xia filed an action to annul the sale in 2025. Has her action prescribed?

alac.answer: No, Xia's action has not prescribed.
alac.basis: Article 1390 of the Civil Code makes voidable a contract where consent is vitiated by fraud. Article 1391 provides that the action for annulment shall be brought within four years, and in case of mistake or fraud, the period begins from the time of the discovery of the same.
alac.application: Here, Yul's false assurance induced Xia to buy the car, so her consent was vitiated by fraud and the sale is voidable. The fraud was discovered only in 2024. Counting four years from discovery, Xia may sue until 2028. She sued in 2025.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Xia's action for annulment was filed on time.

keyPoints: Fraud vitiating consent makes a contract voidable (Art. 1390)
Four years from discovery of the fraud (Art. 1391)
Discovery in 2024; filed in 2025

q: Under the Statute of Frauds (Article 1403(2) of the Civil Code), which agreement is unenforceable unless in writing?
choices: A sale of a pen for P100
An agreement that by its terms is not to be performed within a year from its making
hints: The Statute of Frauds covers only executory contracts.
Long-term agreements are on the list.
why: Art. 1403(2)(a): an agreement that by its terms is not to be performed within a year from the making thereof is unenforceable unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party charged.

q: Without any authority from his aunt Zeny, Allan sold her car in her name to Bert. When Zeny learned of it, she accepted the price from Bert and handed him the car's papers. Later, she changed her mind and sought to recover the car, arguing that Allan had no authority. Will she succeed?

alac.answer: No, Zeny will not succeed.
alac.basis: Article 1317 of the Civil Code provides that a contract entered into in the name of another by one who has no authority shall be unenforceable, unless it is ratified, expressly or impliedly, by the person on whose behalf it has been executed, before it is revoked by the other contracting party. Article 1403(1) lists such contracts as unenforceable unless ratified.
alac.application: Here, Allan had no authority, so the sale was at first unenforceable against Zeny. But Zeny, knowing of the sale, accepted the price and delivered the car's papers to Bert. Her acts impliedly ratified the contract before Bert revoked it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale became binding on Zeny, and she cannot recover the car.

keyPoints: Unauthorized contracts are unenforceable (Arts. 1317, 1403(1))
Ratification may be express or implied
Acceptance of the price and delivery of papers is implied ratification

q: Under Article 1410 of the Civil Code, the action or defense for the declaration of the inexistence of a contract:
choices: Must be filed within one year
hints: A void contract produces no effect.
Time cannot make it valid.
why: Art. 1410: the action or defense for the declaration of the inexistence of a contract does not prescribe; void contracts also cannot be ratified (Art. 1409).

q: In 2005, to hide their land from a possible lawsuit, Spouses Cruz executed a deed of sale of the land to their son Dan for P1 million. No price was ever paid, and the spouses kept possessing the land. After both parents died, Dan's siblings sued in 2025 to declare the sale void. Dan argues that the action has prescribed and that his parents ratified the sale. Decide.

alac.answer: The sale is void, and the action has not prescribed.
alac.basis: Article 1409(2) of the Civil Code declares inexistent and void from the beginning contracts which are absolutely simulated or fictitious, and provides that such contracts cannot be ratified. Article 1410 provides that the action or defense for the declaration of the inexistence of a contract does not prescribe.
alac.application: Here, the parties never intended to be bound by a sale: no price was paid and the parents kept the land. The deed was executed only to hide the property. The sale is therefore absolutely simulated. A void contract cannot be ratified, and the action to declare it void does not prescribe.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the deed of sale to Dan is void, and his siblings' action, though filed twenty years later, may prosper.

keyPoints: Absolutely simulated contracts are void (Art. 1409(2))
Void contracts cannot be ratified
Action to declare inexistence does not prescribe (Art. 1410)

q: Under Article 2142 of the Civil Code, a quasi-contract arises from:
choices: Certain lawful, voluntary and unilateral acts, so that no one is unjustly enriched at the expense of another
hints: There is no agreement in a quasi-contract.
The goal is to prevent unjust enrichment.
why: Art. 2142: certain lawful, voluntary and unilateral acts give rise to the juridical relation of quasi-contract, so that no one is unjustly enriched or benefited at the expense of another.

q: A bank teller mistakenly gave Rosa P10,000 more than her withdrawal. When the bank asked for its return, Rosa argued that she never agreed to return anything, so she has no obligation. Is Rosa correct?

alac.answer: No, Rosa is not correct. She is obliged to return the P10,000.
alac.basis: Article 2142 of the Civil Code provides that certain lawful, voluntary and unilateral acts give rise to the juridical relation of quasi-contract, to the end that no one shall be unjustly enriched at the expense of another. Article 2154 provides that if something is received when there is no right to demand it, and it was unduly delivered through mistake, the obligation to return it arises.
alac.application: Here, the obligation does not come from any agreement of Rosa but from the law on quasi-contracts. Rosa received P10,000 which she had no right to demand, and the bank delivered it by mistake. Allowing her to keep it would unjustly enrich her at the bank's expense.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Rosa must return the P10,000 under the quasi-contract of solutio indebiti.

keyPoints: Quasi-contract arises without agreement (Art. 2142)
Purpose: prevent unjust enrichment
Solutio indebiti: payment by mistake must be returned (Art. 2154)

q: Under Article 2144 of the Civil Code, negotiorum gestio does NOT arise when:
choices: The owner's property is neglected or abandoned
The property or business is not neglected or abandoned, or the manager was tacitly authorized by the owner
The manager had no power from the owner
hints: Negotiorum gestio is the management of another's abandoned affairs without authority.
If there is tacit authority, agency rules apply instead.
why: Art. 2144: negotiorum gestio does not arise when the property or business is not neglected or abandoned, or when the manager was tacitly authorized by the owner.

q: While Ellen was working abroad and her house in Manila stood empty, a typhoon tore off part of its roof. Her neighbor Fred, without any authority from her, hired workers and spent P60,000 to repair the roof to keep the rain from ruining the house. Ellen refuses to reimburse Fred, saying she never authorized the repair. Is she liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Ellen must reimburse Fred.
alac.basis: Article 2144 of the Civil Code provides that whoever voluntarily takes charge of the management of the property of another, without any power from the latter, incurs the juridical relation of negotiorum gestio when the property is neglected or abandoned. Article 2150 provides that the owner who enjoys the advantages of the management shall reimburse the officious manager for the necessary and useful expenses, even without ratification, and that the same obligation exists when the management had for its purpose the prevention of an imminent and manifest loss.
alac.application: Here, Ellen's house was left unattended while she was abroad. Fred, without authority, voluntarily repaired the roof to prevent the rain from damaging the house, an imminent and manifest loss. The repair was a necessary expense that benefited Ellen.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ellen is liable to reimburse Fred the P60,000 he spent, even though she did not authorize or ratify the repair.

keyPoints: Negotiorum gestio: management of abandoned property without authority (Art. 2144)
Owner reimburses necessary and useful expenses (Art. 2150)
Also when meant to prevent an imminent and manifest loss

q: What is the main difference between solutio indebiti and accion in rem verso?
choices: Solutio indebiti requires that the payment was made by mistake; accion in rem verso does not require mistake and is available only when there is no other action
Accion in rem verso requires a contract
Solutio indebiti applies only to land
hints: Solutio indebiti is a quasi-contract under Art. 2154.
Accion in rem verso rests on Art. 22 and is subsidiary.
why: Solutio indebiti (Art. 2154) requires a payment not due and made by mistake. Accion in rem verso (Art. 22) is a subsidiary action against unjust enrichment that does not require mistake and lies only when no other action is available.

q: Because of a clerical error, Bank Z credited P1 million to Gary's account instead of to another depositor's account. Gary withdrew the money. Bank Z sued Gary for its return, invoking Article 22 (accion in rem verso). Gary argues that accion in rem verso is not the proper action. Which action should the bank pursue?

alac.answer: The bank's proper action is one based on solutio indebiti, not accion in rem verso.
alac.basis: Article 2154 of the Civil Code provides that if something is received when there is no right to demand it, and it was unduly delivered through mistake, the obligation to return it arises; this is solutio indebiti. Article 22 provides that every person who acquires something at the expense of another without just or legal ground shall return it. Accion in rem verso under Article 22 is subsidiary: it is available only when there is no other action, such as one based on contract, quasi-contract, crime or quasi-delict.
alac.application: Here, the bank delivered P1 million to Gary through a clerical mistake, and Gary had no right to it. All the elements of solutio indebiti are present, so the bank has a specific action under Article 2154. Since another action is available, the subsidiary accion in rem verso does not apply.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the bank should recover the money from Gary on the basis of solutio indebiti.

keyPoints: Solutio indebiti: payment not due, made by mistake (Art. 2154)
Accion in rem verso is subsidiary (Art. 22)
When solutio indebiti applies, accion in rem verso does not

q: Under Article 2155 of the Civil Code, payment by reason of a mistake in the construction or application of a doubtful or difficult question of law:
choices: May come within the scope of solutio indebiti
hints: Ignorance of the law excuses no one, but there is an exception.
The exception covers doubtful or difficult questions of law.
why: Art. 2155: payment by reason of a mistake in the construction or application of a doubtful or difficult question of law may come within the scope of solutio indebiti.

q: Hector inherited property worth P300,000 from his father, who left debts of P500,000. Believing, after reading conflicting opinions, that heirs are personally liable for all the debts of the deceased, Hector paid the creditor the full P500,000. Can he recover the excess of P200,000?

alac.answer: Yes, Hector may recover the P200,000 excess.
alac.basis: Article 1311 of the Civil Code provides that the heir is not liable beyond the value of the property he received from the decedent. Article 2154 provides that if something is received when there is no right to demand it, and it was unduly delivered through mistake, the obligation to return it arises. Article 2155 provides that payment by reason of a mistake in the construction or application of a doubtful or difficult question of law may come within the scope of Article 2154.
alac.application: Here, Hector was liable only up to the P300,000 value of what he inherited. He paid P200,000 more because he mistakenly believed, on a question of law he found doubtful and difficult, that he was personally liable for all of his father's debts. The creditor had no right to demand the excess from him.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the excess payment comes within solutio indebiti, and Hector may recover the P200,000 from the creditor.

keyPoints: Heir not liable beyond the value inherited (Art. 1311)
Mistake on a doubtful or difficult question of law (Art. 2155)
Excess recoverable as solutio indebiti (Art. 2154)

q: Under Article 2159 of the Civil Code, a person who in BAD faith accepts an undue payment of money must:
choices: Pay legal interest, and answer for loss and damages until the thing is recovered
Keep the money as a donation
hints: Bad faith increases liability.
Compare with Art. 2160 for the payee in good faith.
why: Art. 2159: a payee in bad faith pays legal interest if money is involved (or fruits, if the thing produces them) and answers for any loss or impairment from any cause and for damages, until the thing is recovered.

q: By mistake, Ivan delivered to Jose a specific painting that was meant for Jose's neighbor. Jose, in good faith, believed it was a gift and sold it to a buyer for P200,000. When Ivan discovered the mistake, he demanded that Jose return the painting or pay its value of P300,000. What is Jose liable for?

alac.answer: Jose is liable only to return the P200,000 price or to assign his action to collect it.
alac.basis: Article 2160 of the Civil Code provides that he who in good faith accepts an undue payment of a thing certain and determinate shall only be responsible for the impairment or loss of the same insofar as he has thereby been benefited, and if he has alienated it, he shall return the price or assign the action to collect the sum. By contrast, under Article 2159, a payee in bad faith answers for any loss and for damages.
alac.application: Here, Jose received the painting, a determinate thing, through Ivan's mistake, but he accepted it in good faith, believing it was a gift. He then sold it for P200,000. As a payee in good faith, his liability is limited to what he received from its sale.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Jose must give Ivan the P200,000 price, or assign to Ivan his action to collect it, and is not liable for the full P300,000 value.

keyPoints: Payee in good faith of a determinate thing (Art. 2160)
If alienated: return the price or assign the action to collect it
Contrast with the payee in bad faith (Art. 2159)

q: Under Article 2175 of the Civil Code, a person who is constrained to pay the taxes of another:
choices: Is entitled to reimbursement from the latter
Becomes owner of the property taxed
hints: This is one of the "other quasi-contracts."
The law prevents unjust enrichment of the taxpayer.
why: Art. 2175: any person who is constrained to pay the taxes of another is entitled to reimbursement from the latter.

q: When Lola Maria died, her friend Nena, without the knowledge of Maria's children, paid P150,000 for her funeral. The children, who were obliged to support their mother, refuse to reimburse Nena, saying they never asked her to pay. Must they reimburse her?

alac.answer: Yes, the children must reimburse Nena.
alac.basis: Article 2165 of the Civil Code provides that when funeral expenses are borne by a third person, without the knowledge of those relatives who were obliged to give support to the deceased, said relatives shall reimburse the third person, should the latter claim reimbursement. Under Article 2142, such quasi-contracts arise so that no one is unjustly enriched at the expense of another.
alac.application: Here, Nena, a third person, paid for Lola Maria's funeral without the knowledge of the children, who were obliged to support their mother. By paying, she relieved them of an expense that the law placed on them. Nena now claims reimbursement.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the children must reimburse Nena the P150,000 she spent for the funeral.

keyPoints: Funeral expenses paid by a third person (Art. 2165)
Relatives obliged to support the deceased must reimburse
Quasi-contract prevents unjust enrichment (Art. 2142)

q: Under Article 415(5) of the Civil Code, machinery is immovable when it is:
choices: Placed by the owner of the tenement for an industry carried on in the building or land, and tends directly to meet its needs
Placed by a lessee for his own business
Registered with the Registry of Deeds
hints: The law looks at who placed the machinery and why.
The placer must be the owner of the tenement.
why: Art. 415(5): machinery, receptacles, instruments or implements intended by the owner of the tenement for an industry or works carried on in a building or on a piece of land, and which tend directly to meet the needs of the industry, are immovable.

q: Kalye Corp. leased a building and installed heavy sawmill machinery bolted to cement foundations for its business. The lease said nothing about who would own the machinery at the end of the lease. A creditor of Kalye Corp. levied on the machinery as personal property. Kalye Corp. argues that the machinery is immovable. Who is correct?

alac.answer: The creditor is correct. The machinery is personal property.
alac.basis: Article 415(5) of the Civil Code considers immovable the machinery, receptacles, instruments or implements intended by the owner of the tenement for an industry carried on in a building or on a piece of land, and which tend directly to meet its needs. In Davao Sawmill Co. v. Castillo, G.R. No. L-40411, August 7, 1935, the Supreme Court held that machinery placed by a tenant, who is not the owner of the land or building, does not become immovable under this provision, unless the tenant acted as agent of the owner.
alac.application: Here, the machinery was installed by Kalye Corp., a mere lessee, not by the owner of the building. Nothing shows that it acted as the owner's agent or that the machinery was to pass to the owner. Although it is bolted to the foundation for the business, it was not placed by the owner of the tenement.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the machinery remains personal property and may be levied upon as such.

keyPoints: Art. 415(5) requires placement by the owner of the tenement
Machinery placed by a lessee remains movable (Davao Sawmill Co. v. Castillo)
Exception: lessee acting as the owner's agent
cite: Civil Code, Art. 415(5); Davao Sawmill Co. v. Castillo, G.R. No. L-40411, August 7, 1935

q: Under Article 416 of the Civil Code, electricity, as a force of nature brought under control by science, is:
hints: Art. 416 lists what is deemed personal property.
Forces of nature appear on that list.
why: Art. 416(3): forces of nature which are brought under control by science are deemed personal property.

q: Nilo owns a house and lot. He installed portable air-conditioning units that stand on the floor and can be unplugged and carried out without damaging the house. When he sold the house and lot, the deed said nothing about the units. The buyer claims the units as part of the house. Is the buyer correct?

alac.answer: No, the buyer is not correct. The portable units are movable property that remain Nilo's.
alac.basis: Article 415(3) of the Civil Code treats as immovable everything attached to an immovable in a fixed manner, so that it cannot be separated without breaking the material or deterioration of the object. Article 416(4) provides that, in general, all things which can be transported from place to place without impairment of the real property to which they are fixed are personal property.
alac.application: Here, the portable units merely stand on the floor and can be unplugged and carried away without damaging the house. They are not attached in a fixed manner and were not incorporated into the building. They are therefore movables, which did not pass with the sale of the house and lot.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the units remain Nilo's personal property.

keyPoints: Immovable by incorporation requires fixed attachment (Art. 415(3))
Things transportable without impairment of the realty are movable (Art. 416(4))
Sale of house and lot does not include movables unless agreed

q: Under Article 5 of the Water Code (PD 1067), which of the following belongs to the State?
choices: Rivers and their natural beds, natural lakes, subterranean waters and seawater, among others
None; water belongs to the landowner
hints: The Water Code follows the Regalian doctrine for water.
Even groundwater belongs to the State.
why: PD 1067, Art. 5: rivers and their natural beds, springs and brooks, natural lakes and lagoons, surface waters, atmospheric water, subterranean waters and seawater belong to the State.

q: A natural spring rises on Ramon's private farm. He fenced it off, claiming the spring water as his private property, and began selling it to a bottling company without any permit. Is Ramon the owner of the spring water?

alac.answer: No. The spring water belongs to the State, although Ramon may use it for domestic purposes without a permit.
alac.basis: Article 6 of the Water Code (PD 1067) provides that continuous or intermittent waters rising on private lands belong to the State. The owner of the land where the water is found may use it for domestic purposes without securing a permit, subject to registration when required. Article 13 provides that no person shall appropriate water without a water right evidenced by a water permit.
alac.application: Here, the spring rises on Ramon's land, but the law declares such waters to belong to the State. Ramon may use the water for his household needs without a permit. Selling it to a bottling company, however, is not domestic use; it is an appropriation of State-owned water that requires a water permit.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ramon does not own the spring water and may not sell it commercially without a water permit.

keyPoints: Waters rising on private lands belong to the State (PD 1067, Art. 6)
Landowner may use it for domestic purposes without a permit
Commercial appropriation needs a water permit (Art. 13)

q: Under Article 14 of the Water Code, which use of natural bodies of water does NOT need a water permit?
choices: Supplying water to a bottling plant
Bathing, washing, or watering farm animals
hints: The exemptions are small, everyday uses.
Hand-carried receptacles are also exempt.
why: PD 1067, Art. 14: no permit is needed for appropriation by hand-carried receptacles, and for bathing or washing, watering or dipping domestic or farm animals, and navigation.

q: Blue Resort Corp., 40% owned by Filipinos and 60% by foreigners, applied for a water permit to extract groundwater for its hotel's swimming pools and rooms. Should the permit be granted?

alac.answer: No, the permit should not be granted.
alac.basis: Article 13 of the Water Code (PD 1067) provides that no person shall appropriate water without a water permit. Article 15 provides that only citizens of the Philippines, of legal age, as well as juridical persons, who are duly qualified by law to exploit and develop water resources, may apply for water permits. Under Article XII, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution, the exploration, development and utilization of natural resources is limited to Filipino citizens or corporations at least sixty per centum of whose capital is owned by Filipinos.
alac.application: Here, Blue Resort Corp. needs a permit because extracting groundwater for a hotel is not an exempt use. But only 40% of its capital is Filipino-owned. It is therefore not a juridical person duly qualified by law to exploit and develop water resources.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Blue Resort Corp. is not qualified to apply for, and should not be granted, a water permit.

keyPoints: Water permit required (PD 1067, Art. 13)
Only qualified citizens or juridical persons may apply (Art. 15)
60% Filipino ownership required (Const., Art. XII, Sec. 2)
cite: Water Code (PD 1067), Arts. 13 and 15; 1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Sec. 2

q: Under Article 421 of the Civil Code, patrimonial property of the State is:
choices: Property of the State which is not intended for public use, public service, or the development of national wealth
hints: Patrimonial property is what is left after public dominion.
Compare Art. 420 with Art. 421.
why: Art. 421: all other property of the State, not of the character stated in Art. 420 (public use, public service, development of national wealth), is patrimonial property.

q: A town plaza had not been used for public gatherings for years. Without any law, ordinance or declaration withdrawing it from public use, the mayor sold part of it to a businessman. Is the sale valid?

alac.answer: No, the sale is void.
alac.basis: Article 420 of the Civil Code makes property intended for public use property of public dominion. Article 422 provides that property of public dominion, when no longer intended for public use or public service, shall form part of the patrimonial property of the State. In Heirs of Mario Malabanan v. Republic, G.R. No. 179987, April 29, 2009, the Supreme Court held that there must be an express declaration by the State that the property is no longer intended for public use or public service before it becomes patrimonial. Property of public dominion is outside the commerce of men.
alac.application: Here, the plaza is property for public use. Its non-use for some years does not by itself convert it into patrimonial property; no law, ordinance or other express declaration withdrew it from public use. It therefore remained property of public dominion, outside the commerce of men, when the mayor sold it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale is void.

keyPoints: Plaza for public use is public dominion (Art. 420)
Becomes patrimonial only when no longer intended for public use (Art. 422)
Express declaration required (Heirs of Malabanan v. Republic)
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 420 and 422; Heirs of Mario Malabanan v. Republic, G.R. No. 179987, April 29, 2009

q: Under Article 425 of the Civil Code, property of private ownership includes:
choices: Property belonging to private persons, individually or collectively, besides the patrimonial property of the State, provinces, cities and municipalities
hints: Patrimonial property of the State is held in a private capacity.
Read the opening words of Art. 425.
why: Art. 425: property of private ownership, besides the patrimonial property of the State, provinces, cities, and municipalities, consists of all property belonging to private persons, individually or collectively.

q: For more than 30 years, Rolando openly occupied, as owner, a strip of land that was part of a national road no longer used for traffic but never declared withdrawn from public use. He also occupied, for the same period, an adjoining unregistered lot owned by a private person. Can Rolando acquire both by prescription?

alac.answer: Rolando may acquire the private lot by prescription, but not the road strip.
alac.basis: Article 1113 of the Civil Code provides that all things which are within the commerce of men are susceptible of prescription, unless otherwise provided, but property of the State or any of its subdivisions not patrimonial in character shall not be the object of prescription. Article 425 classifies property belonging to private persons as property of private ownership. Article 1137 provides that ownership over immovables prescribes through uninterrupted adverse possession for thirty years, without need of title or good faith.
alac.application: Here, the road strip remained property of public dominion because it was never withdrawn from public use; it is not patrimonial and cannot be acquired by prescription. The adjoining lot, however, is unregistered land of private ownership, within the commerce of men. Rolando possessed it openly, as owner, for more than thirty years.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Rolando acquired the private lot by extraordinary prescription, but he cannot acquire the road strip, however long he occupies it.

keyPoints: Public dominion property is not subject to prescription (Art. 1113)
Private property is within the commerce of men (Art. 425)
Extraordinary prescription: 30 years (Art. 1137)

q: Under Article 428 of the Civil Code, the owner of a thing has the right to:
choices: Enjoy and dispose of it, without other limitations than those established by law, and to recover it from any holder
Use it only with government approval
Dispose of it only after ten years
Enjoy it but never sell it
hints: Ownership includes enjoyment and disposition.
It also includes an action to recover.
why: Art. 428: the owner has the right to enjoy and dispose of a thing, without other limitations than those established by law, and a right of action against the holder and possessor to recover it.

q: Two years ago, Celso entered Dory's vacant lot and built a shanty there. Dory recently hired men who, without any court order, tore down the shanty and forcibly removed Celso. Dory invokes her right as owner to exclude others under Article 429. Was her act justified?

alac.answer: No, Dory's act was not justified.
alac.basis: Article 429 of the Civil Code provides that the owner or lawful possessor of a thing may use such force as may be reasonably necessary to repel or prevent an actual or threatened unlawful physical invasion or usurpation of his property (the doctrine of self-help). Article 539 provides that every possessor has a right to be respected in his possession and, if disturbed, shall be protected or restored by the means established by the laws and the Rules of Court.
alac.application: Here, Celso's entry was not an actual or threatened invasion that Dory was repelling at the moment; he had been in possession for two years. Self-help under Article 429 applies only to repel or prevent an invasion as it happens, not to recover possession already lost. To recover possession, Dory must go to court.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Dory acted unlawfully; she should have filed the proper action to recover possession.

keyPoints: Self-help only to repel or prevent an actual or threatened invasion (Art. 429)
Possession already lost must be recovered through the courts (Art. 539)
Owner cannot take the law into her own hands

q: Under Article 445 of the Civil Code, whatever is built, planted or sown on the land of another, and the improvements made on it:
choices: Belong to the owner of the land, subject to the rules that follow
Are co-owned by the builder and the landowner
hints: Accession follows the principal thing.
The land is the principal.
why: Art. 445: whatever is built, planted or sown on the land of another and the improvements or repairs made on it belong to the owner of the land, subject to the following articles (e.g., Arts. 448-455).

q: Fermin knew that a lot belonged to Gloria, but he built a store on it anyway while Gloria was abroad. Gloria returned and wants to keep the store without paying anything. Fermin demands reimbursement for the cost of construction. Who is correct?

alac.answer: Gloria is correct. Fermin is not entitled to any indemnity.
alac.basis: Article 445 of the Civil Code provides that whatever is built on the land of another belongs to the owner of the land, subject to the provisions that follow. Article 449 provides that he who builds, plants or sows in bad faith on the land of another loses what is built, planted or sown without right to indemnity.
alac.application: Here, Fermin knew that the lot belonged to Gloria, so he built in bad faith. Gloria, the landowner, did not consent and was in good faith. Under Article 449, Fermin loses the store without any right to be reimbursed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Gloria may keep the store without paying Fermin anything.

keyPoints: Accession belongs to the landowner (Art. 445)
Builder in bad faith loses what is built without indemnity (Art. 449)
Landowner in good faith

q: Under Article 477 of the Civil Code, the plaintiff in an action to quiet title must:
choices: Be in possession of the property
Have legal or equitable title to, or interest in, the real property; possession is not required
hints: Title or interest is required.
Possession is not.
why: Art. 477: the plaintiff must have legal or equitable title to, or interest in, the real property; he need not be in possession.

q: Hermie owns and possesses a lot. He discovered that his cousin had recorded in the Registry of Deeds an affidavit falsely claiming that Hermie had sold the lot to him. The affidavit looks valid on its face. What action may Hermie bring?

alac.answer: Hermie may bring an action to quiet title to remove the cloud cast by the affidavit.
alac.basis: Article 476 of the Civil Code provides that whenever there is a cloud on title to real property by reason of any instrument, record, claim, encumbrance or proceeding which is apparently valid or effective but is in truth invalid, ineffective, voidable or unenforceable, and may be prejudicial to the title, an action may be brought to remove such cloud or to quiet the title. Article 477 requires the plaintiff to have legal or equitable title to or interest in the property.
alac.application: Here, Hermie is the owner, so he has legal title. The recorded affidavit is apparently valid but is false, and it may prejudice his title, for example if he tries to sell or mortgage the lot. It is a cloud on his title.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Hermie may file an action to quiet title to have the affidavit declared void and its annotation cancelled.

keyPoints: Cloud: an instrument apparently valid but in truth invalid (Art. 476)
Plaintiff must have legal or equitable title (Art. 477)
Remedy: action to quiet title

q: Under Article 494 of the Civil Code, co-owners may validly agree to keep the thing undivided for a period not exceeding:
choices: Ten years, which may be extended by a new agreement
hints: No one is obliged to remain in co-ownership forever.
A donor or testator may prohibit partition for up to twenty years.
why: Art. 494: each co-owner may demand partition at any time; an agreement to keep the thing undivided for not more than ten years is valid and may be extended by a new agreement.

q: Units in Tower One Condominium are owned by their buyers, who also co-own the common areas, including the land, in proportion to their units; there is no condominium corporation holding title. A Filipino unit owner sold her unit to a Korean citizen. Is the sale valid?

alac.answer: No, the sale is void.
alac.basis: Section 5 of the Condominium Act (RA 4726) provides that where the common areas in the condominium project are owned by the owners of separate units as co-owners, no condominium unit shall be conveyed or transferred to persons other than Filipino citizens, or corporations at least sixty percent of whose capital stock belong to Filipino citizens, except in cases of hereditary succession. This implements the constitutional restriction on foreign ownership of land.
alac.application: Here, the common areas, including the land, are co-owned by the unit owners. A sale of a unit carries with it an undivided interest in the land. The buyer is a Korean citizen, and the transfer is not by hereditary succession.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale of the unit to the Korean buyer is void.

keyPoints: Condominium unit carries an undivided interest in the common areas (RA 4726, Sec. 2)
Where common areas are co-owned, units may be transferred only to Filipinos or 60% Filipino corporations (Sec. 5)
Exception: hereditary succession

q: Under Article 541 of the Civil Code, a possessor in the concept of owner:
choices: Has in his favor the legal presumption that he possesses with a just title and cannot be obliged to show or prove it
Is presumed to be in bad faith
Has no rights until he registers
hints: The law favors the one who possesses as owner.
The burden is on whoever disputes his title.
why: Art. 541: a possessor in the concept of owner is presumed to possess with a just title and cannot be obliged to show or prove it.

q: Ana's watch was stolen. The thief sold it to Ben, who bought it in good faith for P50,000 from a stranger (not at a public sale). Ana found the watch with Ben and demanded its return. Ben refuses unless Ana pays him P50,000. Must Ana pay?

alac.answer: No, Ana may recover the watch without reimbursing Ben.
alac.basis: Article 559 of the Civil Code provides that the possession of movable property acquired in good faith is equivalent to a title. Nevertheless, one who has lost any movable or has been unlawfully deprived thereof may recover it from the person in possession of the same. If the possessor acquired it in good faith at a public sale, the owner cannot obtain its return without reimbursing the price paid.
alac.application: Here, Ana was unlawfully deprived of her watch by theft. Ben bought it in good faith, but from a private seller, not at a public sale. The exception requiring reimbursement therefore does not apply.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ana may recover the watch from Ben without paying him; Ben's remedy is against the thief.

keyPoints: Possession of movables in good faith is equivalent to title (Art. 559)
Exception: owner who lost it or was unlawfully deprived may recover
Reimbursement only if bought in good faith at a public sale

q: Within what period must an action for forcible entry or unlawful detainer (accion interdictal) be filed?
choices: Within one year from the unlawful deprivation or withholding of possession
hints: It is a summary action to restore physical possession quickly.
After this period, the remedy becomes accion publiciana.
why: Rule 70, Sec. 1 of the Rules of Court: actions for forcible entry and unlawful detainer must be filed within one year after the unlawful deprivation or withholding of possession; they concern physical possession (possession de facto).
cite: Rules of Court, Rule 70, Sec. 1; Civil Code, Art. 539

q: Lessee Tito's lease expired on 31 January. On 1 February, owner Uly sent him a written demand to vacate, which Tito ignored. On 1 September of the same year, Uly filed an action to recover possession in the Municipal Trial Court. Is this the proper action and court?

alac.answer: Yes. Uly properly filed an action for unlawful detainer in the Municipal Trial Court.
alac.basis: Unlawful detainer is a form of accion interdictal under Rule 70 of the Rules of Court, filed when a person unlawfully withholds possession after the expiration or termination of his right to possess. It must be filed within one year from the last demand to vacate, and it falls within the exclusive original jurisdiction of the first-level courts. Article 539 of the Civil Code protects every possessor and allows restoration of possession by the means established by the laws and the Rules of Court.
alac.application: Here, Tito's right to possess as lessee ended on 31 January, and he refused to leave after Uly's written demand on 1 February. His possession became unlawful from then. Uly filed on 1 September, within one year from the demand.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the action is one for unlawful detainer, properly filed in the Municipal Trial Court.

keyPoints: Unlawful detainer: possession was lawful but became unlawful
File within one year from the last demand to vacate (Rule 70)
First-level courts have jurisdiction
cite: Rules of Court, Rule 70, Secs. 1-2; Civil Code, Art. 539

q: Accion publiciana is an action to recover:
choices: The better right of possession (possession de jure), filed when dispossession has lasted more than one year
hints: It is the plenary action for possession.
It is used after the one-year period for ejectment has lapsed.
why: Accion publiciana is a plenary action to recover the better right of possession, independently of title, brought when dispossession has lasted more than one year; jurisdiction depends on the assessed value of the property.
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 428 and 539; Rules of Court, Rule 70

q: Two years ago, Vina secretly fenced in part of Wilma's lot while Wilma was abroad. Wilma discovered it two years ago as well but did nothing until now. She wants to recover possession of the strip. What is her proper remedy?

alac.answer: Wilma's proper remedy is accion publiciana.
alac.basis: Under Rule 70 of the Rules of Court, an action for forcible entry must be filed within one year from the unlawful deprivation, counted from discovery when entry was by stealth. When dispossession has lasted more than one year, the remedy is accion publiciana, a plenary action to recover the better right of possession, filed in the court that has jurisdiction based on the assessed value of the property. Article 428 of the Civil Code gives the owner a right of action against the holder and possessor of the thing to recover it.
alac.application: Here, Vina entered by stealth, and Wilma discovered the entry two years ago. More than one year has passed, so forcible entry is no longer available. Wilma must instead file accion publiciana to recover the better right of possession of the strip.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Wilma should file an accion publiciana in the court with jurisdiction over the assessed value of the strip.

keyPoints: Forcible entry must be filed within one year from discovery (stealth)
After one year: accion publiciana
Recovers the better right of possession
cite: Civil Code, Art. 428; Rules of Court, Rule 70

q: Under Article 434 of the Civil Code, in an action to recover property (accion reivindicatoria), the plaintiff must:
choices: Rely on the weakness of the defendant's claim
Identify the property and rely on the strength of his own title
Prove that the defendant is in bad faith
hints: The plaintiff carries the burden.
Two requirements: identity and title.
why: Art. 434: the property must be identified, and the plaintiff must rely on the strength of his title and not on the weakness of the defendant's claim.

q: Xander sued Yoyong to recover ownership of a parcel of land. Xander presented no deed or title of his own, but proved that Yoyong's tax declarations were irregular and that Yoyong had no title either. Should Xander win?

alac.answer: No, Xander should not win.
alac.basis: Article 434 of the Civil Code provides that in an action to recover, the property must be identified, and the plaintiff must rely on the strength of his title and not on the weakness of the defendant's claim. An accion reivindicatoria is an action to recover ownership.
alac.application: Here, Xander filed an action to recover ownership but did not prove his own title. He relied only on the weakness of Yoyong's claim. Even if Yoyong has no title, that does not prove that Xander owns the land.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Xander's action should be dismissed for failure to prove his own title.

keyPoints: Accion reivindicatoria recovers ownership
Plaintiff must rely on the strength of his own title (Art. 434)
Weakness of the defendant's claim is not enough

q: Under Article 562 of the Civil Code, usufruct gives the right to:
choices: Enjoy the property of another with the obligation of preserving its form and substance, unless the title or law provides otherwise
hints: The usufructuary enjoys but does not own.
Form and substance must be preserved.
why: Art. 562: usufruct gives a right to enjoy the property of another with the obligation of preserving its form and substance, unless the title constituting it or the law otherwise provides.

q: Yolly granted her friend Zeny a usufruct over her apartment building for 20 years. Five years later, Zeny died. Zeny's children claim the right to continue collecting the rents for the remaining 15 years. Are they correct?

alac.answer: No, Zeny's children are not correct. The usufruct ended with Zeny's death.
alac.basis: Article 603(1) of the Civil Code provides that usufruct is extinguished by the death of the usufructuary, unless a contrary intention clearly appears. Article 566 entitles the usufructuary to the natural, industrial and civil fruits, such as rents, only while the usufruct lasts.
alac.application: Here, the usufruct was granted to Zeny for 20 years, but nothing shows a clear intention that it would pass to her heirs. Her death extinguished the usufruct, even though the 20-year period had not yet expired.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the right to the rents reverts to Yolly, and Zeny's children have no right to continue collecting them.

keyPoints: Usufruct is extinguished by the death of the usufructuary (Art. 603(1))
Unless a contrary intention clearly appears
Rents are civil fruits belonging to the usufructuary only while the usufruct lasts (Art. 566)

q: Under Article 613 of the Civil Code, an easement is an encumbrance imposed upon an immovable for the benefit of:
choices: Another immovable belonging to a different owner
Any person who asks for it
hints: The estate that benefits is the dominant estate.
The two estates must have different owners.
why: Art. 613: an easement is an encumbrance imposed upon an immovable for the benefit of another immovable belonging to a different owner; the benefited estate is dominant, the burdened one servient.

q: Mario owned two adjoining lots. On Lot A he built a house with windows overlooking Lot B, less than two meters from the boundary. He later sold Lot B to Nestor; the deed said nothing about the windows, and the windows were not closed before the sale. Nestor now demands that Mario close the windows. Must Mario do so?

alac.answer: No, Mario need not close the windows. An easement of light and view was created.
alac.basis: Article 624 of the Civil Code provides that the existence of an apparent sign of easement between two estates, established or maintained by the owner of both, shall be considered, should either of them be alienated, as a title in order that the easement may continue actively and passively, unless, at the time the ownership of the two estates is divided, the contrary is provided in the title of conveyance, or the sign is removed before the execution of the deed.
alac.application: Here, Mario, as owner of both lots, made the windows of Lot A overlook Lot B. The windows are an apparent sign of an easement. When he sold Lot B, the deed did not provide otherwise, and the windows were not closed before the sale.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the apparent sign serves as a title, and an easement of light and view in favor of Lot A exists over Lot B.

keyPoints: Apparent sign established by the owner of both estates (Art. 624)
Serves as title upon alienation of either estate
Unless the deed provides otherwise or the sign is removed before the sale

q: Under Article 637 of the Civil Code, lower estates are obliged to receive the waters which:
choices: Naturally and without the intervention of man descend from higher estates
Come from factories on higher estates
Are diverted by the owner of the higher estate
hints: This is the natural drainage easement.
Man-made flows are not covered.
why: Art. 637: lower estates must receive the waters which naturally and without the intervention of man descend from higher estates, with the stones or earth they carry.

q: Rain water naturally flows from Olga's hillside farm down to Pablo's lower farm. Pablo built a concrete wall that blocks the flow, flooding Olga's farm. Meanwhile, Olga dug a canal that channels more water onto Pablo's land than before. What are their respective rights?

alac.answer: Pablo must remove the wall, and Olga must undo the canal.
alac.basis: Article 637 of the Civil Code provides that lower estates are obliged to receive the waters which naturally and without the intervention of man descend from the higher estates. The owner of the lower estate cannot construct works which will impede this easement; neither can the owner of the higher estate make works which will increase the burden.
alac.application: Here, Pablo's farm is the lower estate, so it must receive the rain water that naturally flows from Olga's farm. His wall impedes this easement. On the other hand, Olga's canal increases the burden on Pablo's land beyond the natural flow.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Pablo may be compelled to remove the wall, and Olga may be compelled to remove or modify the canal so that only the natural flow reaches Pablo's land.

keyPoints: Lower estate must receive natural flow (Art. 637)
Lower owner cannot impede the easement
Higher owner cannot increase the burden

q: Under Article 650 of the Civil Code, the easement of right of way shall be established:
choices: At the point least prejudicial to the servient estate and, as far as consistent with this, where the distance to the highway is shortest
Always at the shortest distance regardless of damage
hints: Least prejudice comes first.
Shortest distance is secondary.
why: Art. 650: the right of way shall be established at the point least prejudicial to the servient estate and, insofar as consistent with this rule, where the distance to a public highway is shortest.

q: Quintin owned a large lot fronting a highway. He sold the front portion, keeping the rear portion, which became enclosed with no outlet to the highway. He then demanded a right of way through his buyer's front lot. Is he entitled to a compulsory right of way?

alac.answer: No, Quintin is not entitled to a compulsory right of way.
alac.basis: Article 649 of the Civil Code grants the owner of an immovable surrounded by other immovables and without adequate outlet to a public highway the right to demand a right of way through the neighboring estates, after payment of the proper indemnity. However, this easement is not compulsory if the isolation of the immovable is due to the proprietor's own acts.
alac.application: Here, Quintin's rear portion became enclosed only because he himself sold the front portion that gave it access to the highway. The isolation of his property is due to his own act.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Quintin cannot demand a compulsory easement of right of way; he may only negotiate a voluntary easement with the buyer.

keyPoints: Requisites of compulsory right of way (Art. 649)
Not compulsory if isolation is due to the owner's own acts
Owner sold the portion that gave access

q: Under Article 659 of the Civil Code, an easement of party wall is presumed in:
choices: Any wall built by one owner
Dividing walls of adjoining buildings up to the point of common elevation, unless there is a title, exterior sign, or proof to the contrary
Only walls registered with the Registry of Deeds
hints: The presumption can be overcome.
Common elevation is the limit for buildings.
why: Art. 659: a party wall is presumed, unless there is a title, exterior sign or proof to the contrary, in dividing walls of adjoining buildings up to the point of common elevation, in dividing walls of gardens or yards, and in fences dividing rural lands.

q: The dividing wall between the adjoining two-storey houses of Romy and Sara cracked and needed P100,000 in repairs. There is no title or sign showing who owns the wall. Romy refuses to contribute, saying the wall is Sara's. Sara's house leans on the wall, while Romy's does not. Who should pay for the repairs?

alac.answer: Both should share the repairs in proportion to their rights, unless Romy renounces his part-ownership of the wall.
alac.basis: Article 659 of the Civil Code presumes a party wall in dividing walls of adjoining buildings up to the point of common elevation, unless there is a title, exterior sign or proof to the contrary. Article 662 provides that the cost of repairs of party walls shall be borne by all the owners having the party wall in their favor, in proportion to the right of each; nevertheless, any owner may exempt himself by renouncing his part-ownership, except when the party wall supports a building belonging to him.
alac.application: Here, there is no title or sign to the contrary, so the dividing wall between the two houses is presumed a party wall. Romy and Sara must share the cost of repairs. Romy may avoid contributing by renouncing his part-ownership, since the wall does not support his house. Sara cannot do so because the wall supports her house.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the repair cost is shared in proportion to their rights, unless Romy renounces his share in the wall, in which case Sara bears it alone.

keyPoints: Party wall presumed between adjoining buildings (Art. 659)
Repairs shared in proportion to each owner's right (Art. 662)
An owner may renounce, except when the wall supports his building

q: Under Article 670 of the Civil Code, windows with a DIRECT view toward an adjoining land must be at least how far from that property?
hints: Side or oblique views need less distance.
Direct views need more.
why: Art. 670: no windows or similar openings with a direct view upon an adjoining land can be made without leaving two meters; side or oblique views require sixty centimeters. Non-observance does not give rise to prescription.

q: In 2010, Tess built her house with a large window giving a direct view of Ursula's yard, only one meter from the boundary. Ursula did not object until 2025, when she demanded that the window be closed. Tess argues that after fifteen years she has acquired an easement by prescription. Is Tess correct?

alac.answer: No, Tess is not correct. She may be compelled to close or move the window.
alac.basis: Article 670 of the Civil Code prohibits windows that afford a direct view upon an adjoining land without leaving a distance of two meters between the wall and the adjoining property, and provides that the nonobservance of these distances does not give rise to prescription.
alac.application: Here, Tess's window gives a direct view of Ursula's yard but is only one meter from the boundary, violating the two-meter rule. Because the law expressly states that non-observance of the distance does not give rise to prescription, the fifteen years of use gave Tess no easement.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ursula may demand that the window be closed or brought into compliance with the required distance.

keyPoints: Two meters for direct views (Art. 670)
Non-observance does not give rise to prescription
Owner may demand closure

q: Under Article 622 of the Civil Code, discontinuous easements (such as a right of way), whether apparent or not, may be acquired:
choices: Only by virtue of a title
hints: Discontinuous easements depend on acts of man and are used at intervals.
Prescription is not available for them.
why: Art. 622: continuous non-apparent easements and discontinuous ones, whether apparent or not, may be acquired only by virtue of a title. Continuous and apparent easements may be acquired by title or by prescription of ten years (Art. 620).

q: For 25 years, with the tolerance of his neighbor, Victor walked across the neighbor's land along a worn path to reach the river. The neighbor's new owner fenced the path. Victor claims a voluntary easement of right of way acquired by prescription. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, Victor did not acquire a right of way by prescription.
alac.basis: Article 688 of the Civil Code allows owners to establish voluntary easements as they deem suitable, provided they do not contravene the law, public policy or public order. Article 615 defines discontinuous easements as those used at intervals and dependent on the acts of man. Article 622 provides that discontinuous easements, whether apparent or not, may be acquired only by virtue of a title.
alac.application: Here, a right of way is used only when Victor walks across the land, so it is a discontinuous easement, even if the worn path makes it apparent. Such an easement cannot be acquired by prescription, however long the use, and Victor has no title. His use was by mere tolerance.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Victor has no easement, and the new owner may fence the path, unless Victor can establish a compulsory right of way under the requisites of law.

keyPoints: Right of way is a discontinuous easement (Art. 615)
Discontinuous easements acquired only by title (Art. 622)
Use by tolerance creates no right

q: Under Article 695 of the Civil Code, a public nuisance is one that:
choices: Affects a community or neighborhood or any considerable number of persons
hints: The test is how many people it affects.
The extent of harm to individuals may be unequal.
why: Art. 695: a public nuisance affects a community or neighborhood or any considerable number of persons, even if the extent of the annoyance on individuals is unequal; others are private nuisances.

q: A large piggery in the middle of a residential subdivision emits foul odors that sicken many residents. The homeowners' association asks what remedies are available, and whether residents who suffered damage before the piggery is closed can still recover. Advise them.

alac.answer: The piggery is a public nuisance; the remedies are prosecution, a civil action, or abatement, and abatement does not bar recovery of damages for its past existence.
alac.basis: Article 694 of the Civil Code defines a nuisance as anything which, among others, injures or endangers the health or safety of others or annoys or offends the senses. Article 695 classifies as public a nuisance that affects a community or neighborhood. Article 699 provides that the remedies against a public nuisance are a prosecution under the Penal Code or any local ordinance, a civil action, or abatement without judicial proceedings. Article 697 provides that the abatement of a nuisance does not preclude the right of any person injured to recover damages for its past existence.
alac.application: Here, the piggery's odors offend the senses and endanger the health of many residents of the subdivision, so it is a public nuisance. The association may seek prosecution under the applicable law or ordinance, file a civil action, or have it abated through the proper authorities. Residents who were injured may still claim damages for the period before abatement.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the piggery may be abated or stopped through the remedies in Article 699, and the injured residents may still recover damages under Article 697.

keyPoints: Nuisance: injures health or offends the senses (Art. 694)
Public nuisance affects a community (Art. 695)
Remedies (Art. 699); damages despite abatement (Art. 697)

q: Under Article 714 of the Civil Code, can ownership of a piece of land be acquired by occupation?
choices: No, the ownership of a piece of land cannot be acquired by occupation
hints: Occupation applies to things without an owner.
Land without a private owner belongs to the State.
why: Art. 714: ownership of land cannot be acquired by occupation. Occupation applies to things appropriable by nature which are without an owner (Art. 713).

q: Walking home, Yuri found an old wooden chair left beside the street with a sign saying "FREE - PLEASE TAKE." He took it home. The next day, the former owner's son demanded it back, saying his father had no right to give it away. Who owns the chair?

alac.answer: Yuri owns the chair.
alac.basis: Article 713 of the Civil Code provides that things appropriable by nature which are without an owner, such as abandoned movables, are acquired by occupation. Article 712 lists occupation as a mode of acquiring ownership.
alac.application: Here, the chair was a movable that its owner deliberately abandoned, as shown by leaving it on the street with a sign inviting anyone to take it. It became a thing without an owner. Yuri took possession of it with the intention of making it his own.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Yuri acquired ownership of the chair by occupation, and the former owner's son cannot recover it.

keyPoints: Occupation is a mode of acquiring ownership (Art. 712)
Abandoned movables are acquired by occupation (Art. 713)
Abandonment shown by the owner's acts

q: Under Article 1477 of the Civil Code, ownership of the thing sold is transferred to the buyer:
hints: In our law, a contract alone does not transfer ownership.
Tradition (delivery) is the mode.
why: Art. 1477: ownership of the thing sold is transferred to the vendee upon actual or constructive delivery.

q: Aldo sold his unregistered lot to Bella in a notarized deed of sale. The deed did not reserve ownership or possession to Aldo, but Aldo continued to live on the lot for three months more, with Bella's consent. Before Aldo moved out, his creditor levied on the lot as Aldo's property. Who owned the lot at the time of the levy?

alac.answer: Bella owned the lot.
alac.basis: Article 1477 of the Civil Code provides that ownership of the thing sold is transferred to the vendee upon actual or constructive delivery. Article 1498 provides that when the sale is made through a public instrument, the execution thereof shall be equivalent to the delivery of the thing, if from the deed the contrary does not appear or cannot clearly be inferred.
alac.application: Here, the sale was made through a notarized deed, a public instrument, and nothing in the deed shows a contrary intention. Its execution was constructive delivery, which transferred ownership to Bella. Aldo's continued stay was merely with Bella's permission.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the lot already belonged to Bella when Aldo's creditor levied on it, and the levy cannot reach it as Aldo's property.

keyPoints: Ownership passes by delivery (Art. 1477)
Execution of a public instrument is constructive delivery (Art. 1498)
Unless the contrary appears in the deed

q: Under Article 725 of the Civil Code, donation is:
choices: A sale at a low price
An act of liberality whereby a person disposes gratuitously of a thing or right in favor of another, who accepts it
A transfer that needs no acceptance
hints: Donation is gratuitous.
Acceptance is required.
why: Art. 725: donation is an act of liberality whereby a person disposes gratuitously of a thing or right in favor of another, who accepts it.

q: Carmen donated a lot to her niece Dina in a private document signed by both of them, in which Dina accepted the donation. After Carmen's death, her heirs claimed the lot. Dina argues that the donation is valid because she accepted it in writing during Carmen's lifetime. Is the donation valid?

alac.answer: No, the donation is void.
alac.basis: Article 749 of the Civil Code provides that in order that the donation of an immovable may be valid, it must be made in a public document, specifying the property donated and the value of the charges the donee must satisfy, and the acceptance may be made in the same deed or in a separate public document during the lifetime of the donor.
alac.application: Here, the donation of the lot, an immovable, was made only in a private document. The requirement of a public document is essential for the validity of a donation of immovable property. Dina's written acceptance during Carmen's lifetime does not cure the defect in form.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the donation is void, and the lot forms part of Carmen's estate.

keyPoints: Donation of immovable must be in a public document (Art. 749)
Formal requirement is essential for validity
Acceptance during the donor's lifetime does not cure the defect

q: Under Article 1134 of the Civil Code, ordinary acquisitive prescription of immovable property requires possession in good faith and with just title for:
hints: Ordinary prescription is shorter because of good faith and just title.
Extraordinary prescription is 30 years (Art. 1137).
why: Art. 1134: ownership of immovables is acquired by ordinary prescription through possession of ten years; extraordinary prescription requires thirty years without title or good faith (Art. 1137).

q: In 1990, Edgar, knowing he had no title, fenced and occupied an unregistered private lot belonging to Fidel. He possessed it openly, peacefully, continuously and as owner. In 2024, Fidel sued to recover the lot. Who should prevail?

alac.answer: Edgar should prevail. He acquired the lot by extraordinary acquisitive prescription.
alac.basis: Article 1118 of the Civil Code requires possession in the concept of an owner, public, peaceful and uninterrupted. Article 1137 provides that ownership over immovables prescribes through uninterrupted adverse possession for thirty years, without need of title or of good faith. Under Section 47 of PD 1529, registered land cannot be acquired by prescription, but this lot is unregistered.
alac.application: Here, Edgar was in bad faith and had no title, so ordinary prescription is not available. But he possessed the unregistered lot as owner, openly, peacefully and without interruption from 1990. By 2020, thirty years had passed, before Fidel sued in 2024.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Edgar became the owner by extraordinary acquisitive prescription, and Fidel's action should be dismissed.

keyPoints: Possession must be as owner, public, peaceful, uninterrupted (Art. 1118)
Extraordinary prescription: 30 years, no title or good faith needed (Art. 1137)
Not available for registered land (PD 1529, Sec. 47)
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 1118 and 1137; PD 1529, Sec. 47

q: Under the Regalian doctrine (1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Sec. 2), lands of the public domain are:
choices: Owned by whoever occupies them first
Owned by the local government where they are located
hints: The doctrine traces back to the Spanish Crown.
All lands not clearly private are presumed to belong to the State.
why: Art. XII, Sec. 2: all lands of the public domain and other natural resources are owned by the State; with the exception of agricultural lands, they shall not be alienated.

q: Ruben applied for original registration of a parcel of land he has occupied for 30 years. His only proof that the land is alienable and disposable is a certification from the local CENRO. The Republic opposes. Should registration be granted?

alac.answer: No, registration should not be granted on that evidence alone.
alac.basis: Under the Regalian doctrine in Article XII, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution, all lands of the public domain belong to the State, and all lands not otherwise appearing to be clearly within private ownership are presumed to belong to the State. The applicant for registration bears the burden of proving that the land has been classified as alienable and disposable. In Republic v. T.A.N. Properties, Inc., G.R. No. 154953, June 26, 2008, the Supreme Court held that a CENRO certification alone is not enough; the applicant must also prove that the DENR Secretary approved the land classification and released the land as alienable and disposable, through a certified true copy of the original classification.
alac.application: Here, Ruben relies only on a CENRO certification. He has not presented a copy of the original classification approved by the DENR Secretary showing that the land is alienable and disposable. The presumption that the land belongs to the State has not been overcome, however long he has occupied it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ruben's application should be denied for failure to prove that the land is alienable and disposable.

keyPoints: Regalian doctrine: presumption of State ownership (Const., Art. XII, Sec. 2)
Applicant must prove the land is alienable and disposable
CENRO certification alone is insufficient (Republic v. T.A.N. Properties)
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Sec. 2; Republic v. T.A.N. Properties, Inc., G.R. No. 154953, June 26, 2008

q: Under Article XII, Section 8 of the 1987 Constitution, a natural-born Filipino who has lost Philippine citizenship:
choices: Can never own land in the Philippines
May be a transferee of private lands, subject to limitations provided by law
May own land only by inheritance
hints: Section 8 is an exception to Section 7.
Congress sets the limits.
why: Art. XII, Sec. 8: notwithstanding Sec. 7, a natural-born citizen who has lost Philippine citizenship may be a transferee of private lands, subject to limitations provided by law.

q: Lorna, born a Filipino, became an American citizen. She wants to buy a residential lot in Cebu. Her American husband, Mike, who is not a former Filipino, also wants to buy a lot in his own name. Separately, Mike's Filipino father-in-law died and left him, by will, a parcel of land. Can Lorna and Mike acquire these lots?

alac.answer: Lorna may buy a lot within the limits set by law; Mike cannot buy a lot, nor acquire one by will.
alac.basis: Article XII, Section 7 of the 1987 Constitution provides that, save in cases of hereditary succession, no private lands shall be transferred or conveyed except to individuals, corporations, or associations qualified to acquire or hold lands of the public domain, that is, Filipino citizens and qualified corporations. Section 8 allows a natural-born citizen who has lost Philippine citizenship to be a transferee of private lands, subject to limitations provided by law. The exception for hereditary succession refers to intestate succession, not to testamentary dispositions.
alac.application: Here, Lorna is a former natural-born Filipino, so she may buy a residential lot, but only within the area limits set by law. Mike was never a Filipino, so he cannot buy land. As to the land left to him by will, the hereditary succession exception covers only intestate succession, so a devise to a foreigner is not allowed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Lorna may acquire the Cebu lot subject to statutory limits, while Mike cannot acquire either lot.

keyPoints: Aliens cannot acquire private lands, save by hereditary succession (Sec. 7)
Former natural-born Filipinos may be transferees, within legal limits (Sec. 8)
Hereditary succession means intestate succession

q: Under Section 31 of PD 1529, the decree of registration:
choices: Binds only the parties who appeared in the case
Binds the land, quiets title to it, and is conclusive upon all persons, including the Government
May be ignored by the Government
Is valid only for ten years
hints: Land registration is a proceeding in rem.
Notice is addressed "To all whom it may concern."
why: PD 1529, Sec. 31: the decree binds the land and quiets title, subject only to exceptions or liens provided by law, and is conclusive upon all persons, including the National Government, whether named in the application or not.

q: A decree of registration was issued in favor of Sonny after due publication. Two years later, Tina, who was not named in the application and did not receive personal notice, claimed that she owns part of the land and that the decree does not bind her. Is she correct?

alac.answer: No, Tina is bound by the decree.
alac.basis: Section 31 of PD 1529 provides that the decree of registration shall bind the land and quiet title thereto, and that it shall be conclusive upon and against all persons, including the National Government and all branches thereof, whether mentioned by name in the application or notice, the same being included in the general description "To all whom it may concern." Land registration is a proceeding in rem.
alac.application: Here, the decree was issued after due publication, which is notice to the whole world. Tina is included in the general description "To all whom it may concern," even if she was not named or personally notified. More than one year has also passed since the entry of the decree.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the decree binds Tina, and she can no longer question Sonny's registered title in that proceeding.

keyPoints: Registration proceeding is in rem
Decree conclusive upon all persons, named or not (PD 1529, Sec. 31)
Publication is notice to all

q: Under Section 32 of PD 1529, a petition to reopen and review a decree of registration on the ground of actual fraud must be filed:
choices: Not later than one year from the entry of the decree, and not when an innocent purchaser for value has acquired the land
Within four years from discovery of the fraud
hints: After this period, the title becomes incontrovertible.
Innocent purchasers are protected.
why: PD 1529, Sec. 32: a person deprived of land by a decree obtained through actual fraud may petition for review within one year from entry of the decree, but not where an innocent purchaser for value has acquired the land.

q: Ulysses obtained a decree of registration over Vilma's land by falsely declaring that he was its owner and in possession. Vilma discovered this two years after the entry of the decree. Ulysses still holds the title. What is Vilma's remedy?

alac.answer: Vilma can no longer petition for review of the decree, but she may file an action for reconveyance against Ulysses.
alac.basis: Section 32 of PD 1529 allows a petition to reopen and review a decree obtained by actual fraud only within one year from the entry of the decree; after that, the decree and the certificate of title become incontrovertible, but any person aggrieved may pursue his remedy by action for damages against the applicant or any other person responsible for the fraud. Under Article 1456 of the Civil Code, a person who acquires property through fraud is considered a trustee of an implied trust for the benefit of the person from whom the property comes, and the action for reconveyance based on such implied trust prescribes in ten years.
alac.application: Here, more than one year has passed from the entry of the decree, so a petition for review is barred. However, Ulysses obtained the title through fraud and still holds it; no innocent purchaser for value is involved. He holds the land in trust for Vilma.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Vilma may file an action for reconveyance against Ulysses within ten years, or an action for damages.

keyPoints: Petition for review: within one year from entry, for actual fraud (PD 1529, Sec. 32)
After one year, title is incontrovertible
Reconveyance based on implied trust (Civil Code, Art. 1456) if no innocent purchaser

q: Under Section 32 of PD 1529, the phrase "innocent purchaser for value" includes:
choices: Only buyers who paid in cash
An innocent lessee, mortgagee, or other encumbrancer for value
hints: The law protects those who rely on the title and give value.
It covers more than buyers.
why: PD 1529, Sec. 32: the phrase "innocent purchaser for value" is deemed to include an innocent lessee, mortgagee, or other encumbrancer for value.

q: Juan's land was registered in his name. Pedro forged Juan's signature on a deed of sale to himself and obtained a new title in his own name. Pedro then sold the land to Maria, who checked the title in the Registry of Deeds, found it clean and in Pedro's name, inspected the land, and paid the full price. Can Juan recover the land from Maria?

alac.answer: No, Juan cannot recover the land from Maria.
alac.basis: Section 44 of PD 1529 provides that every subsequent purchaser of registered land taking a certificate of title for value and in good faith shall hold the same free from all encumbrances except those noted in the certificate and those provided by law. Under Section 32, the rights of an innocent purchaser for value are protected. Under the mirror principle, a person dealing with registered land may rely on the correctness of the certificate of title.
