A forged deed is void, but an innocent purchaser for value who buys from a registered owner may acquire a good title.
alac.application: Here, Pedro's title came from a forged deed, but Maria bought from Pedro when the land was already registered in his name. She checked the title and found it clean, inspected the land, and paid the full price. She is an innocent purchaser for value.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Maria's title is protected; Juan's remedies are against Pedro for damages and, if Pedro cannot pay, against the Assurance Fund.

keyPoints: Innocent purchaser for value takes the title free of unnoted claims (PD 1529, Sec. 44)
Mirror principle: reliance on the certificate of title
Defrauded owner's remedy: damages and the Assurance Fund

q: Under Section 14(1) of PD 1529, as amended by RA 11573, an applicant for original registration of alienable and disposable public land must show open, continuous, exclusive and notorious possession under a bona fide claim of ownership for at least:
choices: Twenty years immediately preceding the filing of the application
hints: RA 11573 replaced the old June 12, 1945 cut-off.
The period counts back from the filing of the application.
why: PD 1529, Sec. 14(1), as amended by RA 11573: at least twenty years immediately preceding the filing of the application, except when prevented by war or force majeure.
cite: PD 1529, Sec. 14(1), as amended by RA 11573, Sec. 6

q: Since 2002, Cesar has openly, continuously and exclusively possessed, as owner, a lot that the DENR had classified as alienable and disposable in 1990, and which is not covered by any title. In 2023 he applied for original registration. The Republic opposes, arguing that he must prove possession since June 12, 1945. Who is correct?

alac.answer: Cesar is correct. His application may be granted.
alac.basis: Section 14(1) of PD 1529, as amended by RA 11573, allows those who by themselves or through their predecessors-in-interest have been in open, continuous, exclusive and notorious possession and occupation of alienable and disposable lands of the public domain not covered by existing certificates of title or patents, under a bona fide claim of ownership, for at least twenty years immediately preceding the filing of the application, to apply for registration. They are conclusively presumed to have performed all the conditions essential to a Government grant.
alac.application: Here, the lot was classified as alienable and disposable in 1990 and is untitled. Cesar has possessed it in the manner required by law since 2002, which is more than twenty years before he applied in 2023. Under the amended law, he no longer needs to prove possession since June 12, 1945.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Cesar's application for original registration should be granted, upon proof of the land's classification.

keyPoints: Twenty years of qualified possession before filing (PD 1529, Sec. 14(1), as amended by RA 11573)
Land must be alienable and disposable and untitled
June 12, 1945 cut-off replaced
cite: PD 1529, Sec. 14(1), as amended by RA 11573

q: Under Section 48(a) of CA 141, as amended by RA 11573, those who meet the possession requirements over alienable and disposable agricultural public lands are:
choices: Conclusively presumed to have performed all the conditions essential to a Government grant and entitled to a certificate of title
hints: This is judicial confirmation of imperfect title.
The law treats them as if the State had already granted the land.
why: CA 141, Sec. 48(a), as amended by RA 11573: they are conclusively presumed to have performed all the conditions essential to a Government grant and are entitled to a certificate of title.
cite: CA 141, Sec. 48(a), as amended by RA 11573, Sec. 5

q: For 25 years, Danilo has openly and continuously cultivated, as owner, a parcel on a mountainside. The land has never been released from its classification as forest land. He petitions for judicial confirmation of imperfect title under Section 48 of CA 141, as amended. Will the petition prosper?

alac.answer: No, the petition will not prosper.
alac.basis: Section 48(a) of CA 141, as amended by RA 11573, allows judicial confirmation of title only over alienable and disposable agricultural lands of the public domain, possessed in the required manner for at least twenty years immediately preceding the filing of the application. Under Article XII, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution, with the exception of agricultural lands, natural resources such as forest lands shall not be alienated.
alac.application: Here, although Danilo has possessed the land for 25 years, the land is still classified as forest land. It has never been declared alienable and disposable agricultural land. Possession of forest land, however long, cannot ripen into private ownership.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Danilo's petition for judicial confirmation of imperfect title should be denied.

keyPoints: Only alienable and disposable agricultural land may be confirmed (CA 141, Sec. 48(a), as amended)
Forest land is inalienable (Const., Art. XII, Sec. 2)
Length of possession does not matter for forest land
cite: CA 141, Sec. 48(a), as amended by RA 11573; 1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Sec. 2

q: Under Section 48 of PD 1529, a certificate of title:
choices: May be attacked in any proceeding
Shall not be subject to collateral attack and may be altered, modified or cancelled only in a direct proceeding
May be cancelled by the Register of Deeds at will
hints: The validity of a title must be the main issue of the case.
A defense in an ejectment case is not a direct proceeding.
why: PD 1529, Sec. 48: a certificate of title shall not be subject to collateral attack; it cannot be altered, modified or cancelled except in a direct proceeding in accordance with law.

q: Ellen, the registered owner of a lot, sued Fred for unlawful detainer. In his answer, Fred argued that Ellen's title should be declared void because it was obtained through fraud. Can the court cancel Ellen's title in the ejectment case?

alac.answer: No, the court cannot cancel Ellen's title in the ejectment case.
alac.basis: Section 48 of PD 1529 provides that a certificate of title shall not be subject to collateral attack, and it cannot be altered, modified or canceled except in a direct proceeding in accordance with law. An ejectment case involves only physical possession; questions of ownership are resolved only provisionally to determine possession.
alac.application: Here, Fred raises the validity of Ellen's title merely as a defense in an unlawful detainer case, whose main issue is possession. This is a collateral attack on the title, which the law prohibits. To nullify the title, Fred must file a direct action, such as an action for annulment or reconveyance.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court cannot declare Ellen's title void in the ejectment case; Fred must bring a separate direct action.

keyPoints: Title not subject to collateral attack (PD 1529, Sec. 48)
Ejectment involves possession only
Direct action needed to cancel a title

q: Under Section 51 of PD 1529, as far as third persons are concerned, the operative act that conveys or affects registered land is:
hints: Between the parties, the deed is a contract.
Against the world, something more is needed.
why: PD 1529, Sec. 51: a deed or other voluntary instrument operates only as a contract between the parties; the act of registration is the operative act to convey or affect the land insofar as third persons are concerned.

q: Gerry sold his registered lot to Hilda in a notarized deed, but Hilda did not register the sale. A month later, Gerry's creditor, Ike, who did not know of the sale, obtained a writ of attachment against the lot and had it annotated on Gerry's title. Who has the better right: Hilda or Ike?

alac.answer: Ike has the better right as against Hilda.
alac.basis: Section 51 of PD 1529 provides that no deed or other voluntary instrument shall take effect as a conveyance or bind the land, but shall operate only as a contract between the parties; the act of registration is the operative act to convey or affect the land insofar as third persons are concerned. Section 52 provides that every instrument or entry affecting registered land, if registered, is constructive notice to all persons from the time of registration.
alac.application: Here, the unregistered sale binds Gerry and Hilda as a contract, but it does not affect third persons like Ike, who did not know of it. Ike's attachment, on the other hand, was registered and annotated on the title, which is constructive notice to all.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ike's registered attachment prevails over Hilda's unregistered sale, and the lot may answer for Gerry's debt to Ike.

keyPoints: Unregistered deed binds only the parties (PD 1529, Sec. 51)
Registration is the operative act against third persons
Registered attachment is constructive notice (Sec. 52)

q: Under Section 76 of PD 1529, what is the effect of failing to register a notice of lis pendens in a case affecting title to registered land?
choices: The case and any judgment have no effect upon the registered land as against persons other than the parties
hints: Lis pendens warns buyers of a pending case.
Without it, third persons are not bound.
why: PD 1529, Sec. 76: actions directly affecting title to or possession of registered land have no effect against persons other than the parties unless a notice of lis pendens is filed and registered.

q: Jaime sued Karen to annul her title to a lot and had a notice of lis pendens annotated on the title. While the case was pending, Karen sold the lot to Leo, who saw the annotation but bought anyway. Jaime won the case. Is Leo bound by the judgment?

alac.answer: Yes, Leo is bound by the judgment.
alac.basis: Section 76 of PD 1529 provides that no action directly affecting the title to registered land shall have any effect upon the land as against persons other than the parties, unless a notice of lis pendens is filed and registered. Once registered, the notice is constructive notice to all persons (Section 52), and anyone who acquires the land while it is annotated takes it subject to the outcome of the case.
alac.application: Here, Jaime's action directly affected Karen's title, and the notice of lis pendens was annotated before Leo bought the lot. Leo knew of the pending case, and in any event the annotation was notice to him. He therefore bought the lot subject to the result of the litigation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Leo is bound by the judgment in Jaime's favor and cannot claim to be an innocent purchaser for value.

keyPoints: Lis pendens binds third persons to the outcome (PD 1529, Sec. 76)
Registered notice is constructive notice (Sec. 52)
Buyer with notice is not an innocent purchaser

q: Which of the following CANNOT be registered under the Torrens system in the name of a private person?
choices: A residential lot bought from a private owner
Foreshore land and river banks (property of public dominion under Art. 420)
Land acquired by inheritance from a registered owner
Alienable and disposable land possessed for 20 years
hints: Public dominion property is outside the commerce of men.
Art. 420 lists banks and shores.
why: Civil Code, Art. 420: property of public dominion, such as roads, rivers, banks and shores, cannot be registered in the name of private persons.

q: In 1995, Melvin obtained a Torrens title over a strip of foreshore land along Manila Bay. In 2025, the Republic sued to cancel the title. Melvin argues that his title has become incontrovertible and that the action has prescribed. Decide.

alac.answer: The title should be cancelled; the Republic's action has not prescribed.
alac.basis: Article 420 of the Civil Code makes shores and similar property intended for public use property of public dominion, which is outside the commerce of men and cannot be registered. Article 1113 provides that property of the State not patrimonial in character shall not be the object of prescription. A title issued over land of public dominion is void, and the State's action to recover it is imprescriptible.
alac.application: Here, the strip is foreshore land, property of public dominion. It could not have been validly registered in Melvin's name, so his title is void from the beginning. The rule on incontrovertibility after one year does not apply to a void title over non-registrable land, and prescription does not run against the State over public dominion.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should cancel Melvin's title and revert the foreshore land to the State.

keyPoints: Shores are property of public dominion (Art. 420)
Not registrable; a title over it is void
Not subject to prescription (Art. 1113)

q: Under Section 113 of PD 1529, a deed affecting land NOT registered under the Torrens system that is not recorded in the Registry of Deeds is:
hints: Recording affects third persons.
Between the parties, the contract still binds.
why: PD 1529, Sec. 113: no voluntary instrument affecting unregistered land shall be valid, except as between the parties, unless recorded in the Registry of Deeds; recording is without prejudice to a third party with a better right.

q: Nora owned an unregistered lot. In 2020, she sold it to Oscar in a notarized deed, which Oscar did not record. In 2022, Nora sold the same lot to Paula, who promptly recorded her deed in the Registry of Deeds under Section 113 of PD 1529. Who has the better right to the lot?

alac.answer: Oscar has the better right.
alac.basis: Section 113 of PD 1529 provides that instruments affecting unregistered land are valid only between the parties unless recorded, but that any recording made under that section shall be without prejudice to a third party with a better right. Recording of a deed of unregistered land does not by itself give a better right; under the principle that no one can give what he does not have, a seller who has already sold the land has nothing left to sell.
alac.application: Here, Nora sold the lot to Oscar first, in 2020, through a notarized deed, which transferred ownership to him. When Nora sold the same lot to Paula in 2022, she was no longer the owner. Paula's recording under Section 113 is without prejudice to Oscar, a third party with a better right.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Oscar, the first buyer, has the better right to the lot.

keyPoints: Unrecorded instrument valid between the parties (PD 1529, Sec. 113)
Recording is without prejudice to a third party with a better right
The seller had nothing left to sell to the second buyer

q: The Assurance Fund under PD 1529 is meant to:
choices: Pay the taxes of registered owners
Compensate persons who, without negligence, lose land or an interest in it through the operation of the Torrens system and are barred from recovering it
Fund the salaries of Registry personnel
hints: The Torrens system sometimes protects an innocent purchaser at the expense of the true owner.
The Fund compensates that owner.
why: PD 1529, Sec. 95: a person who, without negligence, sustains loss or is deprived of land through the Torrens system, fraud, or errors in the certificate, and is barred from recovering the land, may recover damages from the Assurance Fund.

q: Rita lost her registered land when an impostor forged her signature and sold it, through a series of registered transfers, to an innocent purchaser for value. Rita had kept her owner's duplicate title safely; the impostor used a fake one, and the Register of Deeds' staff failed to detect it. The impostor has disappeared. What remedy does Rita have?

alac.answer: Rita may recover damages from the Assurance Fund.
alac.basis: Section 95 of PD 1529 provides that a person who, without negligence on his part, sustains loss or is deprived of land or any interest therein through fraud or in consequence of any error, omission or mistake in any certificate of title or entry, and who is barred from bringing an action for the recovery of the land, may bring an action for damages to be paid out of the Assurance Fund.
alac.application: Here, Rita was deprived of her land through the fraud of the impostor. She was not negligent, as she kept her owner's duplicate safely. Because the land is now held by an innocent purchaser for value, she is barred from recovering it. The impostor, who should answer for damages, cannot be found.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Rita may file an action for damages against the Assurance Fund.

keyPoints: Loss of land through fraud or error (PD 1529, Sec. 95)
Claimant without negligence
Barred from recovering the land because of an innocent purchaser

q: Which of the following is a condition for recovery from the Assurance Fund under Section 95 of PD 1529?
choices: The claimant is barred under the law from bringing an action to recover the land
The claimant still holds the land
hints: The Fund is a last resort.
Negligence defeats the claim.
why: PD 1529, Sec. 95: the claimant must have suffered loss without negligence on his part, through the operation of the Torrens system, fraud or error, and must be barred from recovering the land.

q: Sonia gave her owner's duplicate title and a signed blank deed of sale to a stranger who promised to find her a buyer. The stranger filled in his own name, registered the sale, and resold the land to an innocent purchaser for value. Sonia now claims compensation from the Assurance Fund. Will her claim prosper?

alac.answer: No, Sonia's claim will not prosper.
alac.basis: Section 95 of PD 1529 allows recovery from the Assurance Fund only by a person who sustains loss or is deprived of land without negligence on his part, and who is barred from recovering the land.
alac.application: Here, Sonia herself handed her owner's duplicate title and a signed blank deed of sale to a stranger. Her own negligence made the fraud possible. Although she is now barred from recovering the land from the innocent purchaser, the condition that she be free from negligence is not met.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Sonia cannot recover from the Assurance Fund; her remedy is against the stranger.

keyPoints: Absence of negligence is required (PD 1529, Sec. 95)
Entrusting the title and a signed blank deed is negligence
Remedy is against the wrongdoer

q: Under Section 96 of PD 1529, if the loss arose wholly through the fraud or negligence of Registry personnel, the action against the Assurance Fund is brought against:
choices: The Register of Deeds of the province or city where the land is situated and the National Treasurer
hints: The State answers for its employees through the Fund.
Two officials are named as defendants.
why: PD 1529, Sec. 96: if the loss arose wholly through Registry personnel, the action is brought against the Register of Deeds and the National Treasurer; if others are at fault, they are joined as co-defendants.

q: Tomas lost his land to an innocent purchaser for value because a private individual, Ulric, forged his signature on a deed. No Registry employee was at fault. Tomas sues for compensation from the Assurance Fund. Whom should he name as defendants?

alac.answer: Tomas should sue the Register of Deeds, the National Treasurer, and Ulric as co-defendants.
alac.basis: Section 96 of PD 1529 provides that if the loss arises through fraud, negligence or misfeasance of a person other than court personnel, the Register of Deeds or his employees, the action shall be brought against the Register of Deeds, the National Treasurer and the other person or persons, as co-defendants. The Solicitor General defends such suits.
alac.application: Here, the loss arose from the forgery of Ulric, a private individual, and not from any fault of Registry personnel. The action must therefore include Ulric, together with the Register of Deeds and the National Treasurer.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Tomas should file his action against the Register of Deeds, the National Treasurer, and Ulric as co-defendants.

keyPoints: Fraud by a private person: Register of Deeds, National Treasurer and the wrongdoer as co-defendants (PD 1529, Sec. 96)
Fault of Registry personnel only: Register of Deeds and National Treasurer
Solicitor General defends

q: Under Section 102 of PD 1529, an action for compensation against the Assurance Fund must be instituted within:
choices: Six years from the time the right to bring the action first occurred
hints: The period is longer than one year but shorter than ten.
Persons under disability get extra time.
why: PD 1529, Sec. 102: six years from the time the right to bring the action first occurred; if the claimant was then under legal disability, within two years after the disability is removed.

q: Vivian was 12 years old when, in 2012, she lost her inherited land to an innocent purchaser for value through a forgery, giving rise to a claim against the Assurance Fund. She turned 18 in 2018. She filed her claim in 2019. Has her action prescribed?

alac.answer: No, Vivian's action has not prescribed.
alac.basis: Section 102 of PD 1529 provides that an action for compensation against the Assurance Fund shall be instituted within six years from the time the right to bring the action first occurred. However, if at that time the person entitled to bring the action was a minor or otherwise under legal disability, the action may be brought at any time within two years after the disability has been removed, notwithstanding the expiration of the original six-year period.
alac.application: Here, Vivian's right of action arose in 2012, when she was a minor. The ordinary six-year period would have ended in 2018. But since she was a minor, she had two years from reaching majority in 2018 to file. She filed in 2019, within that two-year period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Vivian's action against the Assurance Fund was filed on time.

keyPoints: Six years from accrual (PD 1529, Sec. 102)
Minor: two years after the disability is removed
Applies even if the six-year period has expired

q: Under Section 2 of RA 26, the FIRST source in the order of preference for reconstituting a lost or destroyed original certificate of title is:
choices: The owner's duplicate of the certificate of title
hints: The best evidence of the title is a copy of the title itself.
It is usually in the owner's hands.
why: RA 26, Sec. 2(a): the owner's duplicate of the certificate of title is the first source, followed by co-owner's, mortgagee's or lessee's duplicates, certified copies, and other documents in order.

q: A fire destroyed the Registry of Deeds, including the original of Wendy's original certificate of title. Wendy still has her owner's duplicate certificate. What should she do to restore her title, and where may she file?

alac.answer: Wendy should petition for reconstitution of her title based on her owner's duplicate certificate, which may be filed with the Register of Deeds or with the proper court.
alac.basis: Section 2(a) of RA 26 makes the owner's duplicate of the certificate of title the first source for reconstituting a lost or destroyed original certificate of title. Under Section 5 of RA 26, as amended, petitions for reconstitution from sources such as the owner's duplicate may be filed with the register of deeds concerned by the registered owner, accompanied by the necessary sources and an affidavit. Section 10 allows the registered owner to file such a petition directly with the proper court instead.
alac.application: Here, the original title in the Registry was destroyed, but Wendy has her owner's duplicate, the best and first source under the law. She may therefore file a petition for reconstitution with the Register of Deeds, attaching her owner's duplicate and the required affidavit, or file it directly with the proper court.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Wendy should seek reconstitution of her title based on her owner's duplicate certificate.

keyPoints: Owner's duplicate is the first source (RA 26, Sec. 2(a))
Petition may be filed with the Register of Deeds (Sec. 5, as amended)
Or directly with the proper court (Sec. 10)

q: Under Article 1441 of the Civil Code, implied trusts:
choices: Are created by the intention of the trustor
Come into being by operation of law
Must be in a public document
Do not exist in Philippine law
hints: Express trusts come from intention.
Implied trusts come from something else.
why: Art. 1441: express trusts are created by the intention of the trustor or of the parties; implied trusts come into being by operation of law.

q: Mario paid the full price of a lot, but asked that the title be issued in the name of his friend Nestor, to avoid publicity. Separately, Mario paid for another lot and had it titled in the name of his son Oscar. Later, Mario claimed both lots. Who owns each lot?

alac.answer: Mario is the beneficial owner of the lot titled to Nestor, but the lot titled to Oscar is presumed a gift to Oscar.
alac.basis: Article 1448 of the Civil Code provides that there is an implied trust when property is sold and the legal estate is granted to one party but the price is paid by another for the purpose of having the beneficial interest of the property; the former is the trustee, the latter the beneficiary. However, if the person to whom the title is conveyed is a child of the one paying the price, no trust is implied by law, it being disputably presumed that there is a gift in favor of the child.
alac.application: Here, Mario paid the price and had the first lot titled to his friend Nestor, so Nestor holds it as trustee of an implied (purchase money) trust for Mario. The second lot was titled to Mario's son, so the law presumes a gift to Oscar instead of a trust. That presumption is disputable, and Mario may rebut it with proof that he did not intend a gift.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Mario may compel Nestor to reconvey the first lot, while the second lot belongs to Oscar unless Mario proves he did not intend a gift.

keyPoints: Purchase money resulting trust (Art. 1448)
Exception: title in the name of the payor's child
Disputable presumption of a gift to the child

q: In a contract to sell, the seller:
choices: Reserves ownership until full payment of the price, which is a suspensive condition
hints: Compare with a contract of sale (Art. 1458).
Full payment is the condition that triggers the obligation to transfer title.
why: In a contract to sell, ownership is reserved by the seller and does not pass until full payment, which is a positive suspensive condition; non-payment is not a breach but prevents the obligation to convey from arising.
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1458; Coronel v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 103577, October 7, 1996

q: Quality Corp. agreed in writing to sell a commercial lot to Rex for P10 million, payable in a year, with the stipulation that title would remain with Quality Corp. and the deed of absolute sale would be executed only upon full payment. Rex paid only P3 million and stopped. Without going to court, Quality Corp. sold the lot to Sid. Rex argues that Quality Corp. first had to rescind their contract in court. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, Rex is not correct. Quality Corp. could sell the lot to Sid without judicial rescission.
alac.basis: Article 1458 of the Civil Code defines a contract of sale as one where the seller obligates himself to transfer ownership. In a contract to sell, the seller reserves ownership until full payment of the price, which is a positive suspensive condition. In Coronel v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 103577, October 7, 1996, the Supreme Court explained that in a contract to sell, the buyer's failure to pay in full is not a breach but an event that prevents the seller's obligation to convey title from arising, so there is nothing to rescind.
alac.application: Here, the parties expressly agreed that title would remain with Quality Corp. and that the deed of absolute sale would be executed only upon full payment. Their agreement is a contract to sell. Rex did not pay in full, so the suspensive condition did not happen, and Quality Corp.'s obligation to sell never arose. Being a commercial lot, the sale is also outside the Maceda Law.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Quality Corp. remained the owner and could validly sell the lot to Sid without first rescinding its contract with Rex in court.

keyPoints: Contract to sell: ownership reserved until full payment
Non-payment is the non-happening of a suspensive condition, not a breach (Coronel v. CA)
No judicial rescission needed; commercial lot outside the Maceda Law
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1458; Coronel v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 103577, October 7, 1996

q: Under Article 1479 of the Civil Code, an accepted unilateral promise to sell a determinate thing for a price certain binds the promisor if:
choices: It is supported by a consideration distinct from the price
It is in a private document
hints: This is an option contract.
The option needs its own consideration.
why: Art. 1479, par. 2: an accepted unilateral promise to buy or sell a determinate thing for a price certain binds the promisor if supported by a consideration distinct from the price.

q: On 1 March, Tess wrote Ulay: "I give you until 31 March to buy my lot for P2 million." Ulay gave nothing for this promise. On 20 March, before Tess withdrew her offer, Ulay wrote Tess accepting it and tendering P2 million. Tess refused, saying the option had no separate consideration. Is there a perfected sale?

alac.answer: Yes, a contract of sale was perfected when Ulay accepted on 20 March.
alac.basis: Article 1479 of the Civil Code provides that an accepted unilateral promise to sell is binding upon the promisor only if supported by a consideration distinct from the price. In Sanchez v. Rigos, G.R. No. L-25494, June 14, 1972, the Supreme Court held that an option without a separate consideration is a mere offer, which may be withdrawn at any time before acceptance; but if it is accepted before it is withdrawn, a bilateral contract of sale is perfected. Article 1475 provides that a sale is perfected upon a meeting of minds on the thing and the price.
alac.application: Here, Tess's promise had no separate consideration, so it was not a binding option, and she could have withdrawn it at any time. But she did not withdraw it before Ulay accepted on 20 March. Ulay's acceptance created a meeting of minds on the lot and the price of P2 million.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, a contract of sale was perfected, and Tess must sell the lot to Ulay.

keyPoints: Option without separate consideration is a mere offer (Art. 1479; Sanchez v. Rigos)
May be withdrawn before acceptance
Acceptance before withdrawal perfects a sale (Art. 1475)
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 1475 and 1479; Sanchez v. Rigos, G.R. No. L-25494, June 14, 1972

q: A right of first refusal in a lease contract gives the lessee the right to:
choices: Buy the property at any time at any price
Be offered the property first, on the same terms, before the owner sells it to others
hints: It is not an option; no price is fixed in advance.
It is a right of priority.
why: A right of first refusal is a right of priority: before selling to others, the owner must first offer the property to the grantee on the same terms. Its breach makes the owner liable and may lead to rescission of the sale to a third person who knew of the right (Equatorial Realty Development, Inc. v. Mayfair Theater, Inc., G.R. No. 106063, November 21, 1996).
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1159; Equatorial Realty Development, Inc. v. Mayfair Theater, Inc., G.R. No. 106063, November 21, 1996

q: Vic's lease with Wendy gave Wendy, the lessee, a right of first refusal if Vic decided to sell the building. Without offering it to Wendy, Vic sold the building to Xian for P20 million. Xian knew of Wendy's lease and her right. What is Wendy's remedy?

alac.answer: Wendy may have the sale to Xian rescinded and compel Vic to sell the building to her for P20 million.
alac.basis: Article 1159 of the Civil Code provides that obligations arising from contracts have the force of law between the parties and should be complied with in good faith. In Equatorial Realty Development, Inc. v. Mayfair Theater, Inc., G.R. No. 106063, November 21, 1996, the Supreme Court held that a sale made in violation of a lessee's right of first refusal to a buyer who knew of that right is rescissible, and the grantee may compel the owner to sell the property to him on the same terms as the sale to the third person.
alac.application: Here, Vic was bound by the lease to offer the building first to Wendy, but he sold it to Xian without doing so. Xian knew of Wendy's lease and her right, so he is not a buyer in good faith. The sale violated Wendy's right of first refusal.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Wendy may ask the court to rescind the sale to Xian and to order Vic to sell the building to her for P20 million, the price paid by Xian.

keyPoints: Contract has the force of law (Art. 1159)
Sale in violation of a right of first refusal to a buyer with knowledge is rescissible (Equatorial Realty v. Mayfair)
Grantee may buy on the same terms
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1159; Equatorial Realty Development, Inc. v. Mayfair Theater, Inc., G.R. No. 106063, November 21, 1996

q: Under Article 1482 of the Civil Code, earnest money given in a contract of sale is considered:
choices: A separate consideration for an option
Part of the price and proof of the perfection of the contract
A deposit to be returned in all cases
hints: Earnest money differs from option money.
It shows that the sale was perfected.
why: Art. 1482: earnest money is considered part of the price and proof of the perfection of the contract.

q: Yuri agreed to buy Zara's house for P5 million and paid P200,000 as "earnest money." A week later, Yuri told Zara he no longer wanted to buy and asked for the return of the P200,000. Zara argues that there was a perfected sale and wants Yuri to pay the balance. Who is correct?

alac.answer: Zara is correct. A sale was perfected, and she may demand that Yuri pay the balance.
alac.basis: Article 1482 of the Civil Code provides that whenever earnest money is given in a contract of sale, it shall be considered as part of the price and as proof of the perfection of the contract. Under Article 1191, in reciprocal obligations, the injured party may choose between fulfillment and rescission, with damages in either case.
alac.application: Here, Yuri and Zara agreed on the house and the price, and Yuri gave P200,000 as earnest money. The earnest money is part of the price and proof that the sale was perfected. Yuri's change of mind is a breach, not a lawful withdrawal.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Zara may demand that Yuri pay the P4.8 million balance, or she may choose rescission with damages; Yuri cannot simply recover the earnest money and walk away.

keyPoints: Earnest money is part of the price and proof of perfection (Art. 1482)
Buyer's refusal is a breach
Seller may choose fulfillment or rescission with damages (Art. 1191)

q: Under Article 1490 of the Civil Code, spouses may sell property to each other only when:
choices: A separation of property was agreed upon in the marriage settlements, or there has been a judicial separation of property
hints: The rule protects third persons and the weaker spouse.
There are two exceptions.
why: Art. 1490: husband and wife cannot sell property to each other, except when separation of property was agreed upon in the marriage settlements or there has been a judicial separation of property.

q: Anton authorized his agent, Bert, to sell his lot to the highest bidder. Without Anton's consent, Bert bought the lot himself through his cousin as a dummy, at a fair price. Anton later learned of it. Is the sale valid?

alac.answer: No, the sale is void.
alac.basis: Article 1491(2) of the Civil Code provides that agents cannot acquire by purchase, even at a public or judicial auction, either in person or through the mediation of another, the property whose administration or sale may have been entrusted to them, unless the consent of the principal has been given. Article 1409(7) declares void contracts expressly prohibited or declared void by law.
alac.application: Here, Bert was entrusted with the sale of Anton's lot. He acquired it for himself through his cousin, without Anton's consent. The fairness of the price does not matter; the law prohibits the purchase to avoid conflicts of interest.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale is void.

keyPoints: Agents cannot buy property entrusted to them for sale without the principal's consent (Art. 1491(2))
Applies even if through another person
Contracts expressly prohibited by law are void (Art. 1409(7))

q: Under Article 1504 of the Civil Code, unless otherwise agreed, goods sold remain at the seller's risk:
choices: Until ownership is transferred to the buyer
Until the buyer pays in full in all cases
hints: Res perit domino: the thing perishes with its owner.
There are exceptions, such as delay by a party.
why: Art. 1504: goods remain at the seller's risk until ownership is transferred to the buyer, with exceptions such as where delivery is delayed through the fault of a party.

q: Carlo agreed to buy 100 sacks of rice from Dante's warehouse at P50 per kilo, the total price to be computed after weighing. Before the rice was weighed and delivered, a fire destroyed the warehouse and all the rice. Dante demands that Carlo pay. Must Carlo pay?

alac.answer: No, Carlo need not pay. Dante bears the loss.
alac.basis: Article 1480 of the Civil Code provides that should fungible things be sold for a price fixed according to weight, number, or measure, the risk shall not be imputed to the vendee until they have been weighed, counted, or measured and delivered, unless the latter has incurred in delay.
alac.application: Here, the rice was sold at a price fixed per kilo, to be computed after weighing. It was destroyed before it was weighed and delivered, and Carlo was not in delay. The risk had not yet passed to him.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Dante bears the loss, and Carlo is not obliged to pay.

keyPoints: Fungibles sold by weight, number or measure (Art. 1480)
Risk passes only after weighing and delivery
Unless the buyer is in delay

q: Under Article 1495 of the Civil Code, the vendor is bound to:
choices: Transfer the ownership of, deliver, and warrant the thing sold
hints: There are three obligations.
Warranty is one of them.
why: Art. 1495: the vendor is bound to transfer the ownership of and deliver, as well as warrant the thing which is the object of the sale.

q: Elena bought a lot from Felix. The deed said nothing about warranties. A year later, Gina won a final judgment declaring that she had owned the lot since before the sale, and Elena was ousted. Is Felix liable to Elena?

alac.answer: Yes, Felix is liable to Elena for eviction.
alac.basis: Article 1547 of the Civil Code provides that, unless a contrary intention appears, there is an implied warranty that the seller has a right to sell the thing and that the buyer shall have and enjoy its legal and peaceful possession. Article 1548 provides that eviction shall take place whenever, by a final judgment based on a right prior to the sale, the vendee is deprived of the thing purchased, and that the vendor shall answer for the eviction even though nothing has been said in the contract on the subject.
alac.application: Here, Elena was deprived of the lot by a final judgment in favor of Gina, based on Gina's ownership which existed before the sale. Although the deed was silent, the warranty against eviction is implied by law.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Felix is liable to Elena under the warranty against eviction.

keyPoints: Implied warranty of title and peaceful possession (Art. 1547)
Eviction by final judgment based on a prior right (Art. 1548)
Vendor liable even if the contract is silent

q: Under Article 1592 of the Civil Code, in the sale of immovable property with a stipulation for automatic rescission upon non-payment, the buyer may still pay after the due date as long as:
choices: The seller has not sold to another
No demand for rescission has been made upon him judicially or by a notarial act
hints: Automatic rescission clauses are tempered for immovables.
The demand must be in a particular form.
why: Art. 1592: the vendee may pay even after the period, as long as no demand for rescission has been made upon him judicially or by a notarial act.

q: Hugo sold a lot to Ivy in an absolute deed of sale, with the price payable on 30 June and a clause that the sale would be automatically rescinded if Ivy failed to pay on time. Ivy did not pay on 30 June. On 5 July, Hugo sent her an ordinary letter declaring the sale rescinded. On 10 July, Ivy tendered the full price. May Hugo refuse it?

alac.answer: No, Hugo may not refuse Ivy's payment.
alac.basis: Article 1592 of the Civil Code provides that in the sale of immovable property, even though it may have been stipulated that upon failure to pay the price at the time agreed upon the rescission of the contract shall of right take place, the vendee may pay, even after the expiration of the period, as long as no demand for rescission of the contract has been made upon him either judicially or by a notarial act.
alac.application: Here, the sale was of an immovable, with an automatic rescission clause. Ivy failed to pay on time, but Hugo's demand for rescission was made only by an ordinary letter, not judicially or by a notarial act. Ivy tendered payment on 10 July, before any valid demand for rescission.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ivy's tender was timely under Article 1592, and Hugo must accept it.

keyPoints: Applies to sales of immovables (Art. 1592)
Buyer may pay late until demand for rescission
Demand must be judicial or by notarial act

q: Under Article 1544 of the Civil Code, if immovable property is sold to two different buyers, ownership belongs to:
choices: The one who in good faith first recorded it in the Registry of Property; absent registration, the one first in possession in good faith; absent both, the one with the oldest title in good faith
The one chosen by the seller
hints: Good faith is required at every step.
For immovables, registration comes first.
why: Art. 1544: for immovables, ownership belongs to the buyer who in good faith first recorded the sale; if none, the one first in possession in good faith; if none, the one with the oldest title, provided there is good faith.

q: Jose sold his registered lot to Karla, who took possession but did not register the sale. Later, Jose sold the same lot to Leon, who knew of the sale to Karla and saw her house on the lot. Leon registered his deed first. Who owns the lot?

alac.answer: Karla owns the lot.
alac.basis: Article 1544 of the Civil Code provides that if immovable property is sold to different vendees, ownership shall belong to the person who in good faith first recorded it in the Registry of Property; absent registration, to the person who in good faith was first in possession; and absent both, to the person who presents the oldest title, provided there is good faith.
alac.application: Here, Leon registered first, but he knew of the prior sale to Karla and saw her house on the lot. His registration was therefore in bad faith and gives him no preference. Karla, on the other hand, was first in possession, in good faith.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Karla has the better right and owns the lot.

keyPoints: Registration must be in good faith (Art. 1544)
Knowledge of the prior sale is bad faith
Next in order: first possession in good faith

q: Under Article 1484 of the Civil Code (the Recto Law), if the seller of personal property on installments forecloses the chattel mortgage on the thing sold, he:
choices: May still sue for the unpaid balance
Shall have no further action against the buyer to recover any unpaid balance
hints: The three remedies are alternative.
Foreclosure bars a deficiency claim.
why: Art. 1484(3): if the vendor forecloses the chattel mortgage, he shall have no further action against the purchaser to recover any unpaid balance; any agreement to the contrary is void.

q: Mila bought a car on installments from Auto Co., secured by a chattel mortgage on the car. After she missed three installments, Auto Co. foreclosed the mortgage. The car was sold at auction for less than her unpaid balance. Auto Co. now sues Mila for the deficiency, invoking a contract clause allowing it. Will the suit prosper?

alac.answer: No, the suit will not prosper.
alac.basis: Article 1484 of the Civil Code gives the vendor of personal property payable in installments three alternative remedies: exact fulfillment; cancel the sale if the buyer fails to pay two or more installments; or foreclose the chattel mortgage on the thing sold if the buyer fails to pay two or more installments, in which case he shall have no further action against the purchaser to recover any unpaid balance. Any agreement to the contrary is void.
alac.application: Here, Mila bought a car, personal property, on installments, and failed to pay three installments. Auto Co. chose to foreclose the chattel mortgage. Having chosen that remedy, it can no longer recover the deficiency. The clause allowing a deficiency claim is void.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Auto Co.'s suit for the deficiency should be dismissed.

keyPoints: Three alternative remedies (Art. 1484)
Foreclosure bars recovery of the unpaid balance
Contrary stipulation is void

q: Which of the following is EXCLUDED from the coverage of the Maceda Law (RA 6552)?
choices: A residential lot sold on installments
A residential condominium unit sold on installments
A commercial building sold on installments
A house and lot sold on installments
hints: The law protects buyers of residential real estate.
Industrial lots and commercial buildings are excluded.
why: RA 6552, Sec. 3: covers sales or financing of real estate on installments, including residential condominium apartments, but excludes industrial lots, commercial buildings, and sales to tenants under the agrarian laws.

q: Noel bought, on monthly installments, (a) a residential condominium unit for his family, and (b) a small commercial building for his business. After paying installments for three years on each, he defaulted on both. The sellers cancelled both contracts and kept all his payments. Can Noel invoke the Maceda Law on both?

alac.answer: Noel may invoke the Maceda Law for the condominium unit, but not for the commercial building.
alac.basis: Section 3 of RA 6552 (the Maceda Law) applies to all transactions or contracts involving the sale or financing of real estate on installment payments, including residential condominium apartments, but excluding industrial lots, commercial buildings and sales to tenants under the agrarian laws.
alac.application: Here, the residential condominium unit is expressly covered, and Noel paid more than two years of installments, so he is entitled to the protections of the law, including the cash surrender value. The commercial building is expressly excluded, so the Maceda Law does not apply to it, and the rights of the parties depend on their contract and the Civil Code.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Noel may claim the benefits of the Maceda Law only as to the condominium unit.

keyPoints: Maceda Law covers residential real estate on installments, including condominiums (RA 6552, Sec. 3)
Excludes industrial lots and commercial buildings
Commercial building governed by the contract and the Civil Code

q: Under the Maceda Law, in computing the total number of installment payments made by the buyer:
choices: Down payments, deposits or options on the contract are included
Only payments in the last two years are counted
hints: The law favors the buyer.
Every payment toward the property counts.
why: RA 6552, Sec. 3: down payments, deposits or options on the contract are included in the computation of the total number of installment payments made.

q: Olive bought a house and lot on monthly installments and paid regularly for exactly six years, for a total of P1,200,000, including her down payment. She then defaulted. If the seller cancels the contract, how much cash surrender value must it refund, and what grace period was Olive entitled to?

alac.answer: Olive was entitled to a six-month grace period, and if the contract is cancelled, a cash surrender value of P660,000.
alac.basis: Section 3 of RA 6552 provides that a buyer who has paid at least two years of installments is entitled (a) to a grace period of one month for every one year of installment payments made, to pay the unpaid installments without additional interest, and (b) if the contract is cancelled, to a cash surrender value equal to fifty percent of the total payments made, and, after five years of installments, an additional five percent every year, not exceeding ninety percent. Down payments are included in computing the payments made.
alac.application: Here, Olive paid for six years, so she earned a grace period of six months. Her cash surrender value is 50% for the first five years plus 5% for the sixth year, or 55%. Her total payments, including the down payment, are P1,200,000; 55% of that is P660,000.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Olive had a six-month grace period, and upon cancellation the seller must refund P660,000.

keyPoints: One month of grace for every year of installments (RA 6552, Sec. 3(a))
Cash surrender value: 50%, plus 5% per year after five years, up to 90% (Sec. 3(b))
Down payment included in total payments

q: Under Section 6 of the Maceda Law, the buyer has the right to:
choices: Stop paying for one year without penalty
Pay in advance any installment or the full unpaid balance at any time without interest, and have full payment annotated on the title
Rescind the sale at will and get a full refund
hints: The law encourages early payment.
No interest is charged on advance payment.
why: RA 6552, Sec. 6: the buyer may pay in advance any installment or the full unpaid balance any time without interest and have the full payment annotated on the certificate of title.

q: Pia bought a residential lot on monthly installments. After paying for only 18 months, she missed a payment due on 1 March. On 10 March, the developer sent her a notarized notice cancelling the contract effective immediately and forfeiting all her payments. What are Pia's rights?

alac.answer: Pia was entitled to a 60-day grace period, and the cancellation could take effect only after the grace period and 30 days from her receipt of the notarial notice.
alac.basis: Section 4 of RA 6552 provides that where less than two years of installments were paid, the seller shall give the buyer a grace period of not less than sixty days from the date the installment became due; if the buyer fails to pay at the end of the grace period, the seller may cancel the contract after thirty days from the buyer's receipt of the notice of cancellation or demand for rescission by a notarial act. Section 5 allows the buyer to update the account or to sell or assign her rights during the grace period and before actual cancellation.
alac.application: Here, Pia paid for only 18 months, less than two years, so she is not entitled to a cash surrender value. But she was entitled to sixty days from 1 March to pay the missed installment. The developer's cancellation "effective immediately" on 10 March disregarded both the grace period and the thirty-day period after notice.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the cancellation was premature; Pia may still update her account or assign her rights within the grace period, and cancellation can take effect only after the periods required by Section 4.

keyPoints: Less than two years paid: 60-day grace period (RA 6552, Sec. 4)
Cancellation 30 days after receipt of notarial notice
Buyer may update the account or assign rights (Sec. 5)

q: Under Section 3(b) of the Maceda Law, when the buyer has paid at least two years of installments, actual cancellation of the contract takes place:
choices: After thirty days from the buyer's receipt of a notice of cancellation or demand for rescission by notarial act, and upon full payment of the cash surrender value
hints: There are two requirements.
The refund must actually be paid.
why: RA 6552, Sec. 3(b): actual cancellation takes place after thirty days from receipt of a notarial notice of cancellation or demand for rescission and upon full payment of the cash surrender value to the buyer.

q: Quino paid three years of installments on a house and lot, then defaulted. The developer sent him an ordinary letter cancelling the contract and resold the property, without paying him any cash surrender value. Was the contract validly cancelled?

alac.answer: No, the contract was not validly cancelled and remains in force.
alac.basis: Section 3(b) of RA 6552 provides that for a buyer who has paid at least two years of installments, the actual cancellation of the contract shall take place after thirty days from receipt by the buyer of the notice of cancellation or the demand for rescission by a notarial act and upon full payment of the cash surrender value to the buyer. Section 7 declares void any stipulation contrary to these provisions.
alac.application: Here, Quino paid three years of installments, so Section 3 applies. The developer sent only an ordinary letter, not a notarial notice, and did not pay the cash surrender value. Both requirements for a valid cancellation are missing.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the cancellation is void, the contract to sell subsists, and Quino may still pay the balance or claim the protections of the law.

keyPoints: Notarial notice of cancellation required (RA 6552, Sec. 3(b))
Full payment of the cash surrender value required
Without these, the contract remains valid

q: Under Article 1606 of the Civil Code, in a sale with right to repurchase (conventional redemption) with no agreed period, the right lasts:
choices: Four years from the date of the contract
hints: If there is an agreement, the period cannot exceed ten years.
Without agreement, the period is shorter.
why: Art. 1606: absent express agreement, the right to repurchase lasts four years from the date of the contract; an agreed period cannot exceed ten years.

q: Rosa, Sol and Tina co-own a lot. Rosa sold her one-third share to Ugo, a stranger, for P1 million. Sol learned of the sale from neighbors, but Rosa never gave Sol or Tina written notice. Eight months later, Sol offered to redeem Rosa's share. Ugo says it is too late. Is Sol's right of redemption still available?

alac.answer: Yes, Sol may still redeem Rosa's share.
alac.basis: Article 1620 of the Civil Code provides that a co-owner may exercise the right of redemption in case the share of any of the other co-owners is sold to a third person. Article 1623 provides that the right of legal redemption shall not be exercised except within thirty days from the notice in writing by the prospective vendor or by the vendor.
alac.application: Here, Rosa sold her share to Ugo, a stranger, so Sol, a co-owner, has a right of legal redemption. The thirty-day period runs only from written notice by the vendor. Rosa never gave written notice; Sol's knowledge from neighbors does not start the period.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the thirty-day period has not begun to run, and Sol may still redeem Rosa's share by paying Ugo the price.

keyPoints: Co-owner's right of legal redemption (Art. 1620)
Thirty days from written notice by the vendor (Art. 1623)
Knowledge from other sources does not start the period

q: Under Article 1602 of the Civil Code, a contract is presumed to be an equitable mortgage when, among others:
choices: The vendor remains in possession as lessee or otherwise
hints: The law looks behind the form of a sale.
A seller who stays on the property is a warning sign.
why: Art. 1602 lists cases where a sale is presumed to be an equitable mortgage, including an unusually inadequate price, the vendor remaining in possession, an extension of the redemption period, and the vendor paying the taxes.

q: Needing money, Vina signed a "deed of sale with right to repurchase" over her house worth P3 million in favor of Wally for P500,000. She continued living in the house, paying Wally monthly "rent," and kept paying the real property taxes. When she failed to repurchase on time, Wally sought to consolidate ownership. What is the true nature of the contract, and what is Vina's remedy?

alac.answer: The contract is an equitable mortgage, and Vina may ask for reformation of the instrument.
alac.basis: Article 1602 of the Civil Code presumes a contract to be an equitable mortgage when, among others, the price of a sale with right to repurchase is unusually inadequate, the vendor remains in possession as lessee or otherwise, or the vendor binds himself to pay the taxes on the thing sold. Article 1603 provides that, in case of doubt, a contract purporting to be a sale with right to repurchase shall be construed as an equitable mortgage. Article 1605 allows the apparent vendor to ask for the reformation of the instrument.
alac.application: Here, the price of P500,000 is unusually inadequate for a house worth P3 million. Vina remained in the house as a "lessee" and continued paying the taxes. These circumstances show that the real intention was to secure a loan, not to sell.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the contract is an equitable mortgage; Wally cannot consolidate ownership, and Vina may have the instrument reformed into a mortgage and pay her debt.

keyPoints: Presumption of equitable mortgage (Art. 1602)
Inadequate price, vendor in possession, vendor paying taxes
Doubt resolved as equitable mortgage (Art. 1603); reformation (Art. 1605)

q: Under Article 1643 of the Civil Code, a lease of things is NOT valid if its period exceeds:
hints: The law allows very long leases, but with a limit.
The limit is just under a century.
why: Art. 1643: in the lease of things, one party gives another the enjoyment or use of a thing for a price certain and for a definite or indefinite period; no lease for more than ninety-nine years shall be valid.

q: Yna leased an apartment from Zoe for one year, with rent payable monthly. When the year ended, Yna stayed for two more months, paying rent, which Zoe accepted without objection and without any prior notice to leave. Zoe now wants Yna out within the week, claiming the lease has expired. Is there still a lease?

alac.answer: Yes, there is an implied new lease on a month-to-month basis.
alac.basis: Article 1670 of the Civil Code provides that if at the end of the contract the lessee continues enjoying the thing leased for fifteen days with the acquiescence of the lessor, and no notice to the contrary has previously been given by either party, there is an implied new lease, not for the period of the original contract, but for the time established in Articles 1682 and 1687, and the other terms of the original contract are revived. Under Article 1687, when the rent is paid monthly, the period is understood to be from month to month.
alac.application: Here, Yna continued occupying the apartment for more than fifteen days after the lease expired, and Zoe accepted rent without objection and without prior notice. An implied new lease arose. Since the rent is paid monthly, its period is month to month, on the same other terms.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Zoe cannot oust Yna within a week; she must terminate the month-to-month lease at the end of a monthly period, with proper notice.

keyPoints: Implied new lease after fifteen days with the lessor's acquiescence (Art. 1670)
Period not the original one, but per Arts. 1682 and 1687
Monthly rent: month-to-month lease

q: Under Article 1654 of the Civil Code, the lessor is obliged, among others, to:
choices: Make all necessary repairs during the lease to keep the thing suitable for its use, unless otherwise stipulated
Allow the lessee to sell the property
hints: The lessor must keep the thing fit for its intended use.
A stipulation may shift this duty.
why: Art. 1654: the lessor must deliver the thing fit for its intended use, make necessary repairs during the lease (unless otherwise stipulated), and maintain the lessee in peaceful and adequate enjoyment.

q: Arnel leased a restaurant space from Bing. The roof leaked badly, flooding the kitchen every time it rained. Arnel notified Bing repeatedly, but Bing refused to repair it. The lease says nothing about repairs. Arnel had to close for weeks. What are Arnel's remedies?

alac.answer: Arnel may ask for rescission of the lease with damages, or for damages only while keeping the lease in force.
alac.basis: Article 1654 of the Civil Code obliges the lessor to make during the lease all the necessary repairs to keep the thing suitable for its intended use, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary, and to maintain the lessee in the peaceful and adequate enjoyment of the lease. Article 1659 provides that if the lessor fails to comply with these obligations, the aggrieved party may ask for the rescission of the contract and indemnification for damages, or only the latter, allowing the contract to remain in force.
alac.application: Here, the leaking roof made the space unfit for use as a restaurant, and the repair was necessary. The lease does not shift the duty to repair to Arnel. Bing refused to repair despite notice, violating Article 1654.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Arnel may choose to rescind the lease and claim damages, including lost income, or to keep the lease and claim damages only.

keyPoints: Lessor must make necessary repairs (Art. 1654(2))
Lessor must maintain peaceful and adequate enjoyment (Art. 1654(3))
Remedies: rescission and damages, or damages only (Art. 1659)

q: Under Articles 1649 and 1650 of the Civil Code, which is correct?
choices: The lessee may assign the lease without the lessor's consent
The lessee cannot assign the lease without the lessor's consent, but may sublet unless expressly prohibited
hints: Assignment substitutes a new lessee; sublease does not.
Sublease is allowed unless prohibited.
why: Art. 1649: the lessee cannot assign the lease without the lessor's consent, unless otherwise stipulated. Art. 1650: absent an express prohibition, the lessee may sublet, remaining responsible to the lessor.

q: Cora leased a house from Dino. The lease did not prohibit subleasing. Cora sublet the house to Edna, who damaged the walls through careless use. Dino seeks to hold both Cora and Edna liable. Can he?

alac.answer: Yes, Dino may hold both Cora and Edna liable.
alac.basis: Article 1650 of the Civil Code provides that when there is no express prohibition, the lessee may sublet the thing leased, without prejudice to his responsibility for the performance of the contract toward the lessor. Article 1651 provides that, without prejudice to his obligation toward the sublessor, the sublessee is bound to the lessor for all acts which refer to the use and preservation of the thing leased in the manner stipulated between the lessor and the lessee.
alac.application: Here, the sublease was valid because the lease did not prohibit it. Cora remains responsible to Dino for the performance of the lease, including the proper care of the house. Edna, as sublessee, is directly bound to Dino for acts relating to the use and preservation of the house, such as the damage to the walls.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Dino may hold Cora liable under the lease and Edna liable directly for the damage she caused.

keyPoints: Sublease allowed absent express prohibition; lessee remains liable (Art. 1650)
Sublessee directly bound to the lessor for use and preservation (Art. 1651)
Lessor may proceed against both

q: Under Article 1868 of the Civil Code, by the contract of agency a person binds himself to:
choices: Render some service or do something in representation or on behalf of another, with the latter's consent or authority
hints: Representation is the key element.
The principal's consent is required.
why: Art. 1868: by agency, a person binds himself to render some service or do something in representation or on behalf of another, with the consent or authority of the latter.

q: Fely orally authorized her cousin Gil to sell her lot. Gil sold it to Hans in a notarized deed signed by Gil "for Fely." Fely later refused to recognize the sale. Is the sale valid?

alac.answer: No, the sale is void.
alac.basis: Article 1874 of the Civil Code provides that when a sale of a piece of land or any interest therein is through an agent, the authority of the latter shall be in writing; otherwise, the sale shall be void. Article 1878(5) also requires a special power of attorney to enter into any contract by which the ownership of an immovable is transmitted.
alac.application: Here, Gil sold Fely's lot as her agent, but his authority was only oral. The law requires written authority for an agent to sell land, and makes a sale without it void.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale to Hans is void, and Fely is not bound by it.

keyPoints: Agent's authority to sell land must be in writing (Art. 1874)
Otherwise the sale is void
Special power of attorney required (Art. 1878(5))

q: Under Article 1891 of the Civil Code, a stipulation exempting the agent from the obligation to render an account is:
choices: Valid if the agent is unpaid
hints: The agent handles the principal's affairs and money.
The duty to account cannot be waived in advance.
why: Art. 1891: every agent must render an account and deliver to the principal whatever he received by virtue of the agency; any stipulation exempting the agent from rendering an account is void.

q: Ivan appointed Jun as general administrator of his farm. Without any special power of attorney, Jun borrowed P500,000 from a bank in Ivan's name to buy a new car for the farm office. The loan was not urgent or needed to preserve the farm. Ivan refuses to pay. Is Ivan bound?

alac.answer: No, Ivan is not bound unless he ratifies the loan.
alac.basis: Article 1878(7) of the Civil Code requires a special power of attorney to loan or borrow money, unless the latter act be urgent and indispensable for the preservation of the things under administration. Article 1910 provides that the principal must comply with the obligations the agent contracted within the scope of his authority, but as for any obligation wherein the agent has exceeded his power, the principal is not bound except when he ratifies it expressly or tacitly.
alac.application: Here, Jun was only a general administrator and had no special power of attorney to borrow money. The loan to buy a car was not urgent or indispensable for preserving the farm. Jun therefore exceeded his authority.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ivan is not bound by the loan unless he ratifies it; Jun may be personally liable to the bank.

keyPoints: Special power of attorney needed to borrow money (Art. 1878(7))
Exception: urgent and indispensable for preservation
Principal not bound by acts beyond authority unless ratified (Art. 1910)

q: Under Article 1919 of the Civil Code, which of the following extinguishes an agency?
choices: The death of the principal or of the agent
hints: Agency is personal and based on trust.
Art. 1919 lists six causes.
why: Art. 1919: agency is extinguished by revocation, withdrawal of the agent, death, civil interdiction, insanity or insolvency of the principal or agent, dissolution of the firm, accomplishment of the purpose, or expiration of the period.

q: Karl owed Lina P1 million. To pay the debt, Karl appointed Lina as his agent to sell his lot and apply the proceeds to the debt, any balance to go to Karl. Before the sale, Karl died. Karl's heirs claim that Lina's authority ended with his death. Are they correct?

alac.answer: No, the heirs are not correct. Lina's agency continues.
alac.basis: Article 1919(3) of the Civil Code provides that agency is extinguished by the death of the principal. However, Article 1930 provides that the agency shall remain in full force and effect even after the death of the principal if it has been constituted in the common interest of the principal and of the agent, or in the interest of a third person who has accepted the stipulation in his favor.
alac.application: Here, the agency was created not only for Karl's benefit but also for Lina's, as the proceeds of the sale were to pay Karl's debt to her. It is an agency coupled with an interest, constituted in the common interest of the principal and the agent.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Karl's death did not extinguish the agency, and Lina may proceed to sell the lot and apply the proceeds to the debt.

keyPoints: Death of the principal generally extinguishes agency (Art. 1919(3))
Exception: agency in the common interest of principal and agent (Art. 1930)
Agency coupled with an interest survives death

q: Under Article 1933 of the Civil Code, in commodatum:
choices: The bailor retains ownership, and the contract is essentially gratuitous
hints: Commodatum is a loan for use.
If compensation is paid, it is no longer commodatum.
why: Art. 1933: in commodatum, a non-consumable thing is delivered for use for a certain time and returned; it is essentially gratuitous, and the bailor retains ownership. In simple loan (mutuum), ownership passes to the borrower.

q: Ben borrowed his friend Carl's van, free of charge, to move furniture to his new house. Instead, Ben used the van for a weekend trip to the mountains, where a landslide, a fortuitous event, buried it. Is Ben liable for the loss of the van?

alac.answer: Yes, Ben is liable for the loss of the van.
alac.basis: Article 1933 of the Civil Code defines commodatum as a gratuitous loan of a non-consumable thing for use. Article 1942(1) provides that the bailee is liable for the loss of the thing, even if it should be through a fortuitous event, if he devotes the thing to any purpose different from that for which it has been loaned.
alac.application: Here, the free loan of the van was a commodatum for the specific purpose of moving furniture. Ben used it instead for a weekend trip, a purpose different from that agreed. Although the landslide was a fortuitous event, the law makes the bailee answer for it in that case.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ben must pay Carl for the loss of the van.

keyPoints: Free loan of a non-consumable thing for use is commodatum (Art. 1933)
Bailee liable even for fortuitous event if used for a different purpose (Art. 1942(1))
Landslide does not excuse him

q: Under Article 1956 of the Civil Code, interest on a loan is due only when:
choices: It has been expressly stipulated in writing
hints: The rule protects borrowers from claims of unwritten interest.
This is monetary interest, not interest as damages for delay.
why: Art. 1956: no interest shall be due unless it has been expressly stipulated in writing.

q: Dina borrowed P100,000 from Edgar, who required her to sign a promissory note with interest of 5% per month (60% a year). After a year, Edgar sued to collect the principal plus 60% interest. Dina argues that the interest rate is unconscionable. How should the court rule?

alac.answer: The court should strike down the 5% monthly rate as unconscionable and apply the legal rate instead.
alac.basis: Article 1956 of the Civil Code requires interest to be expressly stipulated in writing. Although usury ceilings have been suspended, the Supreme Court has held that stipulated interest rates that are iniquitous or unconscionable are void for being contrary to morals, as in Medel v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 131622, November 27, 1998, which struck down interest of 5.5% per month. Where the stipulated rate is void, the legal rate applies; under Nacar v. Gallery Frames, G.R. No. 189871, August 13, 2013, the legal rate is 6% per annum.
alac.application: Here, the interest was stipulated in writing, but 5% per month, or 60% a year, is excessive, iniquitous and unconscionable. The stipulation is therefore void, although the obligation to pay the principal remains valid.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Dina must pay the P100,000 principal with interest at the legal rate of 6% per annum, not 60%.

keyPoints: Interest must be stipulated in writing (Art. 1956)
Unconscionable rates are void (Medel v. CA)
Legal rate of 6% per annum applies (Nacar v. Gallery Frames)
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1956; Medel v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 131622, November 27, 1998; Nacar v. Gallery Frames, G.R. No. 189871, August 13, 2013

q: Under Article 1962 of the Civil Code, a deposit is constituted when a person receives a thing belonging to another with the obligation of:
choices: Safely keeping it and returning it
hints: Safekeeping is the principal purpose.
If safekeeping is not the main purpose, it is another contract.
why: Art. 1962: a deposit is constituted from the moment a person receives a thing belonging to another, with the obligation of safely keeping it and returning it; if safekeeping is not the principal purpose, there is no deposit.

q: Fe placed P1 million in a savings account with Bank Q. The bank later failed. Fe argues that she is a depositor in the strict sense, so the bank holds her money in trust and she should be paid ahead of the bank's other creditors. Is she correct?

alac.answer: No, Fe is not correct. Her savings deposit is governed by the rules on simple loan.
alac.basis: Article 1980 of the Civil Code provides that fixed, savings, and current deposits of money in banks and similar institutions shall be governed by the provisions concerning simple loan. Under Article 1953, a person who receives a loan of money acquires ownership of it and is bound to pay an equal amount of the same kind.
alac.application: Here, Fe's savings deposit is, in law, a simple loan to the bank. The bank became the owner of the money and Fe its creditor. The bank does not hold the money as a trustee or depositary in the strict sense.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Fe is an ordinary creditor of the bank, without a trust preference, although she may claim deposit insurance under the law on deposit insurance.

keyPoints: Bank deposits are governed by simple loan (Art. 1980)
Bank becomes owner; depositor is a creditor (Art. 1953)
No trust relationship

q: Under Article 1979 of the Civil Code, a depositary is liable for loss of the thing through a fortuitous event when, among others, he:
choices: Kept it in a locked room
Uses the thing without the depositor's permission
hints: The rule mirrors commodatum.
Misuse shifts the risk to the depositary.
why: Art. 1979: the depositary is liable for loss through a fortuitous event if so stipulated, if he uses the thing without permission, if he delays its return, or if he allows others to use it.

q: Gina left her car with her neighbor Hugo for safekeeping while she was abroad. Without her permission, Hugo used the car to drive to work. One day, an earthquake caused a parking structure to collapse on it. Is Hugo liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Hugo is liable for the loss of the car.
alac.basis: Article 1972 of the Civil Code obliges the depositary to keep the thing safely and to return it. Article 1979(2) provides that the depositary is liable for the loss of the thing through a fortuitous event if he uses the thing without the depositor's permission.
alac.application: Here, Hugo received the car for safekeeping, so he is a depositary. He used it without Gina's permission, and it was destroyed by an earthquake, a fortuitous event, while being so used.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Hugo must answer to Gina for the loss of the car.

keyPoints: Depositary must keep the thing safely (Art. 1972)
Liable for fortuitous event if he uses it without permission (Art. 1979(2))
Earthquake does not excuse him

q: Under Article 2054 of the Civil Code, a guarantor:
choices: May bind himself for more than the principal debtor
May bind himself for less, but not for more, than the principal debtor
Must always bind himself for exactly the same amount
hints: The guaranty is accessory to the principal obligation.
Any excess is reduced.
why: Art. 2054: a guarantor may bind himself for less, but not for more, than the principal debtor; if he bound himself for more, his obligation is reduced to the limits of the debtor's.

q: Ivan guaranteed a "loan" from Jack to Kim. It turned out that the loan was really payment for Kim's promise to help Jack rig a public bidding, and the contract was declared void. Jack now sues Ivan as guarantor. Is Ivan liable?

alac.answer: No, Ivan is not liable.
alac.basis: Article 2052 of the Civil Code provides that a guaranty cannot exist without a valid obligation. A guaranty may secure a voidable or an unenforceable contract, or even a natural obligation, but not a void one.
alac.application: Here, the principal obligation was void because its cause, rigging a public bidding, is contrary to law and public policy. Since there is no valid principal obligation, the accessory guaranty has nothing to secure.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ivan's guaranty is also void, and Jack cannot hold him liable.

keyPoints: Guaranty is accessory and needs a valid principal obligation (Art. 2052)
May secure voidable, unenforceable or natural obligations
Not a void obligation

q: Under Article 2058 of the Civil Code, the benefit of excussion means that the guarantor:
choices: Must pay first, before the debtor
Cannot be compelled to pay until the creditor has exhausted all the debtor's property and legal remedies
hints: The guarantor's liability is subsidiary.
The creditor must go after the debtor first.
why: Art. 2058: the guarantor cannot be compelled to pay the creditor unless the latter has exhausted all the property of the debtor and resorted to all legal remedies against him.

q: Lito guaranteed Mon's P500,000 debt to Nina. When the debt fell due, Mon left the Philippines without leaving any representative and cannot be sued here. Nina sued Lito directly. Lito invokes the benefit of excussion. Will his defense succeed?

alac.answer: No, Lito's defense will not succeed.
alac.basis: Article 2058 of the Civil Code gives the guarantor the benefit of excussion: he cannot be compelled to pay unless the creditor has exhausted the debtor's property and legal remedies. However, Article 2059(4) provides that excussion shall not take place when the debtor has absconded or cannot be sued within the Philippines, unless he has left a manager or representative.
alac.application: Here, Mon left the country without a representative and cannot be sued in the Philippines. This is one of the cases where the benefit of excussion does not apply.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Nina may proceed directly against Lito, who must pay as guarantor and then seek reimbursement from Mon.

keyPoints: Benefit of excussion (Art. 2058)
Not available when the debtor has absconded or cannot be sued in the Philippines (Art. 2059(4))
Guarantor may later seek indemnity from the debtor (Art. 2066)

q: Under Article 2076 of the Civil Code, the obligation of the guarantor is extinguished:
choices: Only by payment by the guarantor
At the same time as that of the debtor, and for the same causes as all other obligations
hints: The guaranty follows the principal obligation.
There are also special causes, like an unauthorized extension.
why: Art. 2076: the guarantor's obligation is extinguished at the same time as the debtor's, and for the same causes as all other obligations.

q: Olga guaranteed Pepe's loan from Bank R, due on 1 March 2025. Without telling Olga, the bank agreed with Pepe to extend the due date to 1 March 2026. Pepe defaulted in 2026, and the bank sued Olga. Is Olga still liable?

alac.answer: No, Olga is no longer liable. Her guaranty was extinguished.
