alac.basis: Article 2079 of the Civil Code provides that an extension granted to the debtor by the creditor without the consent of the guarantor extinguishes the guaranty. The mere failure of the creditor to demand payment after the debt became due is not such an extension.
alac.application: Here, Bank R did not merely fail to demand payment; it expressly agreed with Pepe to extend the due date by one year. Olga did not consent to the extension. The extension could prejudice her, since the debtor's ability to pay might change.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the guaranty was extinguished, and the bank cannot hold Olga liable.

keyPoints: Extension without the guarantor's consent extinguishes the guaranty (Art. 2079)
Mere failure to demand is not an extension
Express agreement to extend

q: Under Article 2083 of the Civil Code, if a person bound by law or court order to give a bond cannot do so:
choices: A pledge or mortgage sufficient to cover the obligation shall be admitted in lieu of the bond
hints: The law provides an alternative security.
Real security may replace personal security.
why: Art. 2083: a pledge or mortgage considered sufficient to cover the obligation shall be admitted in lieu of a legal or judicial bond.

q: A court required Quirino, a plaintiff, to post a judicial bond before it would issue a writ of attachment. Quirino offered as bondsman his friend, who had no property and lived abroad. The defendant objected. Quirino also offered, alternatively, a mortgage on his own land sufficient to cover the bond. What should the court do?

alac.answer: The court should reject the proposed bondsman but may accept the mortgage on Quirino's land in lieu of the bond.
alac.basis: Article 2082 of the Civil Code requires a bondsman offered by virtue of law or judicial order to have the qualifications prescribed in Article 2056 and special laws, namely integrity, capacity to bind himself, and sufficient property to answer for the obligation, and, under Article 2056, residence in the Philippines. Article 2083 provides that if the person bound to give a bond cannot do so, a pledge or mortgage considered sufficient to cover his obligation shall be admitted in lieu thereof.
alac.application: Here, Quirino's friend has no property and lives abroad, so he lacks the qualifications of a bondsman. However, Quirino offered a mortgage on his own land sufficient to cover the bond, which the law allows in place of a judicial bond.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should disqualify the proposed bondsman but may accept the sufficient mortgage in lieu of the bond.

keyPoints: Qualifications of a bondsman (Arts. 2056, 2082)
Bondsman without property or residence is not qualified
Sufficient pledge or mortgage may replace the bond (Art. 2083)

q: Which is an essential requisite of a real estate mortgage under Article 2085 of the Civil Code?
choices: The mortgagee must be a bank
The mortgagor must be the absolute owner of the property mortgaged
The loan must exceed P1 million
The mortgage must last ten years
hints: The mortgage secures a principal obligation.
Only the owner can encumber the property.
why: Art. 2085: a mortgage must secure a principal obligation; the mortgagor must be the absolute owner; and he must have free disposal of the property or be legally authorized.

q: Rudy borrowed P2 million from Sol and mortgaged his house and lot. The mortgage contract states that if Rudy fails to pay on time, "ownership of the property shall automatically pass to Sol." Rudy defaulted. Sol now claims to own the property. Is she correct?

alac.answer: No, Sol is not correct. The automatic-transfer clause is void.
alac.basis: Article 2087 of the Civil Code provides that when the principal obligation becomes due, the things mortgaged may be alienated for the payment to the creditor. Article 2088 provides that the creditor cannot appropriate the things given by way of mortgage or dispose of them, and any stipulation to the contrary is null and void. Such a stipulation is known as pactum commissorium.
alac.application: Here, the clause provides that the property automatically becomes Sol's upon Rudy's default, without foreclosure and sale. This is pactum commissorium, which the law declares void. The mortgage itself, however, remains valid as security.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Sol cannot claim ownership by virtue of the clause; her remedy is to foreclose the mortgage and have the property sold.

keyPoints: Mortgaged property may be sold upon default (Art. 2087)
Creditor cannot appropriate it; pactum commissorium is void (Art. 2088)
Remedy is foreclosure

q: Under Act 3135, a real estate mortgage may be foreclosed EXTRAJUDICIALLY only when:
choices: A special power to sell is inserted in or attached to the mortgage
The property is worth less than P1 million
hints: Without the special power, the mortgagee must go to court.
Section 1 of Act 3135 states the condition.
why: Act 3135, Sec. 1: extrajudicial foreclosure applies when a sale is made under a special power inserted in or attached to the real estate mortgage; otherwise, foreclosure must be judicial under Rule 68 of the Rules of Court.
cite: Act No. 3135, Sec. 1; Rules of Court, Rule 68

q: Tito mortgaged his land to Uma to secure a loan. The mortgage contract contains no special power authorizing Uma to sell the land upon default. When Tito defaulted, Uma asked a notary public to sell the land at public auction after posting and publishing notices. Is the sale valid?

alac.answer: No, the extrajudicial sale is not valid.
alac.basis: Section 1 of Act 3135 governs the extrajudicial sale of mortgaged real property only when the sale is made under a special power inserted in or attached to the real estate mortgage. Absent such special power, the mortgagee must foreclose judicially under Rule 68 of the Rules of Court.
alac.application: Here, the mortgage contains no special power to sell. Uma therefore had no authority to foreclose extrajudicially, regardless of compliance with the posting and publication requirements.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the extrajudicial sale is void, and Uma must file an action for judicial foreclosure.

keyPoints: Extrajudicial foreclosure requires a special power to sell (Act 3135, Sec. 1)
Without it, judicial foreclosure under Rule 68
Compliance with notice requirements does not cure the lack of authority
cite: Act No. 3135, Secs. 1 and 3; Rules of Court, Rule 68

q: After the foreclosure of a REAL ESTATE mortgage, if the proceeds of the sale are less than the debt, the mortgagee:
choices: May recover the deficiency from the debtor
hints: Compare with the Recto Law for chattels sold on installments (Art. 1484).
The real estate mortgage is only a security for the debt.
why: The mortgage secures the debt; if the foreclosure sale does not cover it, the mortgagee may recover the deficiency (in judicial foreclosure, by a deficiency judgment under Rule 68, Sec. 6; in extrajudicial foreclosure, by a separate action). The bar on deficiency in Art. 1484 applies only to installment sales of personal property.
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 1484 and 2087; Rules of Court, Rule 68, Sec. 6

q: Bank V lent Wilma P5 million secured by a real estate mortgage with a special power to sell. Wilma defaulted. The bank foreclosed extrajudicially and bought the property at the auction for P3.5 million. The bank then sued Wilma for the P1.5 million balance. Wilma argues that by foreclosing, the bank waived any balance, as in the Recto Law. Is she correct?

alac.answer: No, Wilma is not correct. The bank may recover the deficiency.
alac.basis: A real estate mortgage is an accessory contract that secures the payment of the principal debt; under Article 2087 of the Civil Code, upon maturity, the mortgaged property may be sold for the payment of the creditor. Act 3135 does not prohibit the recovery of a deficiency after extrajudicial foreclosure, and the mortgagee may sue for it in a separate action. The prohibition on recovering a deficiency in Article 1484 (the Recto Law) applies only to sales of personal property on installments secured by a chattel mortgage on the thing sold.
alac.application: Here, the loan was secured by a mortgage on real property, not a chattel mortgage in an installment sale of personal property, so the Recto Law does not apply. The foreclosure sale produced only P3.5 million, leaving P1.5 million of the debt unpaid.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Bank V may recover the P1.5 million deficiency from Wilma.

keyPoints: Mortgage only secures the debt (Art. 2087)
Deficiency recoverable after foreclosure of a real estate mortgage
Recto Law (Art. 1484) applies only to installment sales of personal property
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 1484 and 2087; Act No. 3135

q: Under Section 6 of Act 3135, after an extrajudicial foreclosure sale of real property, the debtor may redeem the property within:
choices: One year from and after the date of the sale
hints: This is the right of redemption.
Jurisprudence counts it from registration of the certificate of sale.
why: Act 3135, Sec. 6: the debtor, his successors, judgment creditors, or subsequent lienholders may redeem within one year from and after the date of the sale (counted, under jurisprudence, from registration of the certificate of sale). Juridical persons whose property is foreclosed by a bank have a shorter period under RA 8791, Sec. 47.

q: XYZ Corp. mortgaged its office building to Bank Z, which foreclosed extrajudicially. The certificate of sale was registered one month after the auction. Four months after the auction, XYZ Corp. tendered the redemption price, claiming it had one year to redeem. Separately, Yuri, an individual whose land was judicially foreclosed by a private lender, wants to know if he can still recover his land after the court confirms the sale. Advise both.

alac.answer: XYZ Corp. can no longer redeem. Yuri has only the equity of redemption, which ends upon confirmation of the sale.
alac.basis: Section 47 of the General Banking Law (RA 8791) provides that, notwithstanding Act 3135, juridical persons whose property is sold in an extrajudicial foreclosure by a bank shall have the right to redeem until, but not after, the registration of the certificate of foreclosure sale, which in no case shall be more than three months after foreclosure, whichever is earlier. In judicial foreclosure under Rule 68 of the Rules of Court, the mortgagor has only an equity of redemption, the right to pay the debt within the period fixed by the court and before the sale is confirmed; there is no right of redemption after confirmation, except when the mortgagee is a bank.
alac.application: Here, XYZ Corp. is a juridical person whose property was foreclosed by a bank. Its right to redeem ended upon registration of the certificate of sale one month after the auction, so its tender four months later is too late. Yuri's land was judicially foreclosed by a private lender, not a bank, so he has only the equity of redemption, which he must exercise before the court confirms the sale.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, XYZ Corp. has lost its right to redeem, and Yuri must pay before confirmation of the sale, after which he can no longer recover his land.

keyPoints: Juridical persons, bank foreclosure: redeem until registration of the certificate of sale, max three months (RA 8791, Sec. 47)
Individuals in extrajudicial foreclosure: one year (Act 3135, Sec. 6)
Judicial foreclosure: equity of redemption only, unless the mortgagee is a bank
cite: RA 8791, Sec. 47; Act No. 3135, Sec. 6; Rules of Court, Rule 68

q: Under Section 12 of the Personal Property Security Act (RA 11057), a security interest may be perfected by:
choices: Registration of a notice, possession of the collateral by the secured creditor, or control of investment property and deposit accounts
hints: Creation is by a security agreement; perfection makes it effective against third parties.
There are three means.
why: RA 11057, Sec. 12: perfection by registration of a notice with the Registry, possession of the collateral by the secured creditor, or control of investment property and deposit accounts.

q: On 1 March, Ace Lending and Zed signed a written security agreement over Zed's delivery truck, but Ace did not register a notice. On 1 April, Bright Finance and Zed signed a security agreement over the same truck, and Bright registered its notice on 2 April. On 10 April, Ace registered its notice. Zed defaulted on both loans. Whose security interest has priority?

alac.answer: Bright Finance's security interest has priority.
alac.basis: Under Sections 5 and 6 of RA 11057, a security interest is created by a written security agreement. Under Section 12, it may be perfected by registration of a notice with the Registry. Section 17 provides that the priority of security interests in the same collateral shall be determined according to the time of registration of a notice or perfection by other means, without regard to the order of creation of the security interests.
alac.application: Here, Ace's security interest was created first, on 1 March, but it registered its notice only on 10 April. Bright's interest was created later but was perfected by registration on 2 April, earlier than Ace's. Priority depends on the time of registration, not of creation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Bright Finance has priority over the truck, and Ace ranks second.

keyPoints: Creation by written security agreement (RA 11057, Secs. 5-6)
Perfection by registration (Sec. 12)
Priority by time of registration or perfection, not creation (Sec. 17)

q: Under Section 30 of RA 11057, a notice of security interest becomes effective:
choices: When the security agreement is signed
At the time it is discoverable on the records of the Registry
hints: The PPSA Registry is electronic and public.
Third parties must be able to find it.
why: RA 11057, Sec. 30(a): a notice is effective at the time it is discoverable on the records of the Registry; it lasts for the term indicated unless continued.

q: Coral Credit registered a notice of security interest over the equipment of Dex Corp., but typed the wrong taxpayer identification number for Dex Corp., so that a search under Dex Corp.'s correct number does not show the notice. A later lender who searched the Registry and found nothing took a security interest and registered it correctly. Is Coral Credit's notice effective against the later lender?

alac.answer: No, Coral Credit's notice is not effective against Dex Corp. as grantor and the later lender.
alac.basis: Section 30(d) of RA 11057 provides that a notice that may not be retrieved in a search of the Registry against the correct identifier of the grantor shall be ineffective with respect to that grantor. Section 31 provides that a notice that does not provide the identification number of the grantor shall be seriously misleading.
alac.application: Here, Coral Credit's notice bore a wrong identification number, so it cannot be retrieved in a search under Dex Corp.'s correct identifier. The later lender searched correctly and found nothing. Coral Credit's notice is therefore ineffective with respect to Dex Corp., and its security interest is not perfected by registration.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the later lender's properly registered security interest prevails over Coral Credit's.

keyPoints: Notice effective when discoverable (RA 11057, Sec. 30(a))
Notice not retrievable under the grantor's correct identifier is ineffective (Sec. 30(d))
Wrong identification number is seriously misleading (Sec. 31)

q: Under Section 47 of RA 11057, a secured creditor may take possession of the collateral without judicial process if:
choices: The debtor is one day late
The security agreement so stipulates and possession can be taken without a breach of the peace
The collateral is worth less than P50,000
hints: Self-help repossession has two conditions.
Entering a private residence is a breach of the peace.
why: RA 11057, Sec. 47(a): the secured creditor may take possession of the collateral without judicial process if the security agreement so stipulates and possession can be taken without a breach of the peace; otherwise, it may apply for an expedited court order.

q: Eli defaulted on a loan secured by a security interest in his car. The security agreement allows repossession without court action. The lender's agents entered Eli's house at night, took the car keys, drove the car away, and sold it the next day without notice to Eli. Did the lender act lawfully?

alac.answer: No, the lender did not act lawfully.
alac.basis: Section 47 of RA 11057 allows a secured creditor to take possession of the collateral without judicial process only if the security agreement so stipulates and possession can be taken without a breach of the peace, which includes entering the private residence of the grantor without permission; otherwise, the creditor must apply for an expedited court order. Sections 50 and 51 require that the disposition of the collateral be commercially reasonable and that the grantor be notified not later than ten days before disposition.
alac.application: Here, although the agreement allowed repossession without court action, the agents entered Eli's house to take the keys, a breach of the peace. They should have applied for an expedited hearing and court order. The lender also sold the car the very next day without the required ten-day notice to Eli.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, both the repossession and the sale violated RA 11057, and the lender may be liable to Eli for damages.

keyPoints: Self-help repossession only without breach of the peace (RA 11057, Sec. 47)
Entering a private residence is a breach of the peace; seek an expedited court order
Commercially reasonable disposition with ten-day notice (Secs. 50-51)

q: Under Article 2197 of the Civil Code, which of the following is a kind of damages?
hints: There are six kinds of damages.
They range from actual to exemplary.
why: Art. 2197: damages may be actual or compensatory, moral, nominal, temperate or moderate, liquidated, or exemplary or corrective.

q: A supplier, acting in good faith, delivered defective machine parts to a factory, causing a two-day shutdown. The factory claims (a) lost profits for the two days and (b) the loss of a big export contract that the supplier could not have known about when the contract was made. For which damages is the supplier liable? Would the answer change if the supplier had acted in bad faith?

alac.answer: In good faith, the supplier is liable for the two days' lost profits but not for the export contract. In bad faith, it would be liable for all damages reasonably attributable to the breach.
alac.basis: Article 2195 of the Civil Code makes the rules on damages applicable to all obligations. Article 2200 includes in indemnification not only the value of the loss suffered but also the profits which the obligee failed to obtain. Article 2201 provides that in contracts, an obligor in good faith is liable for damages that are the natural and probable consequences of the breach and which the parties foresaw or could have reasonably foreseen when the obligation was constituted; in case of fraud, bad faith, malice or wanton attitude, the obligor is responsible for all damages which may be reasonably attributed to the non-performance.
alac.application: Here, a shutdown and the resulting lost profits are natural and probable consequences of delivering defective parts, and the supplier could have foreseen them. The loss of the export contract, which the supplier could not have known about, was not foreseeable when the contract was made. If the supplier had acted in bad faith, the foreseeability limit would not apply.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, a supplier in good faith pays only the foreseeable lost profits, while a supplier in bad faith would also answer for the lost export contract, if reasonably attributable to the breach.

keyPoints: Damages include lost profits (Art. 2200)
Good faith: only natural, probable and foreseeable damages (Art. 2201)
Bad faith: all damages reasonably attributable to the breach

q: Under Article 2199 of the Civil Code, actual or compensatory damages are awarded:
choices: Only for pecuniary loss duly proved
hints: Actual damages compensate real, proven loss.
Receipts and documents are the usual proof.
why: Art. 2199: except as provided by law or stipulation, one is entitled to adequate compensation only for such pecuniary loss as he has duly proved.

q: Fina's car was damaged by Greg's negligence. She claims P150,000 for repairs. She presented receipts totaling P90,000 and her own testimony that she spent another P60,000, without receipts. How much in actual damages should be awarded?

alac.answer: Only P90,000 should be awarded as actual damages.
alac.basis: Article 2199 of the Civil Code provides that one is entitled to adequate compensation only for such pecuniary loss as he has duly proved; such compensation is referred to as actual or compensatory damages. Actual damages must be proved with a reasonable degree of certainty, usually by receipts or other competent evidence, and cannot be based on speculation or a party's bare assertion.
alac.application: Here, Fina proved P90,000 of repair costs with receipts. The other P60,000 rests only on her testimony, without documentary support, so it is not duly proved.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Fina may recover P90,000 as actual damages; for the unproved part, the court may consider temperate damages if it finds that some loss was suffered but cannot be proved with certainty.

keyPoints: Actual damages only for pecuniary loss duly proved (Art. 2199)
Proof by receipts or competent evidence
Unproved loss may support temperate damages (Art. 2224)

q: Under Article 2203 of the Civil Code, the party suffering loss must:
choices: Exercise the diligence of a good father of a family to minimize the damages
hints: The injured party cannot let the damage grow.
Damages he could have avoided are not recoverable.
why: Art. 2203: the party suffering loss or injury must exercise the diligence of a good father of a family to minimize the damages resulting from the act or omission.

q: Henry's supplier failed to deliver the cement he ordered for a building project. Cement was readily available from other dealers at the same price, but Henry did not buy any and let his project stand idle for six months. He now claims six months of lost rentals from the supplier. Should the full claim be granted?

alac.answer: No, the full claim should not be granted.
alac.basis: Article 2203 of the Civil Code provides that the party suffering loss or injury must exercise the diligence of a good father of a family to minimize the damages resulting from the act or omission in question. Damages that the injured party could have avoided by reasonable effort are not recoverable.
alac.application: Here, cement was readily available elsewhere at the same price. A prudent person would have bought it and continued the project within a short time. Henry instead let the project stand idle for six months, so most of the lost rentals resulted from his own failure to mitigate.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Henry may recover only the damages for the reasonable period needed to obtain cement elsewhere, not for the entire six months.

keyPoints: Duty to minimize damages (Art. 2203)
Substitute supply was readily available
Avoidable losses are not recoverable

q: Under Article 2206 of the Civil Code, in case of death caused by a crime or quasi-delict, the defendant is liable, among others, for:
choices: The loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, paid to his heirs
Nothing, if there were mitigating circumstances
hints: Death indemnity is in addition to other damages.
The heirs lose what the deceased would have earned.
why: Art. 2206: in addition to the death indemnity, the defendant is liable for loss of the deceased's earning capacity, support to dependents who are not heirs (up to five years), and moral damages to the spouse, descendants and ascendants for mental anguish.

q: Ivo, aged 40, earning P300,000 a year, was killed when Jun's truck, negligently driven, hit him. Ivo's heirs sue for loss of earning capacity. How should this be computed, and what other damages may they claim?

alac.answer: Loss of earning capacity should be computed by the settled formula, and the heirs may also claim civil indemnity and moral damages, among others.
alac.basis: Article 2206 of the Civil Code provides that in case of death caused by a quasi-delict, the defendant shall be liable for the loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, paid to his heirs, and that the spouse, legitimate and illegitimate descendants and ascendants may demand moral damages for mental anguish. Settled jurisprudence computes the net earning capacity as: two-thirds of (80 minus the age at death), multiplied by (gross annual income less reasonable living expenses, usually fixed at 50% of gross income absent proof).
alac.application: Here, Ivo was 40, so his life expectancy is 2/3 x (80 - 40) = 26.67 years. His net annual income is P300,000 less 50% living expenses, or P150,000. His loss of earning capacity is therefore about 26.67 x P150,000 = P4,000,000. In addition, his heirs may claim the death indemnity and moral damages for their mental anguish, and actual damages such as proven funeral expenses.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the heirs may recover about P4 million for loss of earning capacity, plus death indemnity, moral damages, and proven actual damages.

keyPoints: Loss of earning capacity is recoverable (Art. 2206(1))
Formula: 2/3 x (80 - age) x (gross annual income - living expenses)
Also death indemnity and moral damages for the heirs (Art. 2206(3))

q: Under Article 2208 of the Civil Code, absent stipulation, attorney's fees may be recovered when, among others:
choices: The defendant acted in gross and evident bad faith in refusing to satisfy the plaintiff's plainly valid, just and demandable claim
The lawyer charges a high fee
The case lasts more than a year
hints: The general rule is that attorney's fees are not recoverable.
Art. 2208 lists the exceptions.
why: Art. 2208: absent stipulation, attorney's fees and litigation expenses cannot be recovered, except in the listed cases, such as when exemplary damages are awarded or when the defendant acted in gross and evident bad faith in refusing a plainly valid claim.

q: Karen sued Lyle to collect an unpaid loan evidenced by a promissory note that Lyle admitted signing. Lyle had no defense but refused to pay for two years, telling Karen to "go to court." Karen won. The note says nothing about attorney's fees. May Karen recover attorney's fees?

alac.answer: Yes, Karen may recover attorney's fees.
alac.basis: Article 2208 of the Civil Code provides that, in the absence of stipulation, attorney's fees and expenses of litigation cannot be recovered, except, among others, where the defendant acted in gross and evident bad faith in refusing to satisfy the plaintiff's plainly valid, just and demandable claim, and where the defendant's act compelled the plaintiff to incur expenses to protect his interest.
alac.application: Here, Karen's claim was plainly valid: Lyle admitted signing the note and had no defense. He nonetheless refused to pay for two years and dared Karen to sue. This is gross and evident bad faith that forced her to litigate.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, although the note is silent on attorney's fees, Karen may recover them under Article 2208(5).

keyPoints: General rule: no attorney's fees absent stipulation (Art. 2208)
Exception: gross and evident bad faith in refusing a plainly valid claim
Court must state the factual basis for the award

q: Under Article 2220 of the Civil Code, moral damages may be awarded for breach of contract when:
choices: The defendant acted fraudulently or in bad faith
hints: Simple breach is not enough.
The defendant's state of mind matters.
why: Art. 2220: willful injury to property may justify moral damages; the same rule applies to breaches of contract where the defendant acted fraudulently or in bad faith.

q: Mina booked and paid for a hotel room for her wedding night. On arrival, the hotel told her the room had been given to a higher-paying guest, although the staff knew of her booking, and loudly refused her in front of her wedding guests. She suffered humiliation and anguish. May she recover moral damages for the breach of contract?

alac.answer: Yes, Mina may recover moral damages.
alac.basis: Article 2217 of the Civil Code provides that moral damages include mental anguish, wounded feelings, social humiliation and similar injury, and may be recovered if they are the proximate result of the defendant's wrongful act. Article 2220 provides that moral damages may be awarded for breaches of contract where the defendant acted fraudulently or in bad faith.
alac.application: Here, the hotel breached its contract with Mina by giving her paid room to another guest, knowingly and for profit, which is bad faith. The manner of refusal before her wedding guests caused her humiliation and anguish, which proximately resulted from the hotel's wrongful act.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Mina may recover moral damages, in addition to actual damages for the breach.

keyPoints: Moral damages cover anguish and humiliation (Art. 2217)
In breach of contract, only if fraud or bad faith (Art. 2220)
Knowingly giving away a paid booking for profit is bad faith

q: Under Article 2221 of the Civil Code, nominal damages are awarded:
choices: To vindicate or recognize a right that has been violated, not to indemnify a loss
As a penalty for the public good
hints: No pecuniary loss needs to be shown.
The point is to recognize the right.
why: Art. 2221: nominal damages are adjudicated so that a violated right may be vindicated or recognized, not to indemnify any loss.

q: Nestor's employer dismissed him for a valid cause, but without giving him the notices and hearing required by law. Nestor proved no actual loss from the procedural lapse, since the dismissal itself was justified. Is he entitled to any damages?

alac.answer: Yes, Nestor is entitled to nominal damages.
alac.basis: Article 2221 of the Civil Code provides that nominal damages are adjudicated in order that a right of the plaintiff, which has been violated or invaded by the defendant, may be vindicated or recognized, and not for the purpose of indemnifying the plaintiff for any loss suffered by him. Article 2216 provides that no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary for nominal damages.
alac.application: Here, the dismissal was for a valid cause, so Nestor suffered no compensable loss from losing his job. However, his right to procedural due process, to notice and hearing, was violated. That right deserves to be vindicated even without proof of loss.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Nestor may be awarded nominal damages to recognize the violation of his right to due process.

keyPoints: Nominal damages vindicate a violated right (Art. 2221)
No proof of pecuniary loss needed (Art. 2216)
Violation of procedural due process in dismissal

q: Under Article 2224 of the Civil Code, temperate damages may be recovered when:
choices: No loss at all was suffered
Some pecuniary loss was suffered but its amount cannot, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty
The loss was fully proved with receipts
The defendant acted in bad faith
hints: They are more than nominal but less than compensatory.
They fill the gap where exact proof is impossible.
why: Art. 2224: temperate damages, more than nominal but less than compensatory, may be recovered when some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount cannot be proved with certainty.

q: Ofelia's small sari-sari store was closed for a month because a neighbor's negligent construction work blocked its entrance. She clearly lost sales, but she kept no records and could not prove the exact amount. The trial court denied any damages for lost income for lack of proof. Was this correct?

alac.answer: No, the court should have awarded temperate damages.
alac.basis: Article 2224 of the Civil Code provides that temperate or moderate damages, which are more than nominal but less than compensatory damages, may be recovered when the court finds that some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount cannot, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty.
alac.application: Here, it is clear that Ofelia suffered a loss of income because her store was closed for a month due to the neighbor's negligence. But because of the nature of a small store without records, the exact amount cannot be proved with certainty. This is precisely the situation that temperate damages address.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should award Ofelia a reasonable amount as temperate damages for her lost income.

keyPoints: Pecuniary loss certainly suffered
Amount cannot be proved with certainty from the nature of the case
Temperate damages: more than nominal, less than compensatory (Art. 2224)

q: Under Article 2226 of the Civil Code, liquidated damages are those:
choices: Fixed by the court after trial
Agreed upon by the parties to a contract, to be paid in case of breach
hints: They are fixed in advance.
They may be reduced if unconscionable (Art. 2227).
why: Art. 2226: liquidated damages are those agreed upon by the parties, to be paid in case of breach; Art. 2227: they shall be equitably reduced if iniquitous or unconscionable.

q: A construction contract fixed liquidated damages of P10,000 per day of delay in completing the building. The contractor finished on time, but the building's roof leaked because of defective work. The owner demands P10,000 for every day the roof leaked. Is the owner correct?

alac.answer: No, the owner cannot use the liquidated damages clause for the defective roof.
alac.basis: Article 2226 of the Civil Code defines liquidated damages as those agreed upon by the parties to be paid in case of breach. Article 2228 provides that when the breach committed by the defendant is not the one contemplated by the parties in agreeing upon the liquidated damages, the law shall determine the measure of damages, and not the stipulation.
alac.application: Here, the parties agreed on liquidated damages for delay in completion. The contractor was not late; its breach was defective work on the roof. That breach was not the one the parties contemplated when they fixed the P10,000 daily rate.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the owner must prove his actual damages for the defective roof under the general rules on damages, instead of relying on the liquidated damages clause.

keyPoints: Liquidated damages are agreed in advance (Art. 2226)
Apply only to the breach contemplated (Art. 2228)
Other breaches: damages measured by law

q: Under Article 2234 of the Civil Code, before exemplary damages may be considered, the plaintiff must show that:
choices: He is entitled to moral, temperate or compensatory damages
The case was filed within a year
hints: Exemplary damages are never awarded alone.
They are added to other damages.
why: Art. 2234: the amount of exemplary damages need not be proved, but the plaintiff must show that he is entitled to moral, temperate or compensatory damages before exemplary damages may be considered.

q: A bus company, to save on costs, knowingly let its buses run with worn-out brakes. One bus crashed, injuring Pia, who proved her medical expenses and suffered serious physical pain and anxiety. Besides actual and moral damages, may Pia recover exemplary damages?

alac.answer: Yes, Pia may recover exemplary damages.
alac.basis: Article 2229 of the Civil Code provides that exemplary or corrective damages are imposed, by way of example or correction for the public good, in addition to moral, temperate, liquidated or compensatory damages. Article 2232 provides that in contracts, the court may award exemplary damages if the defendant acted in a wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive, or malevolent manner. Article 2234 requires that the plaintiff first show entitlement to moral, temperate or compensatory damages.
alac.application: Here, the bus company, a common carrier bound by contract to carry Pia safely, knowingly ran buses with worn-out brakes to save costs, which is wanton and reckless. Pia proved her actual damages and her entitlement to moral damages for her physical suffering and anxiety. The requisites for exemplary damages are therefore present.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Pia may recover exemplary damages in addition to her actual and moral damages, to deter such conduct for the public good.

keyPoints: Exemplary damages are for example or correction (Art. 2229)
In contracts, for wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive or malevolent acts (Art. 2232)
Plaintiff must first be entitled to moral, temperate or compensatory damages (Art. 2234)

q: Which of the following is NOT an element of a quasi-delict under Article 2176 of the Civil Code?
choices: Fault or negligence of the defendant
A causal connection between the fault or negligence and the damage
A pre-existing contract between the parties
hints: A quasi-delict is also called culpa aquiliana.
If there is a pre-existing contract, the liability is usually contractual.
why: Art. 2176: whoever by act or omission causes damage to another, there being fault or negligence, must pay for it; such fault or negligence, if there is no pre-existing contractual relation, is a quasi-delict. Elements: damage, fault or negligence, causal connection, and no pre-existing contract.

q: While backing out of his driveway without looking, Ariel hit and injured Bela, a jogger passing on the sidewalk. They had no prior relationship. Bela sues Ariel for damages. On what basis may Ariel be held liable, and what must Bela prove?

alac.answer: Ariel may be held liable for quasi-delict, and Bela must prove damage, Ariel's negligence, and the causal connection between them.
alac.basis: Article 2176 of the Civil Code provides that whoever by act or omission causes damage to another, there being fault or negligence, is obliged to pay for the damage done; such fault or negligence, if there is no pre-existing contractual relation between the parties, is called a quasi-delict.
alac.application: Here, Bela suffered injuries, which is damage. Ariel backed out of his driveway without looking, which is negligence. His negligence directly caused Bela's injuries. Ariel and Bela had no pre-existing contract.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ariel is liable to Bela for quasi-delict once she proves her damage, his negligence, and the causal connection by a preponderance of evidence.

keyPoints: Elements of quasi-delict (Art. 2176)
No pre-existing contract
Proof by preponderance of evidence

q: In culpa contractual (breach of contract), can the employer escape liability by proving due diligence in selecting and supervising the employee who caused the breach?
choices: No; that defense applies to quasi-delicts, not to breach of contract
Yes, if the employee was a minor
Only if the contract is oral
hints: The diligence defense comes from Art. 2180, which governs quasi-delicts.
In contract, the obligor answers for the persons he uses to perform.
why: In culpa contractual, the defendant is liable for breach of the contract itself, and the defense of diligence in the selection and supervision of employees (Art. 2180) does not apply; it applies only to culpa aquiliana (Cangco v. Manila Railroad Co., G.R. No. 12191, October 14, 1918).
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 1170 and 2180; Cangco v. Manila Railroad Co., G.R. No. 12191, October 14, 1918

q: Cesar held a confirmed first-class plane ticket. At boarding, the airline's manager, in front of other passengers, rudely ordered him to give his seat to a "more important" passenger and to move to economy, threatening to have him removed. Cesar sued for breach of contract and for moral damages. The airline argues that only breach of contract is involved, so moral damages cannot be awarded. Is the airline correct?

alac.answer: No, the airline is not correct. Cesar may recover moral damages.
alac.basis: The same act that breaks a contract may also be a tort. In Air France v. Carrascoso, G.R. No. L-21438, September 28, 1966, the Supreme Court held that the wrongful and humiliating ejection of a passenger from his first-class seat was a breach of contract that also amounted to a tort, for which moral damages may be awarded. Article 2220 of the Civil Code allows moral damages for breach of contract where the defendant acted fraudulently or in bad faith, and Article 21 makes liable any person who wilfully causes injury in a manner contrary to morals, good customs or public policy.
alac.application: Here, the airline breached its contract by taking away Cesar's confirmed first-class seat. Its manager also did so in bad faith and in a humiliating manner, in front of other passengers. This conduct is both a breach of contract and a tort.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Cesar may recover moral damages, in addition to damages for the breach of contract.

keyPoints: The same act may be a breach of contract and a tort (Air France v. Carrascoso)
Moral damages for breach in bad faith (Art. 2220)
Wilful injury contrary to morals (Art. 21)
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 21 and 2220; Air France v. Carrascoso, G.R. No. L-21438, September 28, 1966

q: Under Article 19 of the Civil Code (abuse of rights), every person must, in exercising his rights and performing his duties:
choices: Act only for his own benefit
Act with justice, give everyone his due, and observe honesty and good faith
hints: A legal right may still be exercised wrongfully.
The test includes bad faith and intent to prejudice.
why: Art. 19: every person must act with justice, give everyone his due, and observe honesty and good faith. Its elements: a legal right or duty, exercised in bad faith, for the sole intent of prejudicing or injuring another (Globe Mackay Cable and Radio Corp. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 81262, August 25, 1989).

q: An employer suspected its employee Dino of fraud. Even after its own investigation cleared him, the employer's manager kept calling Dino a "crook" in front of co-workers, filed criminal complaints he knew were baseless, and wrote to Dino's prospective employers that he was dishonest. The employer argues that it was merely exercising its right to protect its business. Is the employer liable?

alac.answer: Yes, the employer is liable for damages for abuse of rights.
alac.basis: Article 19 of the Civil Code requires every person, in the exercise of his rights, to act with justice, give everyone his due, and observe honesty and good faith. In Globe Mackay Cable and Radio Corp. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 81262, August 25, 1989, on similar facts, the Supreme Court held the employer liable, explaining that a right exercised in bad faith, with the sole intent of prejudicing or injuring another, gives rise to liability, and that Article 21 likewise makes liable one who wilfully causes injury contrary to morals and good customs.
alac.application: Here, the employer had the right to investigate a suspected fraud. But after Dino was cleared, it continued to insult him publicly, filed baseless complaints, and wrote to his prospective employers to harm him. These acts were done in bad faith and with the intent to injure him.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the employer abused its rights and is liable to Dino for damages, including moral and exemplary damages.

keyPoints: Elements: legal right, exercised in bad faith, to prejudice another (Art. 19)
Continued harassment after clearance shows bad faith
Globe Mackay v. CA
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 19 and 21; Globe Mackay Cable and Radio Corp. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 81262, August 25, 1989

q: Under Article 20 of the Civil Code, a person who, contrary to law, wilfully or negligently causes damage to another:
choices: Is liable only if convicted of a crime
Shall indemnify the latter for the same
Is liable only for intentional acts
Is never liable if the law has no penalty
hints: Art. 20 is a catch-all for violations of law.
Both wilful and negligent acts are covered.
why: Art. 20: every person who, contrary to law, wilfully or negligently causes damage to another shall indemnify the latter.

q: A factory discharged untreated waste into a river in violation of environmental laws. The waste killed the fish in Eddie's fishpond downstream. The factory argues that the environmental law provides only for fines and does not give private persons any right to damages. Can Eddie recover?

alac.answer: Yes, Eddie can recover damages.
alac.basis: Article 20 of the Civil Code provides that every person who, contrary to law, wilfully or negligently causes damage to another shall indemnify the latter for the same. It provides a general sanction for violations of law, even when the specific law does not itself provide a civil remedy.
alac.application: Here, the factory discharged untreated waste in violation of environmental laws, an act contrary to law. That act damaged Eddie by killing the fish in his fishpond. The fact that the environmental law only imposes fines does not prevent Eddie from claiming damages under Article 20.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the factory must indemnify Eddie for his loss.

keyPoints: Damage caused contrary to law must be indemnified (Art. 20)
Applies even if the special law provides only penalties
Wilful or negligent violation

q: Article 21 of the Civil Code makes liable any person who wilfully causes loss or injury to another in a manner that is:
choices: Contrary to a specific statute only
Contrary to morals, good customs or public policy
hints: Art. 21 covers wrongs not punished by any specific law.
The act must be wilful.
why: Art. 21: any person who wilfully causes loss or injury to another in a manner contrary to morals, good customs or public policy shall compensate the latter.

q: Faisal, a foreign student, promised to marry Gemma, a young woman from a conservative family, and on the strength of that promise persuaded her to live with him and have sexual relations. He had no intention of marrying her and later abandoned her. A mere breach of promise to marry is not actionable. Can Gemma recover damages?

alac.answer: Yes, Gemma can recover damages under Article 21.
alac.basis: A mere breach of a promise to marry is not an actionable wrong. However, Article 21 of the Civil Code makes liable any person who wilfully causes loss or injury to another in a manner contrary to morals, good customs or public policy. In Gashem Shookat Baksh v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 97336, February 19, 1993, the Supreme Court held that where a man's promise to marry was the proximate cause of the woman's giving herself to him, and he never intended to keep it, he is liable for damages under Article 21.
alac.application: Here, Faisal did not merely break a promise. He made it with no intention of keeping it, to induce Gemma to live with him and have sexual relations. That deceitful conduct wilfully injured her in a manner contrary to morals and good customs.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Gemma may recover damages, including moral damages, under Article 21.

keyPoints: Mere breach of promise to marry is not actionable
Deceit to obtain sexual relations is contrary to morals (Art. 21)
Gashem Shookat Baksh v. CA
cite: Civil Code, Art. 21; Gashem Shookat Baksh v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 97336, February 19, 1993

q: Under Article 22 of the Civil Code, a person who acquires something at the expense of another without just or legal ground must:
hints: No one should be enriched at another's expense.
The remedy is accion in rem verso.
why: Art. 22: every person who, through an act of performance by another or any other means, acquires or comes into possession of something at the expense of the latter without just or legal ground, shall return it.

q: Hector, a contractor, built a perimeter fence on what he and the lot owner both believed was the owner's lot. It turned out that part of the fence stood on the adjoining lot of Ida, who kept and used the fence as her own. Hector has no contract with Ida, did not act by mistake in paying anyone, and has no other remedy against her. Can he recover the value of the fence portion from Ida?

alac.answer: Yes, Hector may recover from Ida under the principle against unjust enrichment.
alac.basis: Article 22 of the Civil Code provides that every person who through an act of performance by another, or any other means, acquires or comes into possession of something at the expense of the latter without just or legal ground, shall return the same to him. The action (accion in rem verso) requires that the defendant was enriched, the plaintiff suffered a loss, the enrichment was without just or legal ground, and the plaintiff has no other action based on contract, quasi-contract, crime or quasi-delict.
alac.application: Here, Ida acquired and uses the part of the fence on her lot, which Hector built at his expense. She has no just or legal ground to keep the benefit for free, and Hector has no other action against her.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Hector may recover from Ida the reasonable value of the fence portion she kept, under Article 22.

keyPoints: Enrichment without just or legal ground must be returned (Art. 22)
Elements of accion in rem verso
Subsidiary: no other available action

q: Under Article 1314 of the Civil Code, a third person who induces another to violate his contract:
choices: Shall be liable for damages to the other contracting party
Is liable only for a crime
Becomes a party to the contract
hints: This is tortious interference with contract.
The injured party is the other contracting party.
why: Art. 1314: any third person who induces another to violate his contract shall be liable for damages to the other contracting party.

q: Jasmine had a lease on a warehouse for five years. Kenneth, a competitor who knew of the lease, offered the owner a higher rent to cancel Jasmine's lease and lease to him instead; the owner did so. Jasmine sued Kenneth. Kenneth argues he acted only to advance his own business, without malice. Is Kenneth liable?

alac.answer: Kenneth may be enjoined and held liable for interfering with Jasmine's lease, but he is not liable for damages if he acted purely for legitimate business interest without malice.
alac.basis: Article 1314 of the Civil Code provides that any third person who induces another to violate his contract shall be liable for damages to the other contracting party. The elements of tortious interference are the existence of a valid contract, knowledge of it by the third person, and interference without legal justification. In So Ping Bun v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 120554, September 21, 1999, the Supreme Court held that a competitor who induced the cancellation of another's lease committed tortious interference and could be enjoined, but that where the interferer acted from legitimate business motives and not from malice, he is not liable for damages.
alac.application: Here, Jasmine had a valid lease, Kenneth knew of it, and he induced the owner to cancel it by offering higher rent. That is interference with her contract. However, if Kenneth acted only to advance his own business, without malice or bad faith toward Jasmine, damages may not be awarded against him.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Kenneth committed tortious interference and may be restrained, but he is liable for damages only if malice or bad faith is shown; the owner remains liable to Jasmine for breach of the lease.

keyPoints: Inducing breach of contract is actionable (Art. 1314)
Elements: valid contract, knowledge, interference without justification
No damages if motivated only by legitimate business interest (So Ping Bun v. CA)
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1314; So Ping Bun v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 120554, September 21, 1999

q: Under Article 23 of the Civil Code, a person may be liable for damage to another's property even without fault or negligence when:
choices: He was benefited by the act or event that caused the damage
hints: This is liability without fault, based on equity.
The key word is "benefited."
why: Art. 23: even when an act or event causing damage to another's property was not due to the defendant's fault or negligence, he is liable for indemnity if through it he was benefited.

q: A flash flood was about to inundate Lorna's rice field. To save her crop, the barangay, without any fault of Lorna, opened a channel that diverted the water onto Mario's adjoining fishpond, destroying his fish. Lorna's crop was saved. Mario sues Lorna, who argues she did nothing wrong. Is Lorna liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Lorna is liable to indemnify Mario to the extent of the benefit she received.
alac.basis: Article 23 of the Civil Code provides that even when an act or event causing damage to another's property was not due to the fault or negligence of the defendant, the latter shall be liable for indemnity if through the act or event he was benefited.
alac.application: Here, Lorna was not at fault; the barangay diverted the water. But the diversion that destroyed Mario's fish was the same event that saved Lorna's crop. She was benefited at Mario's expense.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Lorna must indemnify Mario, at least to the extent of the benefit she received, even though she was not negligent.

keyPoints: Liability without fault when benefited (Art. 23)
Same event caused the damage and the benefit
Based on equity

q: Under Article 26 of the Civil Code, which act gives rise to a cause of action for damages, even if it is not a crime?
choices: Prying into the privacy of another's residence
hints: Art. 26 protects dignity, privacy and peace of mind.
These are intentional torts.
why: Art. 26: prying into the privacy of another's residence, meddling with private life or family relations, intriguing to alienate friends, and vexing or humiliating another for personal conditions give rise to damages, prevention and other relief.

q: Nonoy installed a CCTV camera on his house that was aimed directly into the bedroom window of his neighbor, Olivia, and he shared clips of her family's private moments with friends. No criminal case was filed. What remedies does Olivia have?

alac.answer: Olivia may sue Nonoy for damages and ask the court to order the camera removed or redirected.
alac.basis: Article 26 of the Civil Code provides that every person shall respect the dignity, personality, privacy and peace of mind of his neighbors and other persons, and that acts such as prying into the privacy of another's residence and meddling with or disturbing the private life of another, though they may not constitute a criminal offense, shall produce a cause of action for damages, prevention and other relief.
alac.application: Here, Nonoy deliberately aimed his camera into Olivia's bedroom and shared clips of her family's private moments. This is an intentional intrusion into the privacy of her residence and private life, even if no crime was charged.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Olivia may recover damages, including moral damages, and obtain an order preventing further intrusion.

keyPoints: Intentional tort: invasion of privacy (Art. 26)
Actionable even if not a crime
Remedies: damages, prevention and other relief

q: Negligent torts differ from intentional torts in that the defendant:
choices: Failed to observe the care required by the circumstances, without intending the harm
Was strictly liable regardless of care
hints: Intent is not needed for negligence.
The test is the care a prudent person would have used.
why: In negligent torts, liability arises from the omission of the diligence required by the circumstances (Arts. 1173 and 2176), not from an intent to cause harm.

q: A store owner, Pablo, left a puddle of cooking oil on the floor of the store's aisle for two hours without cleaning it or putting up a warning sign. A customer, Queenie, slipped and broke her arm. Pablo argues he never intended to hurt anyone. Is he liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Pablo is liable for negligence.
alac.basis: Article 2176 of the Civil Code makes liable whoever by act or omission causes damage to another, there being fault or negligence. Article 1173 defines negligence as the omission of that diligence which is required by the nature of the obligation and corresponds with the circumstances of the persons, of the time and of the place; absent a stated standard, the diligence of a good father of a family is required.
alac.application: Here, a prudent store owner would have cleaned the spill or at least put up a warning, especially after two hours. Pablo's omission fell below that standard and caused Queenie's injury. Intent to harm is not needed in a negligent tort.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Pablo is liable to Queenie for damages.

keyPoints: Negligence: omission of the required diligence (Art. 1173)
Liability for damage caused by negligence (Art. 2176)
Intent is not an element

q: Under Article 2187 of the Civil Code, manufacturers and processors of foodstuffs are liable for death or injuries caused by noxious or harmful substances used:
choices: Only if there is a contract with the consumer
Even though no contractual relation exists between them and the consumers
Only if the product was imported
hints: This is a form of product liability.
Privity of contract is not required.
why: Art. 2187: manufacturers and processors of foodstuffs, drinks, toilet articles and similar goods are liable for death or injuries caused by noxious or harmful substances, although no contractual relation exists with the consumers.

q: Rina bought a bottled juice from a sari-sari store. The juice contained a harmful chemical used by the manufacturer, and Rina was hospitalized. The manufacturer argues that Rina bought the juice from a store, not from it, and that it had no contract with her. Is the manufacturer liable?

alac.answer: Yes, the manufacturer is liable.
alac.basis: Article 2187 of the Civil Code provides that manufacturers and processors of foodstuffs, drinks, toilet articles and similar goods shall be liable for death or injuries caused by any noxious or harmful substances used, although no contractual relation exists between them and the consumers. Article 2183 similarly imposes liability on the possessor of an animal for damage it causes, showing other instances where liability attaches by law.
alac.application: Here, the juice is a drink processed by the manufacturer, and the harmful chemical it used injured Rina. The law makes the manufacturer liable even if Rina bought the product from a store and had no contract with the manufacturer.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the manufacturer must answer to Rina for her injuries.

keyPoints: Product liability of manufacturers of food and drinks (Art. 2187)
No contractual relation needed
Liability imposed by law

q: A direct tortfeasor is one who:
choices: Is liable for the acts of others
Personally causes the damage by his own act or omission with fault or negligence
hints: Contrast with persons made responsible for others (Art. 2180).
Art. 2176 speaks of one's own act or omission.
why: A direct tortfeasor is liable under Art. 2176 for damage caused by his own act or omission with fault or negligence; vicarious liability under Art. 2180 is for the acts of others.

q: Sonny, a delivery rider employed by Fast Co., negligently ran a red light and hit Tomas. Tomas sued only Sonny. Sonny argues that Tomas should have sued his employer, Fast Co., instead. Is Sonny correct?

alac.answer: No, Sonny is not correct. He is directly liable as the tortfeasor.
alac.basis: Article 2176 of the Civil Code makes whoever by act or omission causes damage to another, there being fault or negligence, liable for the damage done. Article 2180 makes employers also responsible for damage caused by their employees, but this liability is in addition to, not in place of, the liability of the employee who committed the act. Under Article 2194, the responsibility of two or more persons liable for a quasi-delict is solidary.
alac.application: Here, Sonny himself negligently ran a red light and hit Tomas, so he is a direct tortfeasor. Fast Co. may also be liable as his employer, but Tomas may choose to sue Sonny, or both.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Tomas may hold Sonny directly liable; the employer's liability does not excuse him.

keyPoints: Direct tortfeasor liable for his own negligence (Art. 2176)
Employer's liability is additional (Art. 2180)
Liability is solidary (Art. 2194)

q: Under Article 2180 of the Civil Code, employers are liable for damages caused by their employees and household helpers:
choices: Acting within the scope of their assigned tasks, even if the employer is not engaged in any business
Only if the employer was present
Only if the employee is a minor
hints: The employee must be acting within the scope of his tasks.
Even households can be employers.
why: Art. 2180: employers are liable for damages caused by employees and household helpers acting within the scope of their assigned tasks, even though the employers are not engaged in any business or industry.

q: Uma's family driver, while driving her children to school, negligently hit a pedestrian, Vic. On Sunday, the same driver took the car without permission for a joyride and hit another pedestrian, Wen. Is Uma liable to Vic and to Wen?

alac.answer: Uma is liable to Vic, but not to Wen, unless she fails to prove due diligence as to Vic.
alac.basis: Article 2180 of the Civil Code provides that employers shall be liable for damages caused by their employees and household helpers acting within the scope of their assigned tasks, even though the employers are not engaged in any business or industry. The responsibility ceases when the employer proves that she observed all the diligence of a good father of a family to prevent damage.
alac.application: Here, when the driver hit Vic, he was performing his assigned task of driving Uma's children to school, so Uma is presumed liable, unless she proves diligence in selecting and supervising him. When he hit Wen, he was on an unauthorized joyride on a Sunday, outside the scope of his assigned tasks.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Uma is liable to Vic (subject to the defense of due diligence), but not to Wen, whose remedy is against the driver.

keyPoints: Employer liable for acts within the scope of assigned tasks (Art. 2180)
Not liable for acts outside that scope
Defense: diligence of a good father of a family

q: Does Article 2176 of the Civil Code (quasi-delict) cover only negligent acts?
choices: No; it also covers voluntary or intentional acts, so persons responsible for others may be liable for their intentional acts too
hints: The Supreme Court gave Art. 2176 a broad reading.
Parents may answer for their minor child's intentional acts.
why: Art. 2176 covers acts that are criminal in character, whether voluntary or negligent (Elcano v. Hill, G.R. No. L-24803, May 26, 1977); thus those responsible for others under Art. 2180 and Family Code Art. 221 may be liable even for intentional acts.
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 2176 and 2180; Family Code, Art. 221; Elcano v. Hill, G.R. No. L-24803, May 26, 1977

q: Xavi, a 16-year-old living with his parents, intentionally stabbed Yoyo during a quarrel. He was acquitted in the criminal case for lack of discernment. Yoyo's family sued Xavi's parents for damages. The parents argue that Article 2176 covers only negligence, not intentional acts, and that Xavi was acquitted. Are the parents liable?

alac.answer: Yes, the parents may be held liable.
alac.basis: In Elcano v. Hill, G.R. No. L-24803, May 26, 1977, the Supreme Court held that Article 2176 covers not only negligent acts but also voluntary and intentional acts, and that an acquittal in the criminal case does not bar a civil action based on quasi-delict for the same act. Article 221 of the Family Code makes parents civilly liable for injuries caused by the acts or omissions of their unemancipated children living in their company and under their parental authority, subject to the appropriate defenses provided by law.
alac.application: Here, Xavi is an unemancipated minor living with his parents. His intentional act injured Yoyo. His acquittal for lack of discernment does not erase the civil liability arising from the act, and Article 2176 covers intentional acts as well.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Xavi's parents may be held liable, unless they prove that they observed the proper diligence to prevent the damage.

keyPoints: Art. 2176 covers intentional acts (Elcano v. Hill)
Acquittal does not bar the civil action for quasi-delict
Parents liable for acts of minor children living with them (FC Art. 221)
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 2176 and 2180; Family Code, Art. 221; Elcano v. Hill, G.R. No. L-24803, May 26, 1977

q: Under Article 2180 of the Civil Code, when an employee causes damage in the course of his work, the employer is:
choices: Presumed negligent in selecting or supervising the employee, but may rebut the presumption by proving the diligence of a good father of a family
hints: The presumption is juris tantum.
Read the last paragraph of Art. 2180.
why: Art. 2180 presumes negligence on the part of persons responsible for others; the responsibility ceases when they prove that they observed all the diligence of a good father of a family to prevent damage.

q: A bus company's driver hit a pedestrian. In the quasi-delict case against the company, the company proved that it hired the driver only after checking his license, driving record and clearances, required him to pass written and actual driving tests, and conducted regular seminars and random checks on its drivers. Can the company escape liability?

alac.answer: Yes, the company may escape liability to the pedestrian.
alac.basis: Article 2180 of the Civil Code makes employers liable for damages caused by their employees acting within the scope of their tasks, based on a presumption of negligence in the selection or supervision of the employee. The last paragraph provides that the responsibility shall cease when the employer proves that it observed all the diligence of a good father of a family to prevent damage.
alac.application: Here, the suit is based on quasi-delict, not on a contract of carriage with the pedestrian. The company overcame the presumption by proving diligence in selection (checking the license, record and clearances, testing) and in supervision (seminars and random checks).
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the company may be absolved, while the driver remains liable as the direct tortfeasor.

keyPoints: Presumption of negligence in selection and supervision (Art. 2180)
Rebuttable by proof of diligence of a good father of a family
Defense available in quasi-delict, not against passengers in contract of carriage

q: The liability of an employer under Article 2180 of the Civil Code for the quasi-delict of an employee is:
choices: Subsidiary, only after the employee is insolvent
Primary and direct, and solidary with the employee
hints: Contrast with the subsidiary liability of employers under the Revised Penal Code.
Art. 2194 makes the liability solidary.
why: Under Art. 2180, the employer's liability for the employee's quasi-delict is primary and direct, not subsidiary (Barredo v. Garcia, G.R. No. 48006, July 8, 1942), and solidary with the employee (Art. 2194); the employer may recover from the employee what it paid (Art. 2181).
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 2180, 2181 and 2194; Barredo v. Garcia, G.R. No. 48006, July 8, 1942

q: A taxi driver negligently killed a pedestrian. Instead of waiting for the criminal case against the driver, the victim's heirs sued the taxi operator directly for quasi-delict. The operator argues that its liability is only subsidiary and arises only if the driver is convicted and proves insolvent. Is the operator correct?

alac.answer: No, the operator is not correct. Its liability under quasi-delict is primary and direct.
alac.basis: Under the Revised Penal Code, an employer's liability for the crime of its employee is subsidiary and arises only upon the employee's conviction and insolvency. But in Barredo v. Garcia, G.R. No. 48006, July 8, 1942, the Supreme Court held that the injured party may instead sue the employer for quasi-delict under Article 2180 of the Civil Code, in which case the employer's liability is primary and direct, independent of the criminal case. Article 2177 provides that responsibility for quasi-delict is entirely separate and distinct from civil liability arising from crime, but the plaintiff cannot recover twice.
alac.application: Here, the heirs chose to sue the operator for quasi-delict, not to enforce the civil liability arising from the driver's crime. The operator is therefore directly and primarily liable, subject only to the defense of due diligence in the selection and supervision of the driver, and need not wait for the driver's conviction or insolvency.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the heirs may proceed against the taxi operator directly, though they cannot recover twice for the same death.

keyPoints: Employer's liability for quasi-delict is primary and direct (Barredo v. Garcia)
Separate from subsidiary liability under the Revised Penal Code (Art. 2177)
No double recovery
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 2177 and 2180; Barredo v. Garcia, G.R. No. 48006, July 8, 1942

q: Under Articles 218 and 219 of the Family Code, a school, its administrators and teachers exercising special parental authority over a minor are:
choices: Not liable for the minor's acts
Principally and solidarily liable for damages caused by the minor's acts or omissions while under their supervision, with the parents subsidiarily liable
Liable only for acts inside the classroom
hints: Special parental authority covers authorized activities inside or outside the school.
Parents come second.
why: FC Arts. 218-219: the school, its administrators and teachers have special parental authority over minors under their supervision, including authorized activities outside the premises, and are principally and solidarily liable for the minors' acts; the parents are subsidiarily liable; diligence is a defense.
cite: Family Code, Arts. 218 and 219; Civil Code, Art. 2180

q: During a school-authorized field trip, a 14-year-old student, Yuan, pushed a classmate off a footbridge, injuring him. The teachers in charge were chatting at a distance and not watching the students. The injured student's parents sue the school, the teachers, and Yuan's parents. Who is liable, and how?

alac.answer: The school and the teachers are principally and solidarily liable; Yuan's parents are only subsidiarily liable.
alac.basis: Article 218 of the Family Code gives the school, its administrators and teachers special parental authority and responsibility over a minor child while under their supervision, including authorized activities outside the school premises. Article 219 makes them principally and solidarily liable for damages caused by the acts or omissions of the unemancipated minor, with the parents only subsidiarily liable, unless they prove that they exercised the proper diligence required under the circumstances.
alac.application: Here, Yuan, a minor, injured his classmate during a school-authorized field trip, while under the school's supervision. The teachers were not watching the students, so they cannot prove the proper diligence. The school and teachers are therefore liable first, and Yuan's parents answer only if the school and teachers cannot pay.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the school and the teachers are principally and solidarily liable, and Yuan's parents are subsidiarily liable.

keyPoints: Special parental authority during authorized activities (FC Art. 218)
School and teachers principally and solidarily liable; parents subsidiarily (FC Art. 219)
Defense of proper diligence not proved

q: Under Article 2194 of the Civil Code, the responsibility of two or more persons liable for a quasi-delict is:
choices: Divided equally by law, with no solidarity
hints: The victim may collect the whole from any of them.
The paying tortfeasor may then seek contribution.
why: Art. 2194: the responsibility of two or more persons liable for quasi-delict is solidary.

q: Two speeding drivers, Abe and Bong, collided at an intersection, and the collision threw Abe's car onto the sidewalk, injuring Cely. Both drivers were negligent. Cely sues only Bong for her entire damages. Bong argues he should pay only half. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No, Bong is not correct. He may be held liable for the entire damages.
alac.basis: Article 2194 of the Civil Code provides that the responsibility of two or more persons who are liable for quasi-delict is solidary. Under the rules on solidary obligations, the creditor may proceed against any one of the solidary debtors for the whole obligation, and the one who pays may recover from the others their shares.
alac.application: Here, Abe and Bong were both negligent, and their concurrent negligence caused Cely's injuries. They are joint tortfeasors, solidarily liable to her. Cely may therefore choose to recover the whole amount from Bong.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Bong must pay Cely's entire damages, without prejudice to his right to recover Abe's share from Abe.

keyPoints: Joint tortfeasors are solidarily liable (Art. 2194)
Victim may collect the whole from any one
Right of contribution among tortfeasors

q: Under the test of negligence laid down in Picart v. Smith, a person is negligent if:
choices: He causes any harm at all
He did not use the reasonable care and caution which an ordinarily prudent person would have used in the same situation
hints: The standard is objective.
Think of the ordinarily prudent person (the good father of a family).
why: Picart v. Smith: did the defendant, in doing the alleged negligent act, use that reasonable care and caution which an ordinarily prudent person would have used in the same situation? If not, he is negligent. This matches the diligence of a good father of a family in Art. 1173.
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1173; Picart v. Smith, G.R. No. L-12219, March 15, 1918

q: Dado, driving on a narrow mountain road at night, saw a carabao-drawn cart ahead on his lane. Although he had ample time and space to slow down and pass on the other side, he kept his speed and passed so close that the carabao panicked and the cart overturned, injuring the driver, Elmer. Was Dado negligent?

alac.answer: Yes, Dado was negligent.
alac.basis: Article 1173 of the Civil Code defines negligence as the omission of that diligence which is required by the nature of the obligation and corresponds with the circumstances of the persons, of the time and of the place; absent a stated standard, the diligence of a good father of a family is required. In Picart v. Smith, G.R. No. L-12219, March 15, 1918, the Supreme Court held that the test is whether the defendant used that reasonable care and caution which an ordinarily prudent person would have used in the same situation, and that a driver who sees a danger ahead and has the chance to avoid it must do so.
alac.application: Here, an ordinarily prudent driver, seeing a carabao cart ahead on a narrow road at night, would have slowed down and given it a wide berth. Dado had ample time and space to do so but kept his speed and passed too close, foreseeably frightening the animal.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Dado failed to observe the care of an ordinarily prudent person and is liable to Elmer for negligence.

keyPoints: Standard: diligence of a good father of a family (Art. 1173)
Test: what an ordinarily prudent person would do in the same situation (Picart v. Smith)
Foreseeable danger that could have been avoided
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1173; Picart v. Smith, G.R. No. L-12219, March 15, 1918

q: Under Article 2185 of the Civil Code, a person driving a motor vehicle is presumed negligent if, at the time of the mishap, he was:
hints: The presumption can be rebutted by proof to the contrary.
Other presumptions: Art. 2184 and Art. 2188.
why: Art. 2185: unless there is proof to the contrary, a driver is presumed negligent if at the time of the mishap he was violating any traffic regulation.

q: Fred, driving without headlights at night in violation of traffic rules, hit a cyclist, Gino. Separately, Hilda, who kept a loaded gun on her dining table, accidentally shot her visitor when it fell. In the suits against them, what presumptions apply?

alac.answer: Fred is presumed negligent for violating a traffic regulation, and Hilda is presumed negligent for possessing a dangerous weapon.
alac.basis: Article 2185 of the Civil Code provides that unless there is proof to the contrary, a person driving a motor vehicle is presumed negligent if at the time of the mishap he was violating any traffic regulation. Article 2188 provides that there is a prima facie presumption of negligence on the part of the defendant if the death or injury results from his possession of dangerous weapons or substances, such as firearms, except when their possession or use is indispensable in his occupation or business.
alac.application: Here, Fred was driving without headlights at night, a traffic violation, when he hit Gino, so the law presumes his negligence. Hilda's visitor was injured by her firearm, a dangerous weapon she possessed, and nothing shows that its possession was indispensable to her occupation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, both Fred and Hilda bear the burden of proving that they were not negligent; otherwise they are liable.

keyPoints: Driver violating a traffic regulation is presumed negligent (Art. 2185)
Injury from possession of dangerous weapons: prima facie negligence (Art. 2188)
Presumptions are rebuttable

q: Which is a requisite for applying res ipsa loquitur?
choices: The accident is of a kind that does not ordinarily occur without negligence, and the thing that caused it was under the defendant's exclusive control
hints: "The thing speaks for itself."
It allows an inference of negligence without direct proof.
why: Res ipsa loquitur applies when (1) the accident is of a kind that ordinarily does not occur in the absence of negligence, (2) it was caused by an instrumentality within the defendant's exclusive control, and (3) the injury was not due to any voluntary action or contribution of the plaintiff (Layugan v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. 73998, November 14, 1988).
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2176; Layugan v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. 73998, November 14, 1988

q: While Ina was walking on a public sidewalk beside a building under construction, a hollow block fell from the scaffolding and hit her head. No one saw how it fell, and the contractor argues that Ina cannot prove any negligent act. Can Ina recover?

alac.answer: Yes, Ina may rely on res ipsa loquitur and recover.
alac.basis: Under the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur, as explained in Layugan v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. 73998, November 14, 1988, negligence may be inferred, without direct proof, when the accident is of a kind that ordinarily does not happen without negligence, the instrumentality causing it was within the defendant's exclusive control, and the plaintiff did not contribute to the injury. Article 2176 of the Civil Code makes the negligent party liable for the damage.
alac.application: Here, hollow blocks do not ordinarily fall from scaffolding onto a sidewalk if proper care is used. The scaffolding and materials were under the contractor's exclusive control. Ina was simply walking on a public sidewalk and contributed nothing to the accident.
