alac.conclusion: Therefore, negligence is inferred against the contractor, which must disprove it; failing that, it is liable to Ina.

keyPoints: Accident ordinarily does not occur without negligence
Instrumentality in the defendant's exclusive control
No contribution by the plaintiff (Layugan v. IAC)
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2176; Layugan v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. 73998, November 14, 1988

q: Under Article 2179 of the Civil Code, if the plaintiff's negligence was only contributory and the defendant's lack of care was the immediate and proximate cause:
choices: The plaintiff may recover, but the court shall mitigate the damages
hints: Contributory negligence reduces, but does not bar, recovery.
The plaintiff's negligence is not the proximate cause.
why: Art. 2179: if the plaintiff's negligence was only contributory, the immediate and proximate cause being the defendant's lack of due care, the plaintiff may recover, but the damages shall be mitigated.

q: In a department store, a heavy, unstable counter that the store had failed to secure fell on 6-year-old Jessa, who had climbed on it while her mother was paying. The store argues that the child's own act of climbing, and the mother's lack of supervision, bar or reduce recovery. Decide.

alac.answer: The store is liable; the child cannot be charged with contributory negligence.
alac.basis: Article 2179 of the Civil Code allows mitigation of damages only when the plaintiff's own negligence is contributory. In Jarco Marketing Corp. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 129792, December 21, 1999, on similar facts, the Supreme Court held that a child under nine years of age is conclusively presumed incapable of contributory negligence, and that the store's failure to secure a dangerous counter was the proximate cause of the injury.
alac.application: Here, Jessa, at six years old, is below nine and cannot be charged with contributory negligence for climbing the counter. The store's failure to secure a heavy, unstable counter in a place frequented by children was the proximate cause of her injury. The mother's brief attention to paying at the counter was not shown to be the proximate cause.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the store is liable to Jessa without mitigation on account of her own act.

keyPoints: Mitigation only for the plaintiff's contributory negligence (Art. 2179)
Child under nine incapable of contributory negligence (Jarco Marketing v. CA)
Unsecured counter was the proximate cause
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2179; Jarco Marketing Corp. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 129792, December 21, 1999

q: Proximate cause is that cause which, in natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause:
choices: Produces the injury, and without which the result would not have occurred
hints: This is the classic definition in Bataclan v. Medina.
It is not merely the last event in time.
why: Proximate cause is that cause which, in natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause, produces the injury, and without which the result would not have occurred (Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957).
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2179; Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957

q: A speeding bus overturned at night because the driver lost control. Passengers trapped inside cried for help. Villagers came with a lighted torch, and gasoline leaking from the bus caught fire, burning the bus and killing a trapped passenger, Kiko. The bus company argues that the fire, not the overturning, caused Kiko's death. Is the company liable?

alac.answer: Yes, the company is liable for Kiko's death.
alac.basis: Proximate cause is that cause which, in natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause, produces the injury, and without which the result would not have occurred. In Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957, on very similar facts, the Supreme Court held that the overturning of the bus through the driver's negligence was the proximate cause of the passengers' death in the ensuing fire, because the arrival of rescuers with a torch at night was a natural and probable consequence of the accident. Common carriers are also bound to observe extraordinary diligence for the safety of passengers (Article 1733 of the Civil Code).
alac.application: Here, the bus overturned because of the driver's speeding. It was natural and probable that rescuers would come at night with a light, and the leaking gasoline came from the overturned bus. The fire was not an independent cause breaking the chain; it flowed naturally from the overturning.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the overturning was the proximate cause of Kiko's death, and the bus company is liable.

keyPoints: Proximate cause: natural and continuous sequence (Bataclan v. Medina)
Rescue with a torch at night was a natural and probable consequence
Carrier bound to extraordinary diligence (Art. 1733)
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1733; Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957

q: In determining proximate cause, foreseeability asks whether:
choices: The exact injury was predicted in detail
A prudent person in the defendant's position could reasonably have foreseen that harm of the general kind would result from his act
hints: The precise manner of injury need not be foreseen.
Unforeseeable, freak results may break liability.
why: Foreseeability: the defendant is liable for harm of the kind that a prudent person would reasonably foresee as a likely result of his negligence; the exact manner of the harm need not be foreseen.
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 1173 and 2176; Picart v. Smith, G.R. No. L-12219, March 15, 1918

q: A hardware store negligently sold a can of highly flammable paint thinner with a leaking cap to Lito, a 12-year-old, without any warning. Lito carried it home, where it leaked near the stove and caught fire, injuring his sister Mila. The store argues that it could not have foreseen a fire in a stranger's kitchen. Is the store liable?

alac.answer: Yes, the store is liable.
alac.basis: Article 2176 of the Civil Code makes liable whoever causes damage by negligence. In determining proximate cause, the test of foreseeability asks whether a reasonably prudent person would have foreseen that harm of the general kind that occurred was likely to result from the negligent act; the exact manner in which the harm happens need not be foreseen.
alac.application: Here, a prudent seller of highly flammable thinner would foresee that handing a leaking can, without warning, to a child could lead to a fire wherever the child took it, including a kitchen with a stove. The fire and Mila's injury were harm of the very kind the danger posed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the store's negligence was the proximate cause of Mila's injury, and the store is liable.

keyPoints: Liability for negligence (Art. 2176)
Foreseeability of harm of the general kind suffices
Exact manner of the injury need not be foreseen

q: How does the IMMEDIATE cause of an injury differ from the proximate cause?
choices: The immediate cause is the last event before the injury, which may not be the proximate cause in law
The immediate cause is always the defendant's fault
The immediate cause is a condition
hints: Closest in time is not necessarily closest in law.
Think of Bataclan: the fire was the immediate cause.
why: The immediate cause is the act or event nearest in time to the injury; the proximate cause is the one that, in natural and continuous sequence, produced it. In Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957, the fire was the immediate cause of death, but the negligent overturning was the proximate cause.
cite: Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957

q: Nilo's truck, parked negligently in the middle of a dark road without lights, forced a motorist, Omar, to swerve; Omar's car hit a post, which fell on a pedestrian, Paz. Nilo argues that the falling post, not his truck, was what hurt Paz. Is Nilo liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Nilo is liable; the falling post was only the immediate cause, while his negligent parking was the proximate cause.
alac.basis: The immediate cause is the event closest in time to the injury, while the proximate cause is that cause which, in natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause, produces the injury (Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957). Article 2176 of the Civil Code makes liable the person whose negligence caused the damage.
alac.application: Here, the post falling on Paz was the immediate cause of her injury. But the post fell only because Omar swerved to avoid Nilo's unlit truck parked in the middle of the dark road. Omar's reaction was a natural and foreseeable response, not an efficient intervening cause. Nilo's negligence set off the unbroken chain of events.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Nilo's negligence was the proximate cause of Paz's injury, and he is liable.

keyPoints: Immediate cause: last event before the injury
Proximate cause: natural and continuous sequence (Bataclan v. Medina)
Natural reaction to the danger is not an efficient intervening cause
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2176; Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957

q: An intervening cause relieves the original negligent party of liability only when it is:
choices: An efficient intervening cause: new, independent, and not reasonably foreseeable, which breaks the chain of causation
hints: Foreseeable intervening acts do not break the chain.
Only an efficient intervening cause relieves the defendant.
why: An intervening cause that is a normal and foreseeable result of the defendant's negligence does not break the causal chain; only an efficient intervening cause, independent and unforeseeable, relieves the original actor.
cite: Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957

q: Quino negligently left an open manhole on a busy street without a cover or warning. At night, Rico, a passer-by, fell into it. While Rico was trapped, a thief stole his wallet. Is Quino liable for Rico's injuries and for the stolen wallet?

alac.answer: Quino is liable for Rico's injuries, but not for the stolen wallet.
alac.basis: A defendant is liable for injuries proximately caused by his negligence, that is, injuries flowing in natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause (Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957). A later independent and unforeseeable act of a third person, such as a crime, may be an efficient intervening cause that breaks the chain of causation as to the harm it produces.
alac.application: Here, a person falling into an open, unmarked manhole at night is exactly the foreseeable result of Quino's negligence, so he is liable for Rico's injuries. The theft of Rico's wallet, however, was the independent, deliberate criminal act of a third person, not a natural consequence of the open manhole.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Quino must answer for Rico's injuries, while the thief alone is liable for the stolen wallet.

keyPoints: Liability for harm in natural sequence (Bataclan v. Medina)
Independent, unforeseeable criminal act may be an efficient intervening cause
Chain broken only as to the harm it produces
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2176; Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957

q: A remote cause is one that:
choices: Is too distant in the chain of events, its connection to the injury broken by an independent cause, so it gives rise to no liability
hints: Remote causes may be causes in fact, but not in law.
The law does not trace liability endlessly.
why: A remote cause is one so far removed from the injury, because of independent intervening events, that the law does not treat it as the proximate cause; it does not give rise to liability.
cite: Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957

q: A car dealer sold Sam a car with a properly working but slightly worn spare tire. Three years later, Sam lent the car to his friend Ted, who drove drunk at high speed and crashed into a store. The store owner sues the dealer, arguing that if the dealer had installed a new spare tire, the accident would not have happened. Is the dealer liable?

alac.answer: No, the dealer is not liable. Its act, if a cause at all, is only a remote cause.
alac.basis: Liability for quasi-delict under Article 2176 of the Civil Code requires that the defendant's fault or negligence be the proximate cause of the damage, the cause that in natural and continuous sequence, unbroken by any efficient intervening cause, produced it (Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957). A remote cause, whose link to the injury is broken by an independent intervening cause, does not give rise to liability.
alac.application: Here, the dealer sold a working spare tire three years earlier, which had nothing to do with the crash. The crash was caused by Ted's drunk and reckless driving, an independent and efficient intervening cause. Any connection between the dealer's sale and the accident is too remote.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the dealer is not liable; Ted (and possibly Sam, if negligent in lending the car) may be.

keyPoints: Proximate cause required for liability (Art. 2176)
Remote cause: link broken by an independent cause
Drunk driving is the efficient intervening cause
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2176; Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957

q: When the negligence of two persons concur to produce a single injury, each being a proximate cause:
choices: Both are liable, and their responsibility is solidary
Only the first in time is liable
Only the richer one is liable
hints: Concurrent causes act together.
See Art. 2194.
why: Where the concurrent negligence of two or more persons produces the injury, each is a proximate cause and they are solidarily liable (Art. 2194).

q: A jeepney driver, Ulo, stopped in the middle of the road to load passengers. A truck driver, Val, speeding behind, rammed the jeepney, injuring passenger Wena. Each driver blames the other. Who is liable to Wena?

alac.answer: Both Ulo (with his operator) and Val (with his employer) are liable to Wena, solidarily.
alac.basis: Where the negligent acts of two or more persons concur to produce a single injury, each act is a concurrent proximate cause, and each person is liable for the whole. Article 2194 of the Civil Code provides that the responsibility of two or more persons who are liable for quasi-delict is solidary. A common carrier is also bound to extraordinary diligence for its passengers (Article 1733).
alac.application: Here, Ulo's negligence in stopping in the middle of the road and Val's negligence in speeding together caused the collision that injured Wena. Neither act alone was an efficient intervening cause of the other; both were concurrent causes.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Wena may hold both drivers (and their respective operator and employer) solidarily liable for her entire damages; the jeepney operator is also liable to her under the contract of carriage.

keyPoints: Concurrent negligence: each is a proximate cause
Solidary liability (Art. 2194)
Carrier's extraordinary diligence toward passengers (Art. 1733)

q: In Phoenix Construction v. IAC, the Supreme Court held that the distinction between a "cause" and a mere "condition":
choices: Always frees the defendant who created a condition
Has been almost entirely discredited; a defendant who creates a dangerous condition remains liable if the later injury was foreseeable
hints: The truck parked carelessly was not a mere passive condition.
Foreseeability is the key.
why: In Phoenix Construction, Inc. v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. L-65295, March 10, 1987, the Court held that the cause-versus-condition distinction is largely discredited: if the defendant created a dangerous situation, and the later injury was a foreseeable result, the defendant remains liable even if another's act was the immediate cause.
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 2176 and 2179; Phoenix Construction, Inc. v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. L-65295, March 10, 1987

q: A construction company's dump truck was parked at night on the wrong side of the street, partly on the road, without any warning lights. Xavier, driving home late and speeding with his headlights off, crashed into it and was injured. The company argues that its truck was a mere passive "condition" and that Xavier's own negligence was the cause. How should liability be resolved?

alac.answer: The company is liable, but Xavier's damages should be reduced because of his contributory negligence.
alac.basis: In Phoenix Construction, Inc. v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. L-65295, March 10, 1987, on almost identical facts, the Supreme Court held that the improper parking of a dump truck was the proximate cause of the collision, rejecting the argument that it was a mere passive condition, since a collision was a foreseeable result. It also found the plaintiff's speeding with headlights off to be contributory negligence. Article 2179 of the Civil Code provides that if the plaintiff's negligence was only contributory, he may recover, but the damages shall be mitigated.
alac.application: Here, parking a dump truck at night on the wrong side, partly on the road and without warning lights, created a foreseeable danger of exactly this kind of collision. It was not a mere passive condition but a proximate cause. Xavier's speeding with headlights off contributed to his injury.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the company is liable to Xavier, but the court should mitigate his damages for his contributory negligence.

keyPoints: Cause-vs-condition distinction discredited (Phoenix Construction v. IAC)
Creating a foreseeable danger makes the defendant liable
Plaintiff's contributory negligence mitigates damages (Art. 2179)
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2179; Phoenix Construction, Inc. v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. L-65295, March 10, 1987

q: An efficient intervening cause is one that:
choices: Was foreseeable from the defendant's negligence
Is new and independent, not reasonably foreseeable, and itself produces the injury, thus breaking the chain of causation
Is any act of the plaintiff
hints: It is the exception that relieves the original wrongdoer.
Foreseeable intervening acts do not qualify.
why: An efficient intervening cause is a new and independent force, not reasonably foreseeable, which itself produces the injury and breaks the causal connection with the original negligence.
cite: Bataclan v. Medina, G.R. No. L-10126, October 22, 1957

q: A school allowed a 15-year-old student to drive a jeep, with the school's permission, during its enrollment campaign. The jeep's steering wheel guide suddenly detached because of a mechanical defect unknown to the school, and the jeep turned over, killing a student passenger. The parents sued the school, arguing that letting a minor drive was the cause of death. Is the school liable for the death?

alac.answer: No, the school is not liable for the death; the detachment of the steering wheel guide was the efficient intervening cause.
alac.basis: In St. Mary's Academy v. Carpitanos, G.R. No. 143363, February 6, 2002, on similar facts, the Supreme Court held that the proximate cause of the accident was the detachment of the steering wheel guide of the jeep, not the negligence of the school or the reckless driving of the minor. The school's liability under Articles 218 and 219 of the Family Code requires that its negligence be the proximate cause of the injury.
alac.application: Here, the jeep turned over because the steering wheel guide suddenly detached due to a mechanical defect unknown to the school. Even if the school was negligent in allowing a minor to drive, that negligence was not shown to have caused the accident; the independent mechanical failure was the efficient intervening cause.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the school is not liable for the death; liability lies, if at all, with whoever was responsible for the jeep's defect.

keyPoints: Liability requires that the defendant's negligence be the proximate cause
Sudden mechanical defect as efficient intervening cause (St. Mary's Academy v. Carpitanos)
School's special parental authority (FC Arts. 218-219) does not change the causation rule
cite: Family Code, Arts. 218 and 219; St. Mary's Academy v. Carpitanos, G.R. No. 143363, February 6, 2002

q: Under the doctrine of last clear chance, when both parties are negligent:
choices: The party who had the last clear opportunity to avoid the harm, but failed to do so, is held liable
The first negligent party is always liable
hints: The doctrine looks at who could still have avoided the accident.
It originated in Picart v. Smith.
why: Last clear chance: where both parties are negligent, the one who had the last fair opportunity to avoid the injury through ordinary care, and failed, is liable (Picart v. Smith, G.R. No. L-12219, March 15, 1918).
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2179; Picart v. Smith, G.R. No. L-12219, March 15, 1918

q: Yeye negligently rode his horse on the wrong side of a bridge. Zandro, driving a car, saw him from a distance, had ample time and space to avoid him, but kept going straight, expecting Yeye to move. When Yeye did not, Zandro passed so close that the horse was struck and Yeye was injured. Who is liable?

alac.answer: Zandro is liable, because he had the last clear chance to avoid the injury.
alac.basis: In Picart v. Smith, G.R. No. L-12219, March 15, 1918, on similar facts, the Supreme Court held that although the plaintiff was negligent in being on the wrong side of the bridge, the defendant driver, who saw him in time and could have avoided the injury by reasonable care, had the last clear chance to avoid the harm and was therefore liable. Article 2176 of the Civil Code makes liable the person whose negligence causes damage.
alac.application: Here, Yeye was negligent in riding on the wrong side, but Zandro saw him in time and had ample opportunity to avoid him. Instead, Zandro chose to continue and passed too close. His failure to use the last clear chance to avoid the accident makes him liable.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Zandro is liable to Yeye, though Yeye's own negligence may be considered in mitigating the damages.

keyPoints: Both parties negligent
Defendant had the last clear opportunity to avoid the harm (Picart v. Smith)
Failure to use it makes him liable
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 2176 and 2179; Picart v. Smith, G.R. No. L-12219, March 15, 1918

q: Which defense is available to persons made responsible for others under Article 2180 of the Civil Code?
choices: Proof that they observed all the diligence of a good father of a family to prevent damage
That the victim was a stranger
That the act happened at night
hints: The presumption of negligence is rebuttable.
The defense is in the last paragraph of Art. 2180.
why: Art. 2180: the responsibility ceases when the persons responsible prove that they observed all the diligence of a good father of a family to prevent damage.

q: An employer was sued for damages caused by its delivery driver. To prove due diligence, it presented only the driver's job application and testified generally that it "always reminds drivers to be careful." It presented no records of tests, training, or monitoring. Has it proved the defense of due diligence?

alac.answer: No, the employer has not proved due diligence.
alac.basis: Article 2180 of the Civil Code presumes the negligence of the employer in the selection or supervision of its employee, and provides that the responsibility ceases only when the employer proves that it observed all the diligence of a good father of a family to prevent damage. This requires concrete proof of diligence both in the selection (such as checking qualifications, experience and records) and in the supervision (such as rules, training, and monitoring of compliance) of the employee.
alac.application: Here, the employer showed only a job application and general testimony that it reminds drivers to be careful. It presented no proof of testing the driver's skills or checking his record, and no proof of training or monitoring. These do not overcome the presumption of negligence.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the employer remains liable for the damage caused by its driver.

keyPoints: Presumption of the employer's negligence (Art. 2180)
Must prove diligence in both selection and supervision
General, unsupported testimony is insufficient

q: Under Article 2179 of the Civil Code, when the plaintiff's own negligence was the immediate and proximate cause of his injury:
choices: The defendant must still pay moral damages
hints: Compare with contributory negligence in the same article.
Here the plaintiff's fault is the main cause.
why: Art. 2179: when the plaintiff's own negligence was the immediate and proximate cause of his injury, he cannot recover damages.

q: Arturo ignored the closed railroad crossing barrier, the flashing lights and the ringing bell, and drove around the barrier onto the tracks, where a train running at a normal speed hit his car. The train operator had complied with all safety rules. Arturo sues the train operator. Can he recover?

alac.answer: No, Arturo cannot recover.
alac.basis: Article 2179 of the Civil Code provides that when the plaintiff's own negligence was the immediate and proximate cause of his injury, he cannot recover damages.
alac.application: Here, the train operator complied with all safety rules: the barrier was closed, the lights were flashing and the bell was ringing, and the train ran at a normal speed. Arturo deliberately drove around the barrier onto the tracks. His own negligence was the immediate and proximate cause of the collision.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Arturo cannot recover damages from the train operator.

keyPoints: Plaintiff's own negligence as proximate cause bars recovery (Art. 2179)
Defendant complied with safety rules
Not mere contributory negligence

q: Under Article 2178 of the Civil Code, is the rule on fortuitous events (Art. 1174) applicable to quasi-delicts?
choices: Yes; but the defendant must be free from negligence that contributed to the harm
Yes, even if he was negligent
hints: Art. 2178 incorporates Arts. 1172 to 1174.
An act of God combined with human negligence is treated as a human act.
why: Art. 2178 makes Arts. 1172-1174 applicable to quasi-delicts, so a fortuitous event is a defense; but if the defendant's negligence concurred with the fortuitous event, he is not exempted.

q: During a strong typhoon, an old tree in Benny's yard, which had been visibly rotting for months and which barangay officials had warned him to cut down, fell onto Carla's house. Benny argues that the typhoon was a fortuitous event. Is he liable?

alac.answer: Yes, Benny is liable.
alac.basis: Article 2178 of the Civil Code makes Article 1174 on fortuitous events applicable to quasi-delicts. However, for a fortuitous event to exempt the defendant, he must be free from any participation in or aggravation of the injury; when his negligence concurs with the fortuitous event, the whole occurrence is humanized and he is not exempted. Article 2191(3) also makes proprietors liable for damage caused by the falling of trees near highways or lanes, if not caused by force majeure.
alac.application: Here, the typhoon was a fortuitous event, but the tree fell because it had been rotting for months and Benny ignored warnings to cut it down. His negligence concurred with the typhoon in causing the damage.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the typhoon does not excuse Benny, and he is liable to Carla.

keyPoints: Fortuitous event applies to quasi-delicts (Arts. 1174, 2178)
No exemption if the defendant's negligence concurred
Ignoring warnings about a rotting tree is negligence

q: Damnum absque injuria means:
choices: Damage without legal injury: loss caused by an act that violates no legal right, for which there is no recovery
hints: There must be both damage and a legal wrong.
Lawful acts may still cause loss.
why: Damnum absque injuria: there can be damage without legal injury; where the loss results from the lawful exercise of a right without violating any legal duty, no damages are recoverable (Custodio v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 116100, February 9, 1996).
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2176; Custodio v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 116100, February 9, 1996

q: For years, Dina's tenants reached the street by passing through a passageway on her neighbors' land, by mere tolerance. The neighbors, who had no legal duty to provide a passage, built a fence on their own land, closing it. Dina's tenants left, and she lost rental income. She sues the neighbors for damages. Will she recover?

alac.answer: No, Dina will not recover damages.
alac.basis: In Custodio v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 116100, February 9, 1996, on similar facts, the Supreme Court held that there is a material distinction between damages and injury: loss resulting from the lawful exercise of a right, without the violation of any legal duty, is damnum absque injuria, for which no damages can be recovered. Article 429 of the Civil Code gives the owner the right to exclude any person from the enjoyment of his property, and Article 430 allows the owner to enclose or fence his land.
alac.application: Here, the neighbors fenced their own land in the exercise of their rights as owners. Dina had no easement or other legal right to the passageway, which existed only by tolerance. Her loss of rental income, though real, did not result from any violation of her legal rights.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, her loss is damnum absque injuria, and the neighbors are not liable for damages, unless she obtains a compulsory right of way with indemnity.

keyPoints: Damage without legal injury is not recoverable (Custodio v. CA)
Owner's right to exclude and to fence (Arts. 429-430)
Use by tolerance creates no right
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 429 and 430; Custodio v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 116100, February 9, 1996

q: Under the doctrine of assumption of risk, a plaintiff may be barred from recovery when he:
choices: Knowingly and voluntarily exposed himself to a known risk inherent in his work or activity
hints: Volenti non fit injuria.
Afialda v. Hisole: a caretaker of an animal assumes the risks of his job.
why: Assumption of risk (volenti non fit injuria): one who knowingly and voluntarily exposes himself to a known danger cannot recover for the resulting injury. In Afialda v. Hisole, G.R. No. L-2075, November 29, 1949, the caretaker of a carabao who was gored could not hold the owner liable, since taking care of the animal was his job and its risk was assumed.
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2183; Afialda v. Hisole, G.R. No. L-2075, November 29, 1949

q: Elmo was hired by Fermin as the caretaker of his carabaos. While Elmo was tending them, one carabao gored him. Elmo's heirs sued Fermin under Article 2183, which makes the possessor of an animal liable for damage it causes. Is Fermin liable?

alac.answer: No, Fermin is not liable.
alac.basis: Article 2183 of the Civil Code makes the possessor of an animal, or whoever may make use of the same, responsible for the damage it may cause. In Afialda v. Hisole, G.R. No. L-2075, November 29, 1949, on similar facts, the Supreme Court held that the article does not apply where the injured person was the caretaker of the animal; it was his job to take care of the animal, and he assumed the risk of being injured by it.
alac.application: Here, Elmo was hired to take care of the carabaos. Being gored while tending them was a risk inherent in his work, which he knowingly and voluntarily assumed. As the caretaker who had custody of the animal, he was himself the one responsible for preventing it from causing harm.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Fermin is not liable under Article 2183 to Elmo's heirs, although other benefits, such as under labor and social legislation, may apply.

keyPoints: Possessor of an animal is liable for damage it causes (Art. 2183)
Caretaker assumes the risk of his work (Afialda v. Hisole)
Volenti non fit injuria
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2183; Afialda v. Hisole, G.R. No. L-2075, November 29, 1949

q: Under Article 34 of the Civil Code, when a city or municipal police officer refuses or fails to render aid to a person in danger of life or property:
choices: The officer is primarily liable for damages, and the city or municipality subsidiarily liable
hints: Public officers may be liable for failing in their duty.
The local government answers secondarily.
why: Art. 34: the peace officer is primarily liable for damages, and the city or municipality subsidiarily; the civil action is independent of any criminal case and needs only a preponderance of evidence.

q: Gloria ran into a police station shouting that armed men were robbing her store next door. The officer on duty refused to respond, saying it was his break time. The robbers took P200,000 and injured her husband. What civil action may Gloria bring, and against whom?

alac.answer: Gloria may sue the police officer, who is primarily liable, and the city or municipality, which is subsidiarily liable.
alac.basis: Article 34 of the Civil Code provides that when a member of a city or municipal police force refuses or fails to render aid or protection to any person in case of danger to life or property, such peace officer shall be primarily liable for damages, and the city or municipality shall be subsidiarily responsible. The civil action is independent of any criminal proceedings and requires only a preponderance of evidence. Article 27 also allows an action for damages against a public servant who refuses or neglects, without just cause, to perform his official duty.
alac.application: Here, a robbery threatening life and property was in progress, and the police officer, without just cause, refused to respond. His refusal exposed Gloria's property and her husband to the harm that followed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Gloria may file an independent civil action for damages against the officer and, subsidiarily, the city or municipality.

keyPoints: Police officer primarily liable for refusing to render aid (Art. 34)
City or municipality subsidiarily liable
Independent civil action; preponderance of evidence

q: Under Article 1146 of the Civil Code, an action based on a quasi-delict must be filed within:
hints: The same period applies to injury to the rights of the plaintiff.
Defamation has a shorter period (Art. 1147).
why: Art. 1146: actions upon an injury to the rights of the plaintiff and upon a quasi-delict must be instituted within four years.

q: Hans was injured in a collision caused by Ivy's negligent driving on 1 March 2021. He filed a civil action for damages based on quasi-delict on 15 March 2025. Ivy moves to dismiss on the ground of prescription. Rule on the motion.

alac.answer: The motion should be granted; the action has prescribed.
alac.basis: Article 1146 of the Civil Code provides that an action upon a quasi-delict must be instituted within four years. The period runs from the day the cause of action accrues, which for a quasi-delict is the time of the injury.
alac.application: Here, Hans's cause of action accrued on 1 March 2021, when he was injured. The four-year period expired on 1 March 2025. He filed his action on 15 March 2025, after the period had lapsed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the action has prescribed and should be dismissed.

keyPoints: Quasi-delict prescribes in four years (Art. 1146)
Counted from the injury
Filed after the period lapsed

q: Which waiver is VOID under the Civil Code?
choices: A release signed by an injured person after the accident, for fair consideration and with full knowledge
A waiver, made in advance, of an action for future fraud
A waiver of a right that does not prejudice third persons
A compromise of a pending claim for damages
hints: Rights may generally be waived (Art. 6).
But not liability for future fraud (Art. 1171).
why: Art. 6 allows waivers not contrary to law, public order, public policy, morals or good customs, nor prejudicial to third persons; Art. 1171 declares void any waiver of an action for future fraud. A release executed after the injury, voluntarily and for fair consideration, is generally valid.

q: After a minor car accident, Jun, who was slightly injured, signed a release in favor of Kurt in exchange for P50,000, after consulting a lawyer and knowing the extent of his injuries. Two months later, Jun sued Kurt for more damages, arguing that waivers of liability are void. Will his suit prosper?

alac.answer: No, Jun's suit will not prosper. The release is valid.
alac.basis: Article 6 of the Civil Code provides that rights may be waived, unless the waiver is contrary to law, public order, public policy, morals or good customs, or prejudicial to a third person with a right recognized by law. What the law forbids is a waiver in advance of an action for future fraud (Article 1171). A release or compromise of an existing claim, entered into voluntarily, with full knowledge, and for a reasonable consideration, is valid and binding.
alac.application: Here, Jun signed the release after the accident, knowing the extent of his injuries, after consulting a lawyer, and in exchange for P50,000. It was a voluntary settlement of an existing claim, not an advance waiver of liability for future fraud, and it prejudices no third person.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the release is valid and bars Jun's later suit for additional damages.

keyPoints: Rights may be waived within the limits of Art. 6
Advance waiver of future fraud is void (Art. 1171)
Voluntary, informed release for fair value is valid

q: Under Article 2177 of the Civil Code, a plaintiff may sue both for civil liability arising from crime and for quasi-delict, but:
choices: He cannot recover damages twice for the same act or omission of the defendant
hints: The two actions are separate and distinct.
But the law prevents unjust enrichment of the plaintiff.
why: Art. 2177: responsibility for quasi-delict is separate and distinct from civil liability arising from crime, but the plaintiff cannot recover damages twice for the same act or omission.

q: Lara was injured by Mike's reckless driving. In the criminal case for reckless imprudence, the court convicted Mike and awarded Lara P300,000 in civil damages, which Mike paid. Lara also filed a separate civil action against Mike for quasi-delict for the same injuries, seeking P300,000 more. Will it prosper?

alac.answer: No, Lara cannot recover a second time for the same injuries.
alac.basis: Article 2177 of the Civil Code provides that responsibility for fault or negligence under quasi-delict is entirely separate and distinct from the civil liability arising from negligence under the Penal Code, but the plaintiff cannot recover damages twice for the same act or omission of the defendant.
alac.application: Here, Lara already recovered and was paid P300,000 in the criminal case for the same reckless driving and the same injuries. Although the quasi-delict action is separate and distinct, a second award for the same act would be a double recovery.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Lara cannot recover again in the quasi-delict action; at most she may recover any amount in excess of what she already received, if proven.

keyPoints: Civil liability from crime and from quasi-delict are separate (Art. 2177)
No double recovery for the same act
Plaintiff may only recover any proven excess

q: In a medical negligence case, which of the following must the patient generally prove?
choices: Duty, breach of the standard of care, injury, and proximate causation, usually through expert testimony
hints: A bad result alone does not prove malpractice.
Expert testimony is usually needed, unless res ipsa loquitur applies.
why: Medical negligence requires duty, breach of the standard of care observed by other members of the profession in similar circumstances, injury, and proximate causation, generally shown by expert testimony; res ipsa loquitur may apply where the matter is within common knowledge (Ramos v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 124354, December 29, 1999).
cite: Civil Code, Art. 2176; Ramos v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 124354, December 29, 1999

q: After Nora's operation in a private hospital, two surgical sponges were found left inside her body, causing infection. The surgeon was an independent consultant, but the hospital held him out to the public as part of its medical staff, and its nurses recorded the sponge count as "incomplete" without acting on it. Nora sues the surgeon and the hospital. Are they liable?

alac.answer: Yes, both the surgeon and the hospital are liable.
alac.basis: Medical negligence is governed by Article 2176 of the Civil Code. Leaving foreign objects inside a patient's body is a matter that speaks for itself (res ipsa loquitur). In Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana, G.R. No. 126297, January 31, 2007, on similar facts, the Supreme Court held the surgeon liable for leaving sponges inside the patient, and held the hospital liable under the doctrine of apparent authority, because it held out the doctor as a member of its staff, and for its own corporate negligence in failing to act on the incomplete sponge count.
alac.application: Here, sponges left inside Nora's body show the surgeon's negligence without need of expert testimony. The hospital presented the surgeon to the public as part of its staff, so it cannot disown him by calling him an independent consultant. Its nurses also noted the incomplete sponge count but did nothing, which is the hospital's own negligence.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the surgeon is liable for his negligence, and the hospital is liable both under apparent authority and for its corporate negligence.

keyPoints: Sponges left inside the patient: res ipsa loquitur
Hospital liable under apparent authority (Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana)
Hospital's own corporate negligence in ignoring the sponge count
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 2176 and 2180; Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana, G.R. No. 126297, January 31, 2007

q: Under the doctrine of forum non conveniens, a Philippine court:
choices: Must always dismiss cases involving foreigners
May, in its discretion, refuse to assume jurisdiction over a case when it is not the most convenient forum, considering the circumstances
Must apply foreign law in every case
hints: It is a discretionary doctrine, not a rule of mandatory dismissal.
It is usually raised as a defense, not a ground for a motion to dismiss.
why: Forum non conveniens allows a court with jurisdiction to decline to exercise it when another forum is more convenient. A Philippine court may assume jurisdiction if (1) it is a convenient forum, (2) it is in a position to make an intelligent decision on the law and facts, and (3) it has or is likely to have power to enforce its decision (Raytheon International, Inc. v. Rouzie, Jr., G.R. No. 162894, February 26, 2008).
cite: Raytheon International, Inc. v. Rouzie, Jr., G.R. No. 162894, February 26, 2008

q: An American engineer, Wade, sued a U.S. corporation in a Philippine court for unpaid commissions under a contract he signed with it in the Philippines for projects in the Philippines. The contract said it would be governed by U.S. law. The corporation moved to dismiss on the ground of forum non conveniens. Should the motion be granted?

alac.answer: No, the motion should be denied.
alac.basis: In Raytheon International, Inc. v. Rouzie, Jr., G.R. No. 162894, February 26, 2008, on similar facts, the Supreme Court held that forum non conveniens is not a ground for a motion to dismiss under the Rules of Court, but a matter of defense addressed to the court's discretion, best considered after the facts are established. A Philippine court may assume jurisdiction if it is a convenient forum, can make an intelligent decision on the law and the facts, and has or is likely to have power to enforce its decision. A choice-of-law clause determines the applicable law, not the court that may hear the case.
alac.application: Here, the contract was signed in the Philippines and the services relate to Philippine projects, so the Philippine court is a convenient forum, can determine the facts and apply U.S. law if proven, and can enforce its decision against a corporation doing business here. The stipulation that U.S. law governs does not oust Philippine courts of jurisdiction.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the court should deny the motion to dismiss and proceed with the case.

keyPoints: Forum non conveniens is a discretionary defense, not a ground for a motion to dismiss (Raytheon v. Rouzie)
Three conditions for assuming jurisdiction
Choice-of-law clause is not a choice-of-forum clause
cite: Raytheon International, Inc. v. Rouzie, Jr., G.R. No. 162894, February 26, 2008

q: Under Article 15 of the Civil Code, the Philippines follows which principle for laws relating to family rights and duties, status, condition and legal capacity of its citizens?
choices: Lex nationalis: such laws bind Filipino citizens even though living abroad
hints: The Philippines follows the nationality principle for personal law.
Common-law countries often use domicile.
why: Art. 15: laws relating to family rights and duties, or to the status, condition and legal capacity of persons, are binding upon Filipino citizens even though living abroad (nationality principle).

q: Yago, a 19-year-old Filipino citizen, has lived for years in Country X, where the age of majority is 21. There he sold his car to Zack, then later sought to annul the sale on the ground that he was a minor without capacity to contract. Under what law is Yago's capacity determined, and can he annul the sale?

alac.answer: Yago's capacity is governed by Philippine law, under which he is of age; he cannot annul the sale on the ground of minority.
alac.basis: Article 15 of the Civil Code provides that laws relating to the status, condition and legal capacity of persons are binding upon citizens of the Philippines, even though living abroad. The Philippines thus follows the nationality principle (lex nationalis) rather than the law of the domicile. Under Article 234 of the Family Code, as amended by RA 6809, majority commences at eighteen.
alac.application: Here, Yago is a Filipino citizen, so his legal capacity is governed by Philippine law even though he lives in Country X. Under Philippine law, he reached majority at 18 and had full capacity to contract at 19.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Yago cannot annul the sale on the ground of minority.

keyPoints: Capacity of Filipinos governed by Philippine law even abroad (Art. 15)
Nationality, not domicile
Majority at 18 (FC Art. 234, as amended)
cite: Civil Code, Art. 15; Family Code, Art. 234, as amended by RA 6809

q: Under the first sentence of Article 16 of the Civil Code, real and personal property are subject to:
choices: The law of the owner's nationality
The law of the country where the property is situated
The law chosen by the buyer
hints: This is lex rei sitae (lex situs).
Succession is the exception in the second sentence.
why: Art. 16: real property as well as personal property is subject to the law of the country where it is situated; but succession is governed by the national law of the decedent.

q: In California, two American citizens, Al and Bud, executed a deed in full compliance with California formalities, by which Al sold to Bud a parcel of land in Makati that Al had inherited from his Filipino mother. Is the transfer valid?

alac.answer: No, the transfer is not valid, even though the deed complied with California formalities.
alac.basis: Article 17 of the Civil Code provides that the forms and solemnities of contracts are governed by the laws of the country in which they are executed. But Article 16 provides that real property is subject to the law of the country where it is situated. Under Article XII, Section 7 of the 1987 Constitution, save in cases of hereditary succession, no private lands shall be transferred to persons not qualified to acquire lands of the public domain, such as aliens.
alac.application: Here, the deed's form is valid under California law. But whether ownership of Makati land can pass to Bud is governed by Philippine law, the lex rei sitae. Al validly acquired the land by hereditary succession, but Bud is an American citizen who is disqualified from acquiring private land in the Philippines by sale.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the sale to Bud is void under Philippine law.

keyPoints: Form governed by the place of execution (Art. 17)
Real property governed by the law of the situs (Art. 16)
Constitutional ban on transfer of land to aliens (Art. XII, Sec. 7)
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 16 and 17; 1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Sec. 7

q: Lex contractus (the proper law of the contract) generally refers to:
choices: The law of the forum always
The law the parties intended or chose to govern the contract, subject to public policy limits
The law of the place of signing only
The law of the stronger party
hints: Party autonomy applies in choice of law.
Prohibitive Philippine laws on public order cannot be evaded (Art. 17, par. 3).
why: Lex contractus is the law intended by the parties to govern the intrinsic validity and effects of their contract; but under Art. 17, par. 3, prohibitive laws and those for public order, public policy and good customs cannot be rendered ineffective by foreign laws or agreements.

q: A Filipino worker was hired by a foreign company to work in Manila under a contract stating that it is governed by the law of Country Y, which allows employers to dismiss workers at will without notice or cause. When dismissed without cause, he sued in the Philippines. The company invoked the choice-of-law clause. Will it prevail?

alac.answer: No, the company will not prevail on the choice-of-law clause.
alac.basis: Under the principle of lex contractus, parties may generally choose the law to govern their contract, within the limits of Article 1306 of the Civil Code, which forbids stipulations contrary to law, morals, good customs, public order or public policy. Article 17, paragraph 3, provides that prohibitive laws concerning persons, their acts or property, and those which have for their object public order, public policy and good customs shall not be rendered ineffective by laws or conventions agreed upon in a foreign country. Security of tenure of workers is a matter of public policy under the Constitution and the Labor Code.
alac.application: Here, the parties chose the law of Country Y, but applying it would allow dismissal at will of a worker employed in the Philippines, defeating the constitutional and statutory guarantee of security of tenure. That is contrary to Philippine public policy.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the choice-of-law clause cannot be enforced to defeat the worker's security of tenure, and Philippine labor law applies to his dismissal.

keyPoints: Party autonomy in choosing the governing law (lex contractus)
Limited by law, public order and public policy (Arts. 1306, 17 par. 3)
Security of tenure is Philippine public policy

q: Under Article 17 of the Civil Code, the forms and solemnities of contracts, wills and other public instruments are governed by:
choices: The national law of the parties
The laws of the country in which they are executed
hints: Locus regit actum: the place governs the act.
Exception: instruments executed before Philippine consuls abroad follow Philippine solemnities.
why: Art. 17: the forms and solemnities of contracts, wills and other public instruments are governed by the law of the country where they are executed (lex loci celebrationis); if executed before Philippine diplomatic or consular officials abroad, Philippine solemnities apply.

q: Bea, a Filipino working in Japan, executed her will in Tokyo following the formalities required by Japanese law, which differ from the Civil Code's requirements for notarial wills. After her death, her heirs sought to probate the will in the Philippines. Can it be probated?

alac.answer: Yes, Bea's will may be probated in the Philippines.
alac.basis: Article 17 of the Civil Code provides that the forms and solemnities of wills shall be governed by the laws of the country in which they are executed. Article 815 provides that when a Filipino is in a foreign country, he is authorized to make a will in any of the forms established by the law of the country in which he may be, and such will may be probated in the Philippines.
alac.application: Here, Bea, a Filipino in Japan, executed her will in compliance with Japanese formalities. Although those formalities differ from the Civil Code's, the law expressly authorizes a Filipino abroad to use the forms of the place where he is.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the will is formally valid and may be probated in the Philippines, upon proof of the Japanese law on formalities.

keyPoints: Forms governed by the place of execution (Art. 17)
Filipino abroad may use the forms of that country (Art. 815)
Foreign law must be proved in probate

q: In Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Court of Appeals, the Supreme Court applied which approach to determine the law governing a tort with foreign elements?
choices: The law of the defendant's nationality, always
The "state of the most significant relationship" approach, considering where the injury and conduct occurred, the parties' domicile and nationality, and where their relationship is centered
The law chosen by the plaintiff
hints: Traditional lex loci delicti looks at where the tort happened.
The Court refined it with the most significant relationship test.
why: Lex loci delicti commissi: torts are governed by the law of the place where the wrong was committed; in Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 122191, October 8, 1998, the Court determined that place using the state of the most significant relationship, and applied Philippine law.
cite: Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 122191, October 8, 1998

q: Celia, a Filipino flight attendant of a foreign airline based in Manila, was asked by her employer in Manila to go to Saudi Arabia supposedly to help in an investigation. There she was unexpectedly tried and convicted for an incident on a layover. She was later cleared and returned to Manila, where she sued the airline for damages under Articles 19 and 21 of the Civil Code. The airline argues Saudi law governs. Which law applies?

alac.answer: Philippine law applies.
alac.basis: Under lex loci delicti commissi, a tort is governed by the law of the place where it was committed. In Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 122191, October 8, 1998, on similar facts, the Supreme Court held that the place having the most significant relationship to the tort was the Philippines, where the airline's deceptive acts toward its Filipino employee began and where her employment was based, so Philippine law, including Articles 19 and 21 of the Civil Code, governs.
alac.application: Here, Celia is a Filipino based in Manila, and the airline's act of inducing her to go to Saudi Arabia, which led to her trial, originated in Manila. The relationship between the parties was centered in the Philippines.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Philippine law governs Celia's claim, and she may recover under Articles 19 and 21 if she proves her case.

keyPoints: Lex loci delicti commissi
State of the most significant relationship (Saudi Arabian Airlines v. CA)
Conduct and relationship centered in the Philippines
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 19 and 21; Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 122191, October 8, 1998

q: Lex loci solutionis refers to:
choices: The law of the place where the contract was signed
The law of the place where the obligation is to be performed
The law of the place where the property is located
hints: Solutio means performance or payment.
It usually governs the manner of performance.
why: Lex loci solutionis is the law of the place of performance; it generally governs matters relating to the manner and mode of performance, such as the time, place and currency of payment.

q: A Singapore company and a Philippine company signed a supply contract in Singapore, silent on governing law, for goods to be delivered and paid for in Manila. A dispute arose over the manner of inspecting the goods upon delivery and the business hours within which delivery could be made. Which law should govern these questions?

alac.answer: Philippine law, as the law of the place of performance, should govern these questions.
alac.basis: Under the principle of lex loci solutionis, the law of the place where the obligation is to be performed generally governs matters relating to the manner and details of performance. Article 17 of the Civil Code governs only the forms and solemnities of the contract, which are subject to the law of the place of execution.
alac.application: Here, the contract was signed in Singapore, so its form is governed by Singapore law. But the goods were to be delivered, inspected and paid for in Manila. The questions on the manner of inspection and the hours of delivery concern performance in the Philippines.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, these performance-related questions are governed by Philippine law as the lex loci solutionis.

keyPoints: Lex loci solutionis governs the manner of performance
Form governed by the place of execution (Art. 17)
Delivery and inspection in Manila

q: Which matters are governed by the lex fori (the law of the forum)?
choices: Procedural matters, such as the rules of procedure and evidence
The formal validity of a will
hints: Courts apply their own procedure.
Substance may be governed by foreign law; procedure is not.
why: Procedural matters, including pleading, procedure and evidence, are governed by the law of the forum, even when the court applies foreign substantive law.

q: In a Philippine case on a contract governed by Japanese law, the plaintiff asked the court to admit a document under Japanese rules of evidence, which would admit it though it does not meet the Philippine Rules on Evidence. Should the court apply the Japanese rules of evidence?

alac.answer: No. The court should apply the Philippine Rules on Evidence.
alac.basis: Under the principle of lex fori, matters of procedure, including the admissibility of evidence, are governed by the law of the forum, even when the substantive rights of the parties are governed by a foreign law. A Philippine court may apply Japanese substantive law to the contract if it is pleaded and proved, but it follows its own Rules of Court on procedure and evidence.
alac.application: Here, the case is being tried in a Philippine court. The question of whether a document is admissible is procedural, not a question of the substantive rights under the contract.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the admissibility of the document is determined by the Philippine Rules on Evidence, not by the Japanese rules.

keyPoints: Lex fori governs procedure and evidence
Foreign law may govern substance if pleaded and proved
Admissibility is procedural

q: Renvoi occurs when:
choices: A court refuses to hear a case
The conflict rule of the forum refers to a foreign law, whose own conflict rule refers the matter back to the forum's law (or to a third law)
Two courts hear the same case
hints: Renvoi means "sending back."
Aznar v. Garcia is the leading Philippine case.
why: Renvoi is the process by which a court, referred by its conflict rule to a foreign law, finds that the foreign law's conflict rule refers the matter back to the forum (or to a third state); in Aznar v. Garcia, G.R. No. L-16749, January 31, 1963, the Court accepted the reference back and applied Philippine law.
cite: Civil Code, Art. 16; Aznar v. Garcia, G.R. No. L-16749, January 31, 1963

q: Edward, a U.S. citizen of State Z, lived in the Philippines for decades and died here. His will left nothing to his acknowledged illegitimate daughter. Under Article 16 of the Civil Code, his national law governs his succession. The conflict rule of State Z provides that succession to movables is governed by the law of the decedent's domicile. Is the daughter entitled to a legitime?

alac.answer: Yes, the daughter is entitled to her legitime under Philippine law.
alac.basis: Article 16 of the Civil Code provides that testamentary succession, including the amount of successional rights, is regulated by the national law of the decedent. In Aznar v. Garcia, G.R. No. L-16749, January 31, 1963, on similar facts, the Supreme Court held that where the national law of the decedent, through its conflict rules, refers the matter back to the law of his domicile in the Philippines, the Philippine court should accept the reference back (renvoi) and apply Philippine internal law, under which an illegitimate child is a compulsory heir entitled to a legitime.
alac.application: Here, Edward's national law is that of State Z, but State Z's conflict rule refers succession to the law of the domicile, the Philippines. Accepting the renvoi, the Philippine court applies Philippine law, under which the daughter, as an illegitimate child whose filiation is established, is a compulsory heir.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the daughter is entitled to her legitime, and the will is inofficious to that extent.

keyPoints: National law governs succession (Art. 16)
Foreign conflict rule refers back to the domicile (renvoi)
Philippine law applies; illegitimate child gets a legitime (Aznar v. Garcia)
cite: Civil Code, Art. 16; Family Code, Art. 176; Aznar v. Garcia, G.R. No. L-16749, January 31, 1963

q: Under the doctrine of processual presumption, when a foreign law is relevant but is not pleaded and proved:
choices: The foreign law is presumed to be the same as Philippine law
The court researches the foreign law on its own
hints: Philippine courts do not take judicial notice of foreign laws.
Foreign law is a question of fact.
why: Foreign laws must be alleged and proved as facts; absent proof, the foreign law is presumed to be the same as Philippine law (processual presumption) (EDI-Staffbuilders International, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. No. 145587, October 26, 2007).
cite: EDI-Staffbuilders International, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. No. 145587, October 26, 2007

q: An overseas Filipino worker, Fely, was dismissed by her foreign employer in Country Q. In her illegal dismissal case, the employer argued that the dismissal was valid under the labor law of Country Q, but presented only a photocopy of a provision without any official publication or certification. How should the tribunal decide which law applies?

alac.answer: The tribunal should apply Philippine law under the doctrine of processual presumption.
alac.basis: Philippine courts and tribunals do not take judicial notice of foreign laws; a foreign law must be alleged and proved as a fact, in the manner required by the Rules of Court (an official publication or a copy attested and authenticated as required). In EDI-Staffbuilders International, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. No. 145587, October 26, 2007, the Supreme Court held that where the foreign law is not properly proved, it is presumed to be the same as Philippine law under the doctrine of processual presumption.
alac.application: Here, the employer relied on the labor law of Country Q but presented only an uncertified photocopy, which does not prove the foreign law. The foreign law is therefore presumed to be the same as Philippine law.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the validity of Fely's dismissal must be judged under Philippine labor law.

keyPoints: Foreign law must be pleaded and proved as fact
Unproved foreign law is presumed the same as Philippine law (EDI-Staffbuilders v. NLRC)
Uncertified photocopy is insufficient proof
cite: EDI-Staffbuilders International, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. No. 145587, October 26, 2007

q: Under Article 777 of the Civil Code, the rights to the succession are transmitted:
choices: From the moment of the death of the decedent
hints: Succession opens at a single moment.
Later acts only confirm or implement the transmission.
why: Art. 777: the rights to the succession are transmitted from the moment of the death of the decedent.

q: Lando died leaving an estate worth P2 million and debts of P3 million. His creditor sued Lando's only son, Mario, for the full P3 million, arguing that Mario, as heir, must pay all his father's debts. Is Mario personally liable for the whole debt?

alac.answer: No, Mario is liable only up to the value of the inheritance, P2 million.
alac.basis: Article 774 of the Civil Code provides that succession is a mode of acquisition by virtue of which the property, rights and obligations to the extent of the value of the inheritance of a person are transmitted through his death to another. Article 1311 provides that the heir is not liable beyond the value of the property he received from the decedent.
alac.application: Here, Lando's estate is worth P2 million, while his debts are P3 million. Mario inherits his father's obligations only to the extent of the value of the inheritance. He does not become personally liable for the excess P1 million.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the creditor can collect only up to P2 million from the estate, and Mario is not personally liable for the balance.

keyPoints: Obligations are transmitted only to the extent of the value of the inheritance (Art. 774)
Heir not liable beyond what he received (Art. 1311)
No personal liability for the excess

q: Under Article 805 of the Civil Code, a notarial (attested) will must be attested and subscribed by at least how many credible witnesses?
hints: A holographic will needs no witnesses.
A notarial will needs more than two.
why: Art. 805: a notarial will must be subscribed by the testator at the end and attested and subscribed by three or more credible witnesses in the presence of the testator and of one another.

q: Spouses Nicanor and Olivia signed one notarized document, with three witnesses, in which each left all of his or her property to the other, and on the death of both, to their nephew. After Nicanor died, Olivia presented the document for probate as Nicanor's will. Should it be allowed?

alac.answer: No, the document cannot be allowed as a will.
alac.basis: Article 818 of the Civil Code provides that two or more persons cannot make a will jointly, or in the same instrument, either for their reciprocal benefit or for the benefit of a third person. Article 838 provides that no will shall pass property unless it is proved and allowed in accordance with the Rules of Court.
alac.application: Here, Nicanor and Olivia executed a single instrument as their will, for their reciprocal benefit and for the benefit of their nephew. This is a joint will, which the law expressly prohibits, regardless of compliance with the other formalities.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the joint will is void and cannot be probated; Nicanor's estate will pass by intestate succession unless he left another valid will.

keyPoints: Joint wills are prohibited (Art. 818)
Whether for reciprocal benefit or a third person
Probate required for a will to pass property (Art. 838)

q: Under Article 859 of the Civil Code, a simple substitution, without a statement of the cases to which it refers, covers the cases where the first heir:
choices: Dies before the testator, does not wish to accept, or is incapacitated to accept
hints: There are three cases.
The testator may limit them expressly.
why: Art. 859: a simple substitution without a statement of cases comprises predecease, renunciation, and incapacity of the first heir, unless the testator provides otherwise.

q: In his will, Pedro instituted his friend Quintin as his sole and universal heir, and gave his car as a legacy to his driver. Pedro did not mention his only legitimate son, Rafael, who was alive. What is the effect of the omission?

alac.answer: There is preterition: the institution of Quintin is annulled, Rafael inherits by intestacy, and the legacy to the driver stands if not inofficious.
alac.basis: Article 854 of the Civil Code provides that the preterition or omission of one, some, or all of the compulsory heirs in the direct line, whether living at the time of the execution of the will or born after the death of the testator, shall annul the institution of heir, but the devises and legacies shall be valid insofar as they are not inofficious. In Acain v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. 72706, October 27, 1987, the Supreme Court held that preterition annuls the institution of heir entirely, resulting in intestate succession, while legacies and devises remain valid within the free portion.
alac.application: Here, Rafael is a compulsory heir in the direct line and was totally omitted from the will. The institution of Quintin as universal heir is therefore annulled. The car given as a legacy to the driver remains valid, provided it does not impair Rafael's legitime.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Quintin inherits nothing as heir, the driver keeps the car if it is within the free portion, and the rest of the estate goes to Rafael by intestate succession.

keyPoints: Total omission of a compulsory heir in the direct line is preterition (Art. 854)
Institution of heir annulled; intestacy follows (Acain v. IAC)
Legacies and devises valid if not inofficious
cite: Civil Code, Art. 854; Acain v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. 72706, October 27, 1987

q: Under Article 874 of the Civil Code, an absolute condition in a will not to contract a first or subsequent marriage is generally:
choices: Considered as not written, unless imposed on the widow or widower by the deceased spouse or by the latter's ascendants or descendants
Void, together with the whole will
hints: The law protects the freedom to marry.
There is an exception for the surviving spouse.
why: Art. 874: an absolute condition not to contract a first or subsequent marriage is considered as not written, unless imposed on the widow or widower by the deceased spouse or by the latter's ascendants or descendants.

q: Teofilo's will left his house to his nephew Uriel "on condition that Uriel first files for the nullity of his marriage to his wife, whom I dislike." Uriel did not do so. Teofilo's other heirs claim that Uriel loses the house. Are they correct?

alac.answer: No, the heirs are not correct. Uriel takes the house; the condition is disregarded.
alac.basis: Article 871 of the Civil Code allows the institution of an heir to be made conditionally. However, Article 873 provides that impossible conditions and those contrary to law or good customs shall be considered as not imposed and shall in no manner prejudice the heir, even if the testator should otherwise provide.
alac.application: Here, the condition requires Uriel to seek the nullity of his marriage merely because the testator disliked his wife. Such a condition is contrary to good customs and to the State policy protecting marriage as an inviolable social institution. It is therefore considered as not imposed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Uriel inherits the house as if no condition had been attached.

keyPoints: Conditional institution allowed (Art. 871)
Conditions contrary to law or good customs are considered not imposed (Art. 873)
Heir is not prejudiced

q: Under Article 888 of the Civil Code, the legitime of legitimate children and descendants is:
choices: One-half of the hereditary estate of the father and of the mother
hints: The other half is the free portion, subject to other compulsory heirs.
The share is collective, divided among the children.
why: Art. 888: the legitime of legitimate children and descendants consists of one-half of the hereditary estate of the father and of the mother; the rest may be freely disposed of, subject to the rights of illegitimate children and the surviving spouse.

q: Vicente died with a will, leaving a net estate of P1,200,000. He was survived by his wife Wilma, one legitimate son Xander, and one illegitimate daughter Yna, whose filiation is proved. His will left everything to a charity. How much is each compulsory heir's legitime, and how much can the charity receive?

alac.answer: Xander's legitime is P600,000, Wilma's P300,000, and Yna's P300,000; nothing remains for the charity.
alac.basis: Article 888 of the Civil Code gives legitimate children one-half of the estate as legitime. Article 892 gives the surviving spouse, concurring with only one legitimate child, one-fourth of the estate, taken from the free portion. Under Article 176 of the Family Code, the legitime of each illegitimate child is one-half of the legitime of a legitimate child, and under Article 895 of the Civil Code, the legitime of illegitimate children is taken from the free portion, after the legitime of the surviving spouse has been fully satisfied.
alac.application: Here, Xander's legitime is one-half of P1,200,000, or P600,000. Wilma, concurring with one legitimate child, gets one-fourth, or P300,000, from the free portion of P600,000, leaving P300,000. Yna's legitime is one-half of Xander's, or P300,000, taken from the remaining free portion, which exhausts it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the legitimes absorb the entire estate, and the gift to the charity is inofficious and cannot be given effect.

keyPoints: Legitimate child: 1/2 of the estate (Art. 888)
Spouse with one legitimate child: 1/4, from the free portion (Art. 892)
Illegitimate child: 1/2 of a legitimate child's legitime (FC Art. 176), after the spouse (Art. 895)
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 888, 892 and 895; Family Code, Art. 176 (as amended by RA 9255)

q: Under Article 916 of the Civil Code, disinheritance can be effected only:
choices: Through a will wherein the legal cause therefor is specified
By court order during the testator's lifetime
hints: Disinheritance deprives a compulsory heir of his legitime.
It must be in a will and state a legal cause.
why: Art. 916: disinheritance can be effected only through a will wherein the legal cause is specified; the other heirs bear the burden of proving the cause if denied (Art. 917).

q: In his 2020 will, Zosimo validly disinherited his son Ariel for maltreating him by deed. In 2022, Ariel apologized; father and son reconciled, lived together again, and Zosimo told everyone he had forgiven Ariel, but he never changed his will. Zosimo died in 2025. Is Ariel disinherited?

alac.answer: No, Ariel is not disinherited.
alac.basis: Article 919(6) of the Civil Code makes maltreatment of the testator by word or deed a sufficient cause for disinheriting a child. However, Article 922 provides that a subsequent reconciliation between the offender and the offended person deprives the latter of the right to disinherit, and renders ineffectual any disinheritance that may have been made.
alac.application: Here, the disinheritance in the 2020 will was for a legal cause. But in 2022, Zosimo and Ariel reconciled, as shown by their living together again and Zosimo's public forgiveness. The reconciliation rendered the earlier disinheritance ineffectual, even though the will was not changed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the disinheritance has no effect, and Ariel is entitled to his legitime.

keyPoints: Maltreatment is a cause for disinheritance (Art. 919(6))
Subsequent reconciliation renders the disinheritance ineffectual (Art. 922)
No need to amend the will

q: Under Article 924 of the Civil Code, what may be the object of a legacy or devise?
choices: All things and rights which are within the commerce of man
Only things owned by the State
hints: Legacies are personal property; devises are real property.
Things outside the commerce of man cannot be given.
why: Art. 924: all things and rights within the commerce of man may be bequeathed or devised.

q: In her will, Belen gave her niece "my diamond ring." In truth, the ring belonged to Belen's sister, who had only lent it to her, but Belen mistakenly believed it was hers. Separately, Belen devised to her nephew "the lot next to my house," which she did not own when she made the will but bought a year later. Are the legacy and the devise valid?

alac.answer: The legacy of the ring is void, but the devise of the lot is valid.
alac.basis: Article 930 of the Civil Code provides that the legacy or devise of a thing belonging to another person is void, if the testator erroneously believed that the thing pertained to him. But if the thing bequeathed, though not belonging to the testator when he made the will, afterwards becomes his, by whatever title, the disposition shall take effect.
alac.application: Here, the ring belonged to Belen's sister, and Belen mistakenly believed it was hers. The legacy is therefore void. The lot, on the other hand, did not belong to Belen when she made the will, but she later acquired it by purchase. The devise therefore takes effect.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the niece gets nothing under the legacy of the ring, while the nephew gets the lot.

keyPoints: Legacy of another's thing, believed by the testator to be his own, is void (Art. 930)
Valid if the thing later becomes the testator's
Things within the commerce of man may be given (Art. 924)

q: Under Article 972 of the Civil Code, in the collateral line, the right of representation takes place only in favor of:
choices: Children of brothers or sisters, whether of the full or half blood
hints: Representation never takes place in the ascending line.
In the collateral line it is limited to nephews and nieces.
why: Art. 972: representation takes place in the direct descending line, never in the ascending; in the collateral line, only in favor of children of brothers or sisters.

q: Celia, a widow, died intestate. Her only legitimate son, Dante, had died before her, leaving an illegitimate son, Ely. Ely claims Celia's estate by right of representation of his father. Celia's legitimate nephews oppose. Can Ely inherit from Celia?

alac.answer: No, Ely cannot inherit from Celia by intestacy.
alac.basis: Article 992 of the Civil Code provides that an illegitimate child has no right to inherit ab intestato from the legitimate children and relatives of his father or mother, nor shall such children or relatives inherit in the same manner from the illegitimate child. In Diaz v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. L-66574, June 17, 1987, the Supreme Court held that this "iron curtain" bars an illegitimate child from inheriting by intestacy, even by right of representation, from the legitimate relatives of his parent.
alac.application: Here, Ely is the illegitimate child of Dante, and Celia is Dante's legitimate mother, a legitimate relative of Ely's father. The barrier in Article 992 therefore prevents Ely from inheriting from Celia ab intestato, including by representation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Ely cannot inherit from Celia's estate by intestate succession.

keyPoints: Iron curtain rule (Art. 992)
Applies even to representation (Diaz v. IAC)
Illegitimate child of a legitimate son cannot inherit ab intestato from the grandparent
cite: Civil Code, Arts. 970 and 992; Diaz v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. L-66574, June 17, 1987

q: Under Article 985 of the Civil Code, in default of legitimate children and descendants, the parents and ascendants of the deceased inherit:
choices: To the exclusion of collateral relatives
Only if there is a will
hints: The descending line comes first, then the ascending line.
Collaterals come later.
why: Art. 985: in default of legitimate children and descendants, the parents and ascendants inherit to the exclusion of collateral relatives.
